findings.headline: Adult Social Care debt grown £2.350m to £20.823m and now represents 87% of all council sundry debt
findings.detail: Adult Social Care debt has increased from £18.473m at outturn to £20.823m at Q1, a 12.7% increase. The over-6-month portion rose from £12.821m to £13.666m. While the council notes that around £3.1m is secured on property (deferred arrangements) and £5.6m is linked to probate/property/deputyship (lower-risk), the trend of growth in difficult-to-collect debt and concentration in one service area signals underlying collection challenges.
findings.matters: Growing ASC debt and particularly the over-6-month segment suggests service users are unable to pay charges or the council is experiencing collection difficulties, indicating financial pressure in adult social care.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care debt £20.823m (up £2.350m from outturn); over-6-months debt £13.666m (up £0.845m); ASC represents 87% of total sundry debt
findings.quote: The total amount of service debt over six months old is £15.517m, this has risen by £1.083m since Outturn, largely within Adult's Social Care

findings.headline: Non-Domestic Rates collection down 2.36 percentage points; Collection Fund in £1.157m deficit
findings.detail: NDR collection rates to 30 June are 27.2%, a significant decline from 29.56% at the same stage in 2025/26. The Non-Domestic Rates Collection Fund is forecasting a £1.157m deficit, of which £0.567m is attributable to Cheshire East. The deficit will be funded from the Collection Fund Earmarked Reserve in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates could indicate weakness in the local business base or economic stress; the deficit requires use of reserves and reduces future liquidity.
findings.figures: Collection rates 27.2% (down 2.36 percentage points from 29.56% prior year); Collection Fund deficit £1.157m (£0.567m to council)
findings.quote: Collection rates for the current year, up to 30 June 2026, are 27.2%. This is a decrease of 2.36% points compared to the same stage in 2025/26

findings.headline: Net financing costs forecast £2.897m above budget for the full year
findings.detail: Borrowing costs to 30 June were £4.677m against a budget of £3.664m, and the full-year forecast is £2.897m in the red on net financing costs. The overrun is driven by higher borrowing requirement, interest rates, and S106 contributions. This is material budget pressure that erodes resources available for services.
findings.matters: A persistent cost overrun signals that the council's budget assumptions are not holding; a lender would view this as evidence of financial pressure and reduced budget resilience.
findings.figures: £2.897m adverse full-year variance; borrowing costs £4.677m actual vs £3.664m budget to Q1
findings.quote: The latest full year forecast is for net financing costs to be £2.897m above budget

findings.headline: LOBO loans resetting to 6.75% and 73% of borrowing matures within 12 months — refinancing risk explicitly flagged as HIGH
findings.detail: The council's £12m LOBO loans are being repaid in August 2026 following a lender rate reset to 6.75%, up sharply from the current portfolio average of 4.54%. Additionally, 73% of all borrowing matures within 12 months, and the council relies on short-term borrowing from other local authorities as its principal liquidity source. The treasury management section explicitly identifies liquidity and refinancing risk as HIGH, with daily cash-flow monitoring and consideration of longer-term PWLB borrowing noted as management actions.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about the council's ability to refinance at acceptable rates in a rising-rate environment and the immediate cost impact of the LOBO reset, which materially increases interest expenses.
findings.figures: £12m at 6.75% reset; 73% of borrowing matures under 12 months; £353m new short-term borrowing April–July 2026 at 4.20%
findings.quote: The Council's remaining £12m of LOBO loans are expected to be repaid in August 2026 following lender rate-reset notices

findings.headline: Care Act Phase 2 ICT scheme exceeded approved budget by £0.363m.
findings.detail: The scheme was approved for £6.314m but prior-year spending reached £6.677m, creating a £0.363m overspend recorded as a negative forecast adjustment. This suggests cost escalation or scope creep on a completed or nearly-complete ICT project.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on capital schemes indicate estimation or cost-control weaknesses; if prior estimates were off, forecast figures for other major ICT programmes may also be understated.
findings.figures: Approved £6.314m; Prior Years £6.677m; Adjustment -£0.363m

findings.headline: Carbon Neutral 2030 Investments scheme shows no forecast spending despite £13.98m approval.
findings.detail: The scheme, originally approved for £13.98m, spent only £0.094m in prior years and forecasts zero expenditure for all of 2026–2030. The scheme was previously titled 'Solar Energy Generation', suggesting it has been reformulated. With 99.3% of the approved budget unspent and no forward plan, this represents a major capital programme delay or de-prioritisation.
findings.matters: A large capital scheme showing no progress for four years signals either delivery risk, changed priorities affecting the council's sustainability commitments, or constrained capital capacity—all material to financial health.
findings.figures: Total Approved Budget £13.980m; Prior Years £0.094m; Forecast 2026–30 £0m
findings.quote: Carbon Neutral 2030 Investments - (previously Solar Energy Generation) 13.980           0.094         -

findings.headline: Multiple Red-rated savings programmes failing to deliver; Council needs to transform capital to reduce borrowing
findings.detail: The review highlights several savings initiatives rated RED: adult social care demand growth £5.497m adverse (budgeted £5.958m growth, now forecasts £11.455m); Children's 16-25 accommodation £1.100m shortfall; Positive Parenting pathway £0.512m shortfall; Environmental Services growth for vehicle replacement £0.464m cost overrun; and multiple income targets (BNG, advertising, commercialisation) coming in at zero to 9% of target. The capital section explicitly notes: 'The Council will need to continue to transform the capital programme to reduce the number of schemes requiring Cheshire East Resources and the need to borrow.'
findings.matters: A lender reads multiple RED ratings and underachieving transformation as evidence that the council's financial strategy is not delivering as assumed. The council is frank about needing to cut the capital programme to reduce borrowing, which means the current plan already assumes cuts to services or assets.
findings.figures: Adult care demand growth variance £5.497m; Children's S8 saving shortfall £1.100m; S11 shortfall £0.512m; G29 overspend £0.464m; total capital programme 2026-30 £576.360m with prudential borrowing of £87.583m
findings.quote: The Council will need to continue to transform the capital programme to reduce the number of schemes requiring Cheshire East Resources and the need to borrow.

findings.headline: General reserves rising to £11.328m but council acknowledges this remains insufficient
findings.detail: The Q1 review shows general reserves forecast to rise from £7.789m opening to £11.328m closing. However, the commentary explicitly states: 'The current balance on reserves is insufficient to provide adequate protection against established and newly emerging risks.' The council is drawing down earmarked reserves (£4.871m net reduction) and repurposing transformation reserves to the general fund to build up the balance, but even with this, the council considers reserves inadequate.
findings.matters: A council that acknowledges its reserves are inadequate, even after topping them up with one-off transformation reserve transfers, signals ongoing structural financial pressure. This is not a position of strength for a borrower.
findings.figures: Opening general reserve £7.789m; closing forecast £11.328m; opening earmarked reserves £20.731m; closing forecast £15.860m; net fall in total reserves £1.332m
findings.quote: The current balance on reserves is insufficient to provide adequate protection against established and newly emerging risks, however, there are proposals to contribute to the reserve in future years.

findings.headline: Insurance reserve depleted and insufficient to cover current overspend
findings.detail: Insurance costs are forecast to overspend by £0.840m, driven by increased premiums. The Insurance Reserve shows a balance of £0 at 1 April 2026 — the reserve has been emptied. During 2026/27, £1.183m is forecast to be drawn from insurance claim settlements and added back to the reserve, but this is intended to manage future excess costs, not to cover the current £0.840m overspend. The council does not have a funded reserve to absorb this pressure without using contingency.
findings.matters: Insurance reserves exist to absorb unplanned risk events. A zero opening balance means the council enters the year with no protection for claims inflation or unexpected exposures. A £0.840m overspend means the council is reliant on contingency to cover a cost it knew it would face.
findings.figures: Insurance Reserve opening balance £0.000m; Insurance overspend £0.840m; forecast drawdown for claims £1.183m; contingency used £0.797m (Finance, Legal and Enforcement)
findings.quote: Insurance is forecast to overspend by £0.840m mainly due to increased premiums cost, and insufficient funds available in the Insurance Reserve to offset the pressure

findings.headline: NHS partner in financial turnaround: Cheshire and Merseyside ICB required to cut £170m with unknown impact on council
findings.detail: The Adult Social Care commentary flags that Cheshire and Merseyside ICB is undergoing significant restructuring with a 50% cut to administrative costs. The ICB is formally in financial turnaround and required to make cashable savings of approximately £170m. The commentary notes this 'has the potential to drive costs to local authorities through areas such as Continuing Health Care, S117 Mental Health aftercare, changes to Service Level Agreements, as well as through the Better Care Fund.' The council notes some funding has been included in the MTFS for this risk, but the full implications remain unquantified and under review.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know about external financial shocks to the council's partner bodies that could push costs back onto the council. The ICB is described as 'one of the most financially challenged ICBs in the country' — a material risk to health and social care funding flows.
findings.figures: Cheshire and Merseyside ICB required to make £170m of cashable savings; 50% reduction in ICB administrative costs mandated; ICB formally in financial turnaround
findings.quote: Cheshire and Merseyside ICB is one of the most financially challenged ICBs in the country and is formally in financial turnaround and required to make cashable savings of approximately £170 million. This has the potential to drive costs to local authorities through areas such as Continuing Health Care, S117 Mental Health aftercare, changes to Service Level Agreements, as well as through the Better Care Fund.

findings.headline: Capital receipts shortfall of £3.719m: council budgeted £14.0m, now forecasts only £10.281m
findings.detail: The council's financial plan depends on capital receipts (asset sales) to reduce borrowing need. It budgeted £14.0m for 2026/27 but now forecasts only £10.281m, a £3.719m shortfall. This shortfall is being absorbed by using the general contingency budget (£5.022m contingency spend across central budgets). The reduction in receipts directly increases the council's need to borrow, raising future MRP (debt repayment) charges.
findings.matters: A lender cares about a council's capacity to fund capital without growing debt. A £3.7m shortfall in one year signals either that asset sales are slower than planned or that the council has over-optimistic assumptions about its property disposals pipeline.
findings.figures: Budgeted capital receipts £14.000m; forecast capital receipts £10.281m; shortfall £3.719m; MRP 2026/27 £20.185m; external loan interest £19.705m
findings.quote: S41 Using Capital Receipts to Support Service Improvements (14.000) (10.281) 3.719 Red - reduced forecast of capital receipts

findings.headline: Biodiversity Net Gain income target 96.7% short: £0.033m received of £1.000m budgeted
findings.detail: The council budgeted £1.0m of new income from piloting the sale of Biodiversity Net Gain credits from 180 hectares of council-owned land (woodland and former landfills). As of Q1, only £0.033m has been realised. The commentary simply notes the challenge of delivering the MTFS item, with no recovery plan detailed. This is rated RED — not achieved, no clear fix.
findings.matters: A lender sees a council that identified new revenue income, built it into budget, and has received 3% of the target with no explanation of why the market for these credits has not materialised. If the full £1.0m does not arrive, it falls back to service budgets or contingency drawdown.
findings.figures: £1.000m budgeted, £0.033m forecast realised; variance (0.967m) shortfall; 180 hectares of land identified, up to 450 BNG units potentially available
findings.quote: We are exploring a new way to generate income by piloting the selling of Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) credits... We have around 180 hectares of land that could be used, which might create up to 450 BNG units. [Forecast outturn £0.033m vs £1.000m budgeted]

findings.headline: Schools budget deficit ballooning: £155.943m brought forward, £46.995m further deficit budgeted for 2026/27
findings.detail: The DSG position shows a cumulative deficit of £155.943m carried forward from prior years, with an in-year budgeted deficit of £46.995m. The council notes they are awaiting formal DfE feedback on their SEND reform recovery plan. This is not a year-to-date position — this is the accumulated shortfall over multiple years. The in-year position alone is close to twice the council's general fund reserve.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are statutory liabilities that must eventually be recovered from the council's own revenue. A cumulative deficit of £155.9m hanging over a council with total general reserves of £11.3m represents systematic over-commitment to special education. The DfE feedback mentioned has not yet arrived.
findings.figures: Cumulative DSG deficit £155.943m; in-year budgeted deficit £46.995m; no Q1 forecast provided; total council general reserves £11.328m
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) position has a cumulative deficit brought forward of £155.943m with an in-year budgeted deficit of £46.995m, there is no Q1 forecast for the DSG deficit. An update on the SEND Reform plan and the DSG recovery position will be provided when DfE have provided formal feedback on the Council's recent submission.

findings.headline: Children's placements driven £3.885m overspend with 617 children in care, up 83 in six months
findings.detail: Placements forecast to spend £52.469m against a revised budget of £50.189m. The number of children in care rose sharply from 534 at end 2025/26 to 617 by 27 June 2026. Two major transformation savings programmes have failed to deliver: the 16-25 supported accommodation project lacks tenders for Lot 3, and the Edge of Care 0-10 scheme was delayed until October 2026. Both drive a £1.612m cost pressure. Agency staffing costs are £3.660m, showing the service continues to rely on temporary workers to manage caseload.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if a council's biggest cost pressures are structural or temporary. A surge of 83 children in one quarter, combined with failed savings programmes that assumed fewer admissions, signals demand-side risk the council cannot currently control.
findings.figures: 617 children in care vs 534 end 2025/26; placements budget £50.189m, forecast spend £52.469m; agency staffing £3.660m; placement cost pressure £1.612m from delayed schemes; Special Guardianship Orders additional cost £1.244m
findings.quote: the number of children in care remains significantly higher at 27th June 617 children, compared to 534 at the end of 2025/26. Continued demand for placements remains a significant cost pressure for the service.

findings.headline: Total usable reserves are forecast to decline from £28.520m to £27.188m, but the S151 officer warns the increase in General Fund Reserve (from £7.789m to £11.328m) 'largely represents a transfer from earmarked reserves rather than growth in the Council's overall resources.'
findings.detail: The council's earmarked reserves are forecast to fall from £20.731m to £15.860m (net drawdown of £4.871m for service expenditure and contributions). The General Fund Reserve rises to £11.328m, but only because earmarked funds are being moved across. The S151 officer explicitly flags this as not real growth: 'Total usable reserves are forecast to reduce from £28.520m to £27.188m and remain insufficient when assessed against the scale of the Council's financial risks.'
findings.matters: If the General Fund Reserve is growing only via reallocation from earmarked reserves, the council has no genuine reserve cushion. This is a sustainability warning. Reserves that are 'insufficient' per the S151 officer mean the council has limited headroom to absorb a shock (a recession, a demand spike, a grant cut).
findings.figures: Total usable reserves forecast: £27.188m (down from £28.520m). General Fund Reserve: £11.328m (up from £7.789m, but largely transfer). Earmarked Reserves: £15.860m (down from £20.731m). Ringfenced reserves: £3.854m.
findings.quote: This increase largely represents a transfer from earmarked reserves rather than growth in the Council's overall resources. Total usable reserves are forecast to reduce from £28.520m to £27.188m and remain insufficient when assessed against the scale of the Council's financial risks.

findings.headline: Adult social care placements are driving £0.352m adverse variance, with 'externally commissioned care costs, demographic and complexity growth' continuing to outpace budget.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is the second-largest portfolio and is forecasting £177.759m gross spend against a £169.492m budget. The council notes the pressure is driven by 'externally commissioned care costs, demographic and complexity growth,' and that delivering transformation savings and increasing client income are both required but uncertain. This is a structural, demand-led pressure rather than a one-off.
findings.matters: Demographic growth in adult social care placements is predictable and ongoing. It signals that the council's base budget for adult social care is structurally underfunded relative to actual demand. This is a lender red flag because it will recur every year unless statutory demand changes or the council restricts eligibility.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care budget: £169.492m. Forecast outturn: £177.759m. Variance: £0.352m (after contingency draw of £6.564m).
findings.quote: For Adult Social Care, the pressure is driven by externally commissioned care costs, demographic and complexity growth. The need to sustain delivery of transformation savings and increased client income remains.

findings.headline: Financing costs are £2.897m higher than budget for the full year, because interest rates rose after budget-setting and base rate reductions did not occur as expected.
findings.detail: The council budgeted borrowing costs at £3.664m but is forecasting £4.677m to end-June (and £2.897m additional pressure for the full year). The council expected base rates to decline during 2026/27 but 'due to macro-economic conditions the prospect of rate increases is a reality.' Short-term borrowing from other local authorities is running at 4.50% average, similar to 2025/26's 4.46%, but the volume of borrowing has increased. The council is using short-term borrowing to manage cash shortfalls because it remains 'considerably cheaper than other sources.'
findings.matters: Financing cost overruns reduce the council's flexibility and compress future budgets. A £2.897m in-year pressure on a £467m funding base is material. If base rates rise further, or if short-term borrowing rates shift, the council may face additional pressure. The council's reliance on short-term inter-authority loans creates roll-over risk.
findings.figures: Budget borrowing cost: £3.664m. YTD actual to 30 June: £4.677m. Full-year forecast additional pressure: £2.897m. Average short-term borrowing rate: 4.50%.
findings.quote: borrowing costs are also higher than budgeted at £4.677m compared to the budget of £3.664m. The projected cash flows for the remainder of 2026/27 being the net difference in financing costs (borrowing less investment interest) is expected to be £2.897m higher than that budgeted.

findings.headline: Capital spending is forecast to overrun by £25.837m (13.4% above the revised budget), driven by £17.340m of new supplementary capital estimates approved since February.
findings.detail: The February 2026 capital budget was £166.683m, revised to £192.842m after outturn, and is now forecast at £218.679m. The Q1 forecast includes £17.340m of new Supplementary Capital Estimates (SCEs) plus further project reprofiling. The council notes that 'as at Q1 reporting capital budgets associated with Growth and Regeneration are all located in the portfolio for Planning, Housing and Regeneration' and may be transferred presentationally in Q2.
findings.matters: A capital programme that grows 13% in a single quarter suggests planning uncertainty. Growing the capital programme increases borrowing and future financing costs (MRP and interest), which compress the revenue budget in future years. The council is already forecasting £2.897m additional interest pressure above budget.
findings.figures: Q1 capital forecast: £218.679m. Revised 2026/27 budget: £192.842m. Increase: £25.837m. SCEs since outturn: £17.340m.
findings.quote: The Q1 forecast is reporting an increase of £25.837m against the Revised Outturn Budget due to increases for Supplementary Capital Estimates (SCEs) from Outturn and Q1, of £17.340m

findings.headline: The S151 officer's assurance is explicitly qualified, stating the balanced forecast 'does not demonstrate that the Council's underlying financial position is yet sustainable' and flagging that 'targeted intervention is required now to prevent deterioration.'
findings.detail: The S151 officer states the Q1 forecast is balanced only after 'significant use of Transformation and General Contingency budgets,' notes that 'forecast use of contingency also reduces the capacity to absorb any further pressures later in the year,' and concludes: 'wider financial resilience remains fragile.' The officer requires 'active intervention now' in areas including expenditure controls, delivery of transformation savings, management of placement and agency costs, and maximisation of income.
findings.matters: A qualified S151 assurance is a formal statement that the council is not yet financially sustainable. It means the chief finance officer has concerns about whether current measures will hold and whether reserves are adequate. This directly informs a lender's risk assessment of whether the council will need to call on external support.
findings.figures: £24.995m exceptional financial support (EFS) drawn. Contingency use: £5.799m Transformation Contingency + £10.336m General Contingency = £16.135m. Total contingency deployed: £15.358m of forecast.
findings.quote: The balanced forecast depends on the delivery of savings and mitigations, containment of social care demand, achievement of capital receipts and management of higher financing costs. My assurance is qualified.

findings.headline: Transformation savings are missing by £1.612m (13% of planned £12.347m), concentrated in Children's Services where a tender for 16–25 supported accommodation received no bids.
findings.detail: The 16–25 Supported Accommodation project is forecasting £1.000m saving against £2.100m budgeted (£1.100m shortfall) because the council received no bids for its Lot 3 tender. The Edge of Care project is also delayed, starting in October instead of on-budget, creating a £0.512m shortfall. A third shortfall of £0.404m is in Resources, where the transformation project started two months late.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors track whether savings plans actually land or slip into permanent unfunded gaps. A 13% miss on transformation savings in year one signals difficulty in execution, and a tender with no bidders means the council has identified a problem it may not be able to solve in-year.
findings.figures: £1.612m total shortfall out of £12.347m budgeted. Supported Accommodation: £1.000m vs £2.100m budgeted. Edge of Care: £0.257m vs £0.769m budgeted.
findings.quote: the 16 to 25 Supported Accommodation project is not currently expected to deliver the full planned saving as there were no responses to the tender for the Lot 3 Procurement exercise

findings.paper_title: Cheshire East Growth, Investment and Regeneration Programme - Procurement of intelligent client and technical support and a strategic approach for Crewe.Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Council operating under Non-Statutory Best Value Notice with need to improve financial sustainability
findings.detail: The report explicitly references a revised Non-Statutory Best Value Notice issued 15 July 2026 and emphasises the Council's continuing need to improve financial sustainability, indicating regulatory scrutiny over financial management.
findings.matters: A council under regulatory financial scrutiny is viewed as higher risk by lenders and demonstrates existing financial management concerns.
findings.figures: Best Value Notice issued 15 July 2026
findings.quote: given the revised Non-Statutory Best Value Notice issued on 15 July 2026 and the continuing need to improve financial sustainability

findings.paper_title: Cheshire East Growth, Investment and Regeneration Programme - Procurement of intelligent client and technical support and a strategic approach for Crewe.Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Programme assumes external funding from Combined Authority and Government that have not been confirmed
findings.detail: The programme depends on external contributions from the Cheshire and Warrington Combined Authority and Government departments, but these have not been secured. The Section 151 Officer explicitly lists this as a principal financial risk.
findings.matters: Councils committing to spending based on anticipated external funding creates financial risk if those contributions are lower, arrive later, or do not materialise.
findings.figures: Programme relies on unconfirmed external contributions
findings.quote: The principal financial risks are that external contributions are lower or later than assumed

findings.paper_title: Cheshire East Growth, Investment and Regeneration Programme - Procurement of intelligent client and technical support and a strategic approach for Crewe.Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Year 1 funding includes one-off drawdown from earmarked reserve
findings.detail: The 2026/27 activity is to be funded partly through a drawdown from an existing earmarked reserve. The Section 151 Officer approves this 'in principle' and notes the reserve use is 'one-off and non-recurrent', yet the underlying programme is multi-year.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund current-year activity rather than from operations or external sources suggests cash-flow pressure and is not sustainable for ongoing programmes.
findings.figures: 2026/27 funding includes proposed reserve drawdown
findings.quote: This includes a proposed drawdown from an existing earmarked reserve. The use of the earmarked reserve is one-off and non-recurrent.

findings.paper_title: Cheshire East Growth, Investment and Regeneration Programme - Procurement of intelligent client and technical support and a strategic approach for Crewe.Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Council approving a three-year Growth programme with funding secured only for year 1
findings.detail: Cabinet is approving a three-year Cheshire East Growth, Investment and Delivery Programme, but the Council explicitly acknowledges that funding for years 2-3 has not been secured. The Section 151 Officer warns this must not be interpreted as approval to create unfunded commitments.
findings.matters: Multi-year programme commitments without secured funding create contingent liabilities and future budget pressures that present financial risk.
findings.figures: Three-year programme; funding identified for 2026/27; years 2-3 unfunded
findings.quote: Funding for later years has not yet been fully secured. The recommendations must therefore not be interpreted as approval to create an unfunded commitment across the full programme or contract term.

findings.paper_title: Adults Commissioning and Procurement forward plan 2026/27Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Market sustainability and provider capacity identified as key risks to adult care service delivery
findings.detail: Risk section identifies market sustainability and provider capacity challenges as key risks. These will be managed through established governance and market engagement, but no detail is provided on current provider capacity position or whether the market is under strain.
findings.matters: If providers cannot sustain services at current contract values, the council may face service disruption or be forced into emergency procurement at unfavourable rates, creating cost volatility.
findings.figures: Risk applies across all five major procurements: Supported Living (£53m/year), NHS Health Checks (£394k/year), 0–19 Service (£6.2–6.8m/year), Extra Care Housing (£1.4–1.5m/year), Carers Support Service (£600k–£700k/year)
findings.quote: Market sustainability and provider capacity challenges

findings.paper_title: Adults Commissioning and Procurement forward plan 2026/27Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Council identifies inflation and increasing demand as affordability pressures in £53 million annual adult social care spending
findings.detail: Risk Management section explicitly flags affordability pressures arising from inflation and increasing demand as key risks to the commissioning programme. Supported Living, Outreach and Day Opportunities Framework alone represents approximately £53 million per annum. Council states these will be managed through market engagement and contract management, but the paper does not confirm whether budget provision has been made for the inflationary impact or demand growth.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a major, demand-driven council budget area. Unbudgeted inflation or demand growth could force either service reductions or unbudgeted spending increases.
findings.figures: Supported Living, Outreach and Day Opportunities Framework approximately £53 million per annum (estimated total value approximately £371 million over maximum seven-year term)
findings.quote: Affordability pressures arising from inflation and increasing demand

findings.paper_title: Capital Disposal Programme 2026-2029 - Revised Approach
findings.headline: Council explicitly identifies market volatility as key risk affecting asset disposal values and timing.
findings.detail: Risk management section identifies market volatility as primary risk impacting asset values and disposal timing. Council proposes to manage through phased delivery aligned to market conditions and physical implementation of service change projects to achieve vacant possession.
findings.matters: Real estate market exposure creates material volatility in financial forecast; Council cannot control realization of projected receipt values or timing.
findings.figures: Phased delivery approach; market timing identified as key risk variable
findings.quote: Key risks associated with the programme include: (a) Market volatility impacting values and timing of disposals

findings.paper_title: Capital Disposal Programme 2026-2029 - Revised Approach
findings.headline: Disposal programme procurement costs expected to be funded from transformation contingency subject to demonstrating return on investment.
findings.detail: S151 Officer indicates costs may access transformation funding if business case demonstrates ROI. Requires 'known and affordable maximum value' at contract award and clear return on investment. No double-funding permitted between transformation contingency, capital receipts offset, and service budgets. Financial risks include receipts lower/later than forecast and costs exceeding offsettable amounts.
findings.matters: Indicates council drawing on contingency reserves to fund transformation; limits available contingency for other purposes; success depends on achieving forecast ROI.
findings.figures: Costs subject to maximum contract value; limited offsettable amount (4% of receipts); access to transformation funding contingent on ROI business case
findings.quote: As the commission forms part of the Council's transformation and improvement plan, the Section 151 Officer considers that it is likely to meet the criteria for access to transformation funding, subject to the contract award establishing a known and affordable maximum value and the business case demonstrating a return on investment consistent with the Council's transformation principles.

findings.paper_title: Capital Disposal Programme 2026-2029 - Revised Approach
findings.headline: S151 Officer warns capital receipt forecasts must not be committed in advance and are subject to material realization risks.
findings.detail: Officer emphasizes receipts must only be recognized when realized and cautions against advance commitment of unconfirmed proceeds. Identifies key risks: market volatility, legal and planning constraints, timing of completion, and requirement to obtain best consideration. Risks include receipts lower or later than forecast, and eligible costs exceeding offsettable amounts.
findings.matters: Signals material financial risk to recovery plan if receipts do not materialize; limits forward financial certainty; constrains ability to commit forecast receipts.
findings.figures: Receipts must be realized to be recognized; market conditions, title, planning and due diligence requirements apply
findings.quote: Capital receipt forecasts remain subject to market conditions, purchaser demand, title, planning and other due diligence, timing of completion and the requirement to obtain best consideration. Receipts must therefore be recognised only when realised and should not be committed in advance on the basis of unconfirmed disposal proceeds.

findings.paper_title: Capital Disposal Programme 2026-2029 - Revised Approach
findings.headline: Council lacks internal capacity for disposal programme and is procuring external legal and property professionals at material cost.
findings.detail: Despite existing mixed internal/external expertise, Council has identified that internal capacity is a major constraint. Council is procuring integrated legal and property services via Bloom Framework for initial three-year period with potential 12-18 month extension. External provider will control asset assessment, pipeline development, and disposal advancement.
findings.matters: Indicates complexity and scale of disposal programme; highlights dependency on external advisors; signals material procurement costs to deliver recovery plan.
findings.figures: Three-year term with 12-18 month extension potential; costs to be offset against receipts or funded from transformation contingency
findings.quote: This is capacity is a major constraint and this will continue to lead to delays in legal completions

findings.paper_title: Capital Disposal Programme 2026-2029 - Revised Approach
findings.headline: Council is implementing a three-year accelerated disposal programme to generate capital receipts for financial recovery.
findings.detail: Cabinet seeks approval for a revised approach to dispose of surplus assets over three years via an externalised delivery model. The programme is described as integral to financial strategy and transformation plan, intended to accelerate pace and deliver capital receipts supporting the MTFS and improvement objectives.
findings.matters: Direct evidence of council financial dependency on asset sales; material for creditworthiness assessment and understanding sustainability of financial recovery plan.
findings.figures: Three-year programme; up to 4% of capital receipts can be offset against disposal costs
findings.quote: The release of surplus assets and timely disposal will provide income to the Council, via capital receipts, to support the Council's Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX1_ProgressTrackerImprovementandTransformationDeliveryPlanendJuneFINA
findings.headline: Tatton Park initiative aims to reduce the council's ongoing financial subsidy through a revised operating model.
findings.detail: The Tatton Park transformation programme is marked Amber at Risk with no change in direction. Following a meeting with Lead Members, the project has been sent for scope review to 'determine the vision and workstreams required', specifically to 'drive a reduction in the council's financial subsidy through a revised operating model'. This indicates Tatton Park is currently a material ongoing cost that the council is actively trying to eliminate.
findings.matters: An ongoing subsidy to a leisure facility that the council is now actively trying to exit suggests discretionary spending that strains finances and/or assets that are not self-sustaining.
findings.figures: No specific subsidy figure provided. Status: Amber at Risk, under review for scope redefinition.
findings.quote: the Tatton Park project will be subject to a review of the current scope to determine the vision and workstreams required to deliver the council's ambition for Tatton Park including driving a reduction in the council's financial subsidy through a revised operating model, and lease in collaboration with the National Trust.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX1_ProgressTrackerImprovementandTransformationDeliveryPlanendJuneFINA
findings.headline: Mandatory finance training for elected members is delayed with no scheduled dates through June.
findings.detail: Finance training for all elected members on the council's financial challenges and members' roles in financial distress was originally due by July 2026. The initiative is marked Amber at Risk with 'Deteriorated' status. As of end June, Member Services is reviewing appropriate dates as there were no dates supplied for July, with availability only being sought for August and September.
findings.matters: Members are responsible for approving budgets and major financial decisions. Delayed training for a council in financial distress is a governance weakness that affects the quality of financial oversight and decision-making.
findings.figures: Original deadline: July 2026 for all members; follow-on training for Cabinet members also due July 2026. Current position: dates being awaited for August/September.
findings.quote: Member services team is reviewing appropriate dates. There were no dates supplied for July, awaiting availability for August and September.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX1_ProgressTrackerImprovementandTransformationDeliveryPlanendJuneFINA
findings.headline: Budget governance control is slipping: budget statements from February 2026 are still being collected in July through manual process.
findings.detail: Budget holders were required to sign budget statements in February 2026 confirming they understood their budgets and did not have authority to overspend. The initiative is now marked Amber at Risk with 'Deteriorated' status. Physical confirmation statements are being collected through July as part of Q1 closedown, five months after the deadline, suggesting budget holder compliance and control oversight is weak.
findings.matters: A council in Early Financial Support cannot afford delays in basic budget control. Inability to ensure budget holders are formally engaged with their budget accountability five months after budget setting indicates governance weakness at a critical control point.
findings.figures: Original deadline: February 2026. Actual collection: July 2026. Status: Amber - At Risk, Deteriorated.
findings.quote: Budget statements have been assigned through the Budget Manager System (BMS). Physical confirmation statements being collected through July in line with the Q1 reporting and closedown process.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX1_ProgressTrackerImprovementandTransformationDeliveryPlanendJuneFINA
findings.headline: Financial Leadership Improvement Plan has been extended to three years and reframed from stabilisation to resilience.
findings.detail: The original Financial Leadership Improvement Plan with a March 2027 deadline has been superseded by version 2.0, extending the timeframe to three years to align with longer-term financial sustainability objectives. This shift from 'stabilisation to resilience' suggests the council's financial position stabilisation was not achieved within the original timeline.
findings.matters: A three-year resilience program signals the council will remain in a vulnerable financial position longer than originally planned, affecting debt servicing capacity and confidence in turnaround timing.
findings.figures: Original deadline: March 2027. New deadline: three-year programme. Original plan framed as 'stabilisation'; revised plan framed as 'stabilisation to resilience'.
findings.quote: The Financial Leadership Improvement Plan has been superseded by the development of the Financial Leadership Improvement Plan v2.0. This new plan has longer term timeframes to align to the financial sustainability objectives, moving from stabilisation to resilience. The timeframe is a three year programme compared to the March 2027 completion timeframe within the original FLIP.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_006327_0013329_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateQ1202627AppendixACabinet03092026
findings.headline: Children's Services received £10m growth in 2026/27 and multi-year investment of £20m as part of improvement from inadequate Ofsted rating
findings.detail: Children's services received an Ofsted grading of inadequate in March 2024. The MTFS includes growth of up to £10m for 2026/27 plus a substantial multi-year investment of £20m held in Corporate Contingency to address placement and staffing pressures. Despite this investment, the service faces significant ongoing action to deliver savings and live within budget as demand, complexity and cost are expected to continue increasing.
findings.matters: A £20m multi-year commitment to a failing service signals prolonged financial pressure in children's placements and supported accommodation; continued service growth despite improvement activity suggests underlying demand pressures are not being controlled
findings.figures: £10m growth 2026/27; £20m multi-year investment in Corporate Contingency; Ofsted rating inadequate (March 2024)
findings.quote: Growth to address budget pressures within placement and staffing in MTFS – up to £10m 26/27. MTFS includes a substantial multi-year investment of £20m into Children's Services improvement. This will be held in Corporate Contingency.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_006327_0013329_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateQ1202627AppendixACabinet03092026
findings.headline: Best Value notice revised on 15 July 2026 citing leadership gaps and high turnover as barriers to substantial progress
findings.detail: MHCLG issued a revised non-statutory Best Value notice on 15 July 2026 after Q1 ended, recognizing early signs of improvement but remaining concerned about the scale of challenge facing the authority. Ministers specifically identified gaps in key leadership roles, high turnover, and reliance on interim staff as preventing the council from making and embedding substantial progress. Risk of Section 114 notice if transformation fails.
findings.matters: A revised Best Value notice signals continued government concern about management competence and indicates statutory intervention (commissioners) remains a live possibility if improvement does not accelerate, which would damage the council's credibility with lenders and markets
findings.figures: Best Value notice issued May 2025; revised 15 July 2026; risk of Section 114 notice creating cost liability (government commissioners' costs borne by council)
findings.quote: Whilst MHCLG recognised constructive engagement from the senior leadership team, and early signs of improvement, including the transition to the Leader and Cabinet model of governance, and an improved trajectory in Children's Services, and commitment to improving our medium term financial position, Ministers remain concerned about the scale of challenge still facing the authority, and identified gaps in key leadership roles, high turnover and reliance on interims in preventing the authority from making and embedding substantial progress.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_006327_0013329_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateQ1202627AppendixACabinet03092026
findings.headline: Middlewich Eastern Bypass project entered construction with risk allowance insufficient due to earlier delays and cost inflation
findings.detail: The MEB scheme, the council's largest strategic growth project, commenced construction in April 2026 under a standard NEC contract. Delays to the DfT decision and the council's Capital Programme Review significantly increased estimated outturn costs due to inflation, reducing the risk allowance below optimal levels. Client-side risks (weather, ground conditions) during delivery could force costs above budget, requiring additional funding from other capital budgets or increased borrowing. Combined Authority governance uncertainty adds theoretical risk that the CA may not support funding.
findings.matters: A major capital project running over budget would either force difficult reallocation within the capital programme or require additional borrowing, both of which impact the council's financial resilience and demonstrate governance/delivery capability concerns
findings.figures: Construction contract commenced April 2026; increased scheme estimate costs due to inflation; risk allowance clearly identified as insufficient; DfT funding provided as single lump sum in 26/27 with pressure emerging in 27/28
findings.quote: The scheme has commenced construction in April 2026... The construction contract is a standard NEC construction contract... The financial pressures caused by the delays outlined above have resulted in a less than optimal amount being included in the scheme estimate for risk. So, there is an increased risk that if client side risks occur during scheme delivery (e.g. weather related or unforeseen ground conditions) then the project costs could increase beyond the current scheme budget.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_006327_0013329_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateQ1202627AppendixACabinet03092026
findings.headline: Financial sustainability risk remains critical; 2027/28 budget must be balanced without Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: SR11 maintains a net score of 16 (target 8). The council continues to rely on Exceptional Financial Support from government but must deliver a balanced budget for 2027/28 without EFS as a critical element of achieving longer financial sustainability. A successful Section 25 statement demonstrates the financial sustainability challenges and the requirement to rebuild reserves over the MTFS period.
findings.matters: Dependency on Exceptional Financial Support signals government intervention and uncertainty about the council's ability to manage its finances independently; the 2027/28 deadline creates a hard constraint for service delivery and spending decisions
findings.figures: Net score 16; target score 8; general reserves target minimum £25m by 2030; budget 2027/28 must be balanced without EFS
findings.quote: The budget for 2027/28 must be balanced without the use of EFS. This is a critical element of achieving longer financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_006327_0013329_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateQ1202627AppendixACabinet03092026
findings.headline: DSG deficit stands at £155.943m with statutory override ending March 2028
findings.detail: The cumulative Dedicated Schools Grant deficit grew to £155.943m as at 31 March 2026, with an in-year deficit of £43.217m in Q4. The government has indicated a potential High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the eligible deficit, but this remains subject to confirmation and does not address ongoing in-year pressures. The statutory accounting override allowing the DSG to be held outside the General Fund is due to end in March 2028, creating significant medium-term financial risk.
findings.matters: A £155m+ unresolved education deficit will transfer to the general fund in 2028/29 unless the government provides a solution, creating a potentially catastrophic financial hole for the council and raising fundamental questions about long-term solvency
findings.figures: £155.943m cumulative deficit; £43.217m in-year deficit Q4 2025/26; potential High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of eligible deficit
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, the cumulative DSG deficit stands at £155.943m, including an in-year deficit of £43.217m. In Q4 2025/26 the Government indicated that a High Needs Stability Grant will be introduced, which could cover 90% of the eligible deficit at March 2026. While this offers a potential route to reducing the Council's risk, it remains subject to confirmation and does not address ongoing in-year pressures.

findings.paper_title: 20260825102353_006577_0013325_Annex4Quarter12627Section151AssuranceStatement
findings.headline: High proportion of gross debt of £456.159m is due within 12 months, creating material refinancing and liquidity exposure.
findings.detail: Gross external debt at 30 June 2026 was £456.159m. The maturity profile is explicitly described as 'a material risk, with a high proportion of borrowing due within 12 months'. While short-term local authority borrowing provides value, it 'creates refinancing and liquidity exposure' that requires active management.
findings.matters: Refinancing risk is acute: a large portion of £456m debt must be rolled over within 12 months at potentially higher rates; this creates cash-flow and cost volatility.
findings.figures: Gross external debt: £456.159m; Treasury investments: £62.424m; Net debt: £393.735m; Sundry debt: £23.970m (£15.517m more than 6 months old)
findings.quote: The maturity profile remains a material risk, with a high proportion of borrowing due within 12 months. Short-term local authority borrowing continues to provide value compared with longer-term alternatives, but creates refinancing and liquidity exposure. Daily cash-flow management and consideration of an appropriate balance between short-term and longer-term borrowing remain essential.

findings.paper_title: 20260825102353_006577_0013325_Annex4Quarter12627Section151AssuranceStatement
findings.headline: Capital receipts shortfall of £3.719m and borrowing requirement increase creating £2.897m adverse financing pressure.
findings.detail: Central budget pressures include a £3.719m shortfall in planned capital receipts and £2.897m of additional financing costs. The 2026/27 capital programme of £218.679m requires 'continued scrutiny of deliverability, affordability, funding certainty, whole-life revenue consequences and the need for prudential borrowing'.
findings.matters: Undelivered capital receipts and rising financing costs are consuming budget and creating pressure; capital affordability requires continued scrutiny during a period of refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £3.719m shortfall in planned capital receipts; £2.897m adverse net financing pressure; Capital expenditure forecast: £218.679m
findings.quote: Gross pressures include a £3.719m shortfall in planned capital receipts and £2.897m of additional financing costs... The 2026/27 capital programme is forecasting expenditure of £218.679m. The programme requires continued scrutiny of deliverability, affordability, funding certainty, whole-life revenue consequences and the need for prudential borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 20260825102353_006577_0013325_Annex4Quarter12627Section151AssuranceStatement
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £202.938m is a material balance-sheet and sustainability risk with no clear resolution path.
findings.detail: Opening DSG deficit is £155.943m and the 2026/27 budgeted in-year deficit is £46.995m, resulting in a mitigated cumulative deficit of £202.938m. The CFO notes the position is 'subject to national funding and accounting arrangements and formal feedback from the Department for Education' and requires 'continued separate and transparent monitoring'.
findings.matters: A £202.938m balance-sheet liability with contingency on Department for Education funding decisions represents a material financial risk that could threaten the council's financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Opening DSG deficit: £155.943m; 2026/27 budgeted in-year deficit: £46.995m; Cumulative mitigated deficit forecast: £202.938m
findings.quote: The opening deficit is £155.943m and the 2026/27 budgeted in-year deficit is £46.995m, giving a mitigated cumulative deficit forecast of £202.938m. The DSG position is a significant financial and balance-sheet risk.

findings.paper_title: 20260825102353_006577_0013325_Annex4Quarter12627Section151AssuranceStatement
findings.headline: Total usable reserves are forecast to reduce and remain insufficient for the council's size, complexity and risk exposure.
findings.detail: While the General Fund Reserve increases from £7.789m to £11.328m, total usable reserves reduce by £1.332m from £28.520m to £27.188m. Critically, the CFO states that the General Fund Reserve rebuild is 'principally achieved by repurposing existing earmarked reserves rather than by increasing the Council's total resources'. The CFO explicitly judges reserves insufficient for the authority's risk profile.
findings.matters: Rebuilding reserves by moving money between pots is not genuine financial improvement; reserves remain below the level needed to absorb shocks in a complex, volatile council.
findings.figures: Usable reserves: opening £28.520m, forecast closing £27.188m (reduction of £1.332m); General Fund Reserve: £7.789m to £11.328m; Earmarked Reserves: £15.860m; Public Health Reserve ring-fenced: £3.854m
findings.quote: The forecast increase in the General Fund Reserve from £7.789m to £11.328m is a positive step and the reserve remains protected from unplanned drawdown. However, the increase is principally achieved by repurposing existing earmarked reserves rather than by increasing the Council's total resources. Total usable reserves continue to reduce and a significant proportion of earmarked reserves is held for specific purposes or identified risks. My judgement remains that the Council's reserves are insufficient for an authority of its size, responsibilities, financial volatility and risk exposure.

findings.paper_title: 20260825102353_006577_0013325_Annex4Quarter12627Section151AssuranceStatement
findings.headline: Eleven transformation projects delivering £12.347m of savings have identified shortfalls in two major areas, and savings delivery is conditional on successful implementation.
findings.detail: Most transformation projects are forecasting delivery, but shortfalls remain in Children's Services and Resources. The CFO explicitly warns that 'forecast savings must not be treated as delivered until the benefit is evidenced in the financial ledger and is sustainable', and notes that financial monitoring should operate as a controlled single process.
findings.matters: A significant portion of the budget balance rests on £12.347m of savings that are not yet proven to be deliverable or sustainable; delays in Children's transformation are already visible.
findings.figures: £12.347m of budgeted savings from eleven transformation projects; shortfalls identified in Children's Services and Resources
findings.quote: There are eleven transformation projects that contribute £12.347m of budgeted savings in 2026/27. At Quarter 1, most projects are forecasting delivery, but identified shortfalls remain in Children's Services and Resources. Forecast savings must not be treated as delivered until the benefit is evidenced in the financial ledger and is sustainable.

findings.paper_title: 20260825102353_006577_0013325_Annex4Quarter12627Section151AssuranceStatement
findings.headline: Adult Social Care and Children's Services remain in overspend even after contingency support is applied.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is forecast to overspend by £0.352m after contingency support. Children's Services is forecast to overspend by £1.978m after contingency support, with principal risks in placement demand and cost, agency staffing, and delays in transformation projects.
findings.matters: Services that overspend despite contingency buffers signal inability to manage within allocated resources; Children's overspend is material and driven by volatile demand.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care: £0.352m overspend after contingency; Children's Services: £1.978m overspend after contingency
findings.quote: Adult Social Care is forecast to overspend by £0.352m after contingency support. The forecast remains sensitive to commissioned care demand, complexity, client income, transformation delivery and potential cost transfer from NHS financial recovery actions. Children's Services is forecast to overspend by £1.978m after contingency support. The principal risks are placement demand and cost, agency staffing and delays in the supported accommodation and positive parenting transformation projects.

findings.paper_title: 20260825102353_006577_0013325_Annex4Quarter12627Section151AssuranceStatement
findings.headline: Budget balance depends entirely on £24.995m of conditional Exceptional Financial Support and contingency drawdowns.
findings.detail: The Q1 forecast reports a balanced position, but only after planned application of £24.995m of conditional Exceptional Financial Support. Before contingencies, service and central pressures remain significant. The CFO's overall assurance is explicitly qualified, not unqualified.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether budget balance reflects underlying financial health or external life-support. This council cannot balance without support.
findings.figures: £24.995m conditional Exceptional Financial Support; £5.799m Transformation Contingency applied; £15.358m General Contingency applied (including £10.336m for services and £5.022m for central pressures)
findings.quote: The reported balanced forecast is dependent on the planned application of £24.995m of conditional Exceptional Financial Support, substantial of General Contingency budgets, delivery of savings and mitigations, containment of demand-led expenditure, achievement of capital receipts and management of increased financing costs.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_005788_0013328_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateAppendixACabinet060826
findings.headline: Children's services received Ofsted 'inadequate' rating with £20m multi-year MTFS investment required
findings.detail: Children's services received an 'inadequate' Ofsted grading following March 2024 inspection. An improvement plan is in place but churn in leadership and workforce has hampered progress. Demand for children's services remains high, particularly in placements and supported accommodation, creating significant budget pressure. The MTFS includes growth up to £10m for 26/27 and a substantial £20m multi-year investment to be held in Corporate Contingency. Significant action is still required to deliver savings to live within budget as demand, complexity and cost are expected to continue increasing.
findings.matters: The inadequate rating creates reputational and operational risk. The council is betting on improvement delivery within a tight financial envelope. If the transformation fails, further government intervention and additional costs are likely.
findings.figures: £10m growth 26/27; £20m multi-year investment in Corporate Contingency; Ofsted monitoring visit April 2026
findings.quote: Cheshire East children's services received an Ofsted grading of 'inadequate' following an inspection in March 2024... The service received growth through the MTFS to help address the pressures but the challenge to deliver to budget and achieve the required savings remains present.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_005788_0013328_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateAppendixACabinet060826
findings.headline: Social care market fragility with care home embargoes, escalating waiting times, and provider instability
findings.detail: Q4 saw sustained fragility across adult social care with six care homes operating under full embargoes or placement restrictions. Brokerage waiting times for accommodation with care reached up to seven weeks. Complex care waiting times increased further, reaching 45 weeks maximum in March, driven by limited specialist provision and geographical constraints. Care concerns reached their highest recorded level in March. Provider exits and international recruitment challenges (sponsorship licence issues) continue to create market uncertainty.
findings.matters: Acute care market pressures force the council to pay more for the services it can access, constrain placement options, and create service delivery risk. This directly impacts both revenue budget pressure and the council's ability to meet its statutory duties.
findings.figures: 6 care homes under full embargoes; brokerage waiting times up to 7 weeks (AWC), 1 week (CAH); Complex Care waiting times 45 weeks maximum in March
findings.quote: Accommodation with Care (AWC), market pressure increased during the quarter, with six care homes operating under full embargoes or placement restrictions. This represented a deterioration from earlier in the year and further reduced placement flexibility within the borough... Complex Care continued to present the highest level of sustained risk. Waiting times increased further, reaching a maximum of 45 weeks in March.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_005788_0013328_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateAppendixACabinet060826
findings.headline: £11m in development costs for A500 Corridor project at risk of becoming abortive if scheme removed from government programme
findings.detail: The council has spent approximately £11m to date developing the A500 Corridor scheme through outline business case stage and a revised business case after the government cancelled HS2 north of Birmingham. A recent government announcement on the major scheme programme did not include the A500 project. If the scheme is removed from the national programme, all expenditure to date would become abortive costs charged to revenue accounts, severely impacting the council's financial sustainability.
findings.matters: This represents a significant unrecoverable loss of capital investment that would be charged to revenue, worsening the council's already tight financial position at a critical moment.
findings.figures: £11m spent to date on development; scheme absent from recent government major scheme programme announcement
findings.quote: If the scheme is removed from the Government's Major Scheme Programme then there is a risk that all expenditure the council has incurred to date will become abortive costs and will need to be charged to revenue accounts, which will severely impact on the Councils financial sustainability, given the other existing pressures on revenue budgets.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_005788_0013328_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateAppendixACabinet060826
findings.headline: Middlewich Eastern Bypass faces inflation-driven cost overruns with reduced contingency buffers
findings.detail: The MEB scheme, the council's largest capital project and strategic growth enabler, commences construction in April 2026. Delays to DfT approval and the capital programme review increased estimated outturn costs due to inflation, making the scheme less affordable. The increased costs have eroded risk allowances in the scheme budget. The contract is a Target Price Option C NEC contract where inflation above 2.5% base rate is a client risk. Recent Middle East tensions are likely to create further inflationary pressure.
findings.matters: The MEB is a strategic scheme needed to unlock economic growth. Cost overruns would require funding from other capital budgets or increased borrowing, impacting the council's financial flexibility during a period of tight financial control.
findings.figures: Construction starts April 2026; recent government announcement did not confirm A500 Corridor project (separate scheme, £11m already spent on development)
findings.quote: The increased costs made the scheme less affordable and this has impacted on the risk allowances that have been included in the current scheme estimate, which increases the risk of the budget being insufficient.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_005788_0013328_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateAppendixACabinet060826
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support requirement reduced to £22.315m but financial sustainability remains critical risk
findings.detail: The council's financial position improved at Financial Reporting 4 compared to FR3 by £2.946m, reducing the EFS requirement from £25.261m to £22.315m. The risk register identifies that delivery of the MTFS depends on organisational change and implementation of savings, with the S151 officer warning of possible Section 114 notice if these are not achieved. The financial sustainability risk carries the highest net score (16/16, target 8).
findings.matters: The council remains dependent on exceptional government support to balance its budget. A Section 114 notice would trigger external intervention, commissioners' costs borne by the council, and restrictions on spending.
findings.figures: EFS requirement £22.315m (down from £25.261m); Financial Sustainability risk net score 16/16
findings.quote: The financial position at Financial Reporting 4 (FR4) has shown an improvement when compared to FR3 and as such requires less Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) that was initially budgeted for. The position has improved since FR3 by £2.946m and hence the EFS requirement has reduced from £25.261m to £22.315m.

findings.paper_title: 20260825110212_005788_0013328_StrategicRiskRegisterUpdateAppendixACabinet060826
findings.headline: Dedicated School Grant deficit of £112.1m with contingent funding from DfE approval
findings.detail: The DSG deficit stood at £112.1m at 31 March 2025 (£113.7m high needs, offset by £1.6m early years underspend). Interest payments on borrowing to cover the deficit total £5.8m for 2025/26. The council is eligible for a DfE High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the DSG deficit accrued by end 2025/26, but only if the Local SEND Reform Plan is approved in the first round of assessment. The threshold for approval and the treatment of deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28 remain unknown.
findings.matters: This is the largest single financial liability on the council's books. It reduces the council's financial flexibility and creates dependency on government decision-making outside the council's control.
findings.figures: £112.1m deficit; £5.8m annual interest on borrowing; 90% of cumulative forecast deficit (approx. £139m) may be covered by DfE grant if reform plan approved
findings.quote: The overall DSG deficit figure reported within the accounts at 31 March 2025 is £112.1 million. This is made up of high needs deficit of £113.7 million plus an underspend of early years DSG of £1.6 million.

findings.headline: Council received a Best Value Notice requiring continued urgent progress on financial sustainability
findings.detail: The council received a revised Non-Statutory Best Value Notice in July 2026. It 'recognises early improvement but requires continued urgent progress on financial sustainability.' The document notes the register is 'an important component of the Council's evidence that risks are being identified, owned and managed' but emphasises 'the existence of controls is not sufficient on its own.'
findings.matters: A Best Value Notice signals regulatory concern and puts the council on notice. If progress is not demonstrated, the council risks escalation to statutory intervention or external management of finances.
findings.figures: Notice issued July 2026
findings.quote: The revised Non-Statutory Best Value Notice issued in July 2026 recognises early improvement but requires continued urgent progress on financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Safeguarding Children risk escalated to Critical in Q4 2025-26 due to scale of required improvements
findings.detail: SR05 – Safeguarding Children increased from Material (8) to Critical (12). The register states this escalation is 'due to the scale of required improvements now being fully understood', with current expectation the increase can be reversed by Q4 2026-27. This is a statutory service where failure triggers intervention.
findings.matters: Critical safeguarding risk indicates service improvement is now known to require substantial investment or restructuring. Failure to deliver improvements risks external inspection or DfE intervention.
findings.figures: Increased from Material (8) to Critical (12); expected reversal Q4 2026-27
findings.quote: SR05 – Safeguarding Children. It saw an increase from Material (8) to Critical (12) due to the scale of required improvements now being fully understood.

findings.headline: Operation Decker police investigation is creating unquantified pressures on senior officer capacity and financial sustainability
findings.detail: An ongoing police investigation following a raid on 29 April 2026 is impacting safeguarding children risk, financial sustainability risk, and stakeholder communication risk. The council notes 'heightened external scrutiny, additional resource demands associated with investigations and reviews, pressures on senior officer capacity, staff wellbeing concerns, and the need to implement improvement actions within challenging timescales.' These impacts are not yet separately quantified.
findings.matters: Unquantified demands on officer time divert capacity from financial recovery and capital delivery. Heightened scrutiny increases the risk that inspection or intervention could force accelerated spending or borrowing.
findings.figures: Investigation began 29 April 2026; impacts noted but not quantified
findings.quote: the impact upon the Council from Operation Decker, the ongoing police investigation following a raid on a religious organisation at Webb House in Crewe on 29 April 2026 is beginning to show an impact on some of the existing strategic risks, including SR05 Safeguarding Children, SR11 Financial Sustainability

findings.headline: Capital project delivery is Critical with slippage and cost escalation pressures
findings.detail: SR15 – Capital Projects Management and Delivery is rated Critical (16) with no improvement pathway. The register identifies 'capital programme slippage and cost escalation' as key financial exposures. The section 151 commentary warns of risks from 'under-delivery of capital receipts, capital programme slippage and cost escalation'.
findings.matters: Capital receipt shortfalls and project slippage reduce cash available for revenue needs and borrowing servicing. Cost escalation forces choices between completion and financial viability.
findings.figures: Critical (16); net score equals target score (no improvement indicated)
findings.quote: SR15 - Capital Projects Management and Delivery – Critical (16)... capital programme slippage and cost escalation

findings.headline: The council is relying on Exceptional Financial Support to meet its Medium-Term Financial Strategy
findings.detail: Financial Sustainability is a strategic risk with target resolution dated March 2030. The key financial exposures include 'continuing reliance on Exceptional Financial Support and other one-off resources' alongside demand pressures, DSG deficit, capital receipts under-delivery, and cost escalation. The S151 Officer warns that risk owners must prioritise mitigation within approved budgets and that the financial consequences may be significant.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support is emergency government funding, not sustainable revenue. A council depending on it has structural deficits it cannot resolve alone, making repayment of borrowing contingent on continued government help.
findings.figures: Target date March 2030 for risk resolution; no net score improvement indicated
findings.quote: continuing reliance on Exceptional Financial Support and other one-off resources, demand and price pressures in statutory services

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Inadequate reserve levels requiring future build-up to reach appropriate levels
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies reserves as currently low and requires a plan to increase them in later years to achieve 'more appropriate reserves levels'. Low reserves mean minimal buffer against revenue shortfalls or unexpected costs.
findings.matters: Reserve adequacy is a core indicator of financial resilience. Low reserves combined with recurring multi-year deficits leave the council with no financial cushion and vulnerable to any income volatility or cost shock.
findings.figures: Target reserve level not specified
findings.quote: The medium term forecast also includes the plan to increase reserves in later years to bring the Council up to more appropriate reserves levels to assist with future financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Historic borrowing that cannot be refinanced at rates lower than currently being paid
findings.detail: The council carries capital financing costs from historic borrowing that are 'sunk' costs and cannot be replaced more cheaply in the current environment. With interest rates having risen since the borrowing was taken, any refinancing would increase annual costs, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.matters: This represents a structural cost pressure the council cannot control or escape, reducing the flexibility to respond to other shocks. Higher debt service reduces resources available for service delivery and further strains an already tight budget.
findings.figures: Amounts not disclosed
findings.quote: capital financing costs that are a result of historic borrowing and are 'sunk' and will be very difficult to refinance in the current environment at a lower cost than they currently cost.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: 2027/28 funding shortfall of £15.271m requiring total savings of £28.573m (5.97% of expenditure budget)
findings.detail: After already-planned savings of £13.302m, the council faces a further £15.271m gap for 2027/28. Closing this gap requires total savings of £28.573m, equivalent to cutting 5.97% of the entire expenditure budget. The paper asserts this is 'achievable' but provides no implementation plan.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether a council can credibly deliver savings at this scale without service collapse. Savings of nearly 6% of budget are substantial and politically difficult. If not achieved, the 2027/28 position worsens, widening the rolling deficit.
findings.figures: £15.271m shortfall; £13.302m planned savings; £28.573m total savings required; 5.97% of expenditure budget
findings.quote: When taking into account the savings already included within the MTFS, closing the gap would require a total level of savings of £28.573m for 2027/28 that is equal to 5.97% of the expenditure budget.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Section 114 notice risk (insolvency declaration) if Exceptional Financial Support is unavailable in future years
findings.detail: The council has warned that without ongoing emergency support, it faces a Section 114 notice—the formal declaration that a council cannot meet its financial obligations. This risk is driven by low reserve levels, a DSG deficit, and historic borrowing costs that cannot be refinanced more cheaply as interest rates have risen.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals potential insolvency and triggers government intervention. For a lender, this is the most serious warning signal short of actual administration and indicates extreme financial distress.
findings.figures: Not quantified; triggered if ongoing EFS unavailable
findings.quote: Without Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), this will result in a Section 114 notice based on the Council's current low levels of available reserves and balances alongside the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit and capital financing costs that are a result of historic borrowing and are 'sunk' and will be very difficult to refinance in the current environment at a lower cost than they currently cost.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balanced only through £24.995m Exceptional Financial Support via capitalisation direction, acknowledged as unsustainable
findings.detail: The council cannot balance its current budget from normal revenue and required emergency government support. The paper explicitly states this is not sustainable and must be addressed to achieve financial sustainability. This form of support masks underlying budget imbalance and cannot be repeated.
findings.matters: A lender must establish whether a council can meet its obligations from normal income. Reliance on deficit financing via emergency government support indicates the council is operating outside sustainable parameters and is dependent on government rescue.
findings.figures: £24.995m Exceptional Financial Support, 2026/27
findings.quote: The budget for the financial year 2026/27 could only be balanced using Exceptional Financial Support (£24.995m) by way of an 'in-principle' capitalisation direction. This is not sustainable and needs to be addressed in this year for the Council to become financially sustainable.

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26Cabinet and Committee Report Template
findings.headline: Capital programme spent only £122.180m of £208.491m revised budget (41% underspend)
findings.detail: The council revised its capital budget upward to £208.491m in-year (from £173.077m original), then spent only £122.180m at outturn.
