findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 , item 7.
findings.headline: Council received a non-statutory Best Value Notice from government, signalling formal concern about performance
findings.detail: In May 2025, the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government issued a non-statutory Best Value Notice, indicating government concern about the council's governance and performance. The council is required to develop an improvement plan with regular quarterly monitoring and reporting to MHCLG.
findings.matters: A Best Value Notice is a formal government intervention signal. It indicates official concern about the council's ability to deliver statutory functions, and subjects the council to enhanced scrutiny and accountability.
findings.figures: Notice issued May 2025; MHCLG quarterly update process in place
findings.quote: In May 2025, the Council received a non-statutory Best Value Notice.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 , item 7.
findings.headline: Chief Executive resigned in June 2026 with no permanent successor appointed
findings.detail: The Chief Executive resigned at the beginning of June 2026. An Executive Director is serving as Acting Chief Executive whilst recruitment for an interim replacement proceeds. This creates leadership continuity risk during a critical period of transformation and government improvement monitoring.
findings.matters: Loss of the top executive during a period of major transformation, financial stress, and government oversight creates execution risk. Lenders need confidence in executive leadership stability and continuity of improvement delivery.
findings.figures: Resignation June 2026; Acting Chief Executive in place; interim replacement being sought
findings.quote: Following the resignation of the Chief Executive at the beginning of June, the Council's Executive Director of Adults, Health and Integration is continuing as the Acting Chief Executive, whilst arrangements for an interim Chief Executive are made.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 , item 7.
findings.headline: Internal audit opinion has been 'Limited' for three consecutive years with no improvement expected
findings.detail: The Annual Internal Audit Opinion was 'Limited' for the first time in 2023/24, remained 'Limited' in 2024/25, and is not expected to change for 2025/26. A 'Limited' opinion indicates that while improvements are being implemented, they are not consistently achieving required impacts, meaning control weaknesses persist.
findings.matters: A limited internal audit opinion indicates the council's internal control framework is not operating effectively. This creates risk that errors, fraud, or non-compliance could occur undetected.
findings.figures: Three consecutive years: 2023/24, 2024/25, 2025/26 (anticipated)
findings.quote: The Annual Internal Audit Opinion for 2023/24 was, for the first time, given as 'Limited'. Whilst recognising significant progress, the Annual Internal Audit Opinion for 2024/25 was also 'limited'... The Annual Internal Audit Opinion for 2025/26 will be confirmed to the Audit and Governance Committee, but as indicated to the committee in progress update reports through the year, it is not expected to change from Limited.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 , item 7.
findings.headline: External auditor will disclaim opinion on accounts due to evidence gaps and scope limitations
findings.detail: EY confirmed a disclaimed audit opinion on the 2025/26 Statement of Accounts due to continued evidence gaps, delays in financial reporting, and scope limitations, particularly affecting the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement. This means auditors cannot express confidence in the accuracy of the financial statements.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion means financial statements are unreliable. Lenders and stakeholders cannot trust the reported financial position, making it impossible to assess true solvency or borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Draft audit results reported to Audit and Governance Committee February 2026
findings.quote: At the February 2026 Audit and Governance Committee meeting, EY confirmed in their draft audit results report that a disclaimed audit opinion would be issued due to continued evidence gaps, delays in financial reporting, and limitations of scope, particularly affecting the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26 , item 7.
findings.headline: Council remains in structural deficit and dependent on Exceptional Financial Support to balance its budget
findings.detail: The council achieved a balanced revenue position only after applying £18.510m of Exceptional Financial Support against a planned use of £23.5m. Critically, the underlying position before EFS remained in overspend, indicating the council cannot balance its budget from its own resources. Under-delivery of transformation savings and pressures in Children and Families services were the principal drivers.
findings.matters: A lender must know whether a council can balance its budget from its own revenues. Structural overspend means the council's income does not cover its ongoing commitments, making it dependent on government bailouts.
findings.figures: £18.510m EFS applied in 2025/26 against £23.5m planned; underlying position remained in overspend
findings.quote: the Council achieved a balanced revenue position only after applying £18.510m of EFS against a planned use of £23.5m. Although this represents reduced reliance on EFS compared to budget, the underlying position before EFS remained in overspend, demonstrating that the Council is not yet operating within its recurrent financial means

findings.paper_title: Draft Annual Governance Statement 2025-26
findings.headline: Council identifies financial sustainability, leadership capacity, and children's services improvement as ongoing governance issue areas
findings.detail: The draft AGS identifies multiple areas requiring continued improvement during 2025/26, specifically flagging financial sustainability, leadership capacity, and children's services improvement as significant ongoing governance issues. The council reports no new major governance issues have emerged since February 2026, but these existing areas require sustained remediation effort.
findings.matters: Financial sustainability is fundamental to a lender's credit assessment; leadership capacity gaps suggest management constraints; children's services is typically a cost-pressure area in councils. A lender needs to understand the scope of these issues and management's remediation timeline
findings.figures: Specific numbers not provided in covering report; detail is contained in full Annual Governance Statement (Appendix 1)
findings.quote: This includes the Council's continuing work on financial sustainability, improvement and transformation, governance and internal control, leadership capacity, children's services improvement, partnership working and other areas identified through the annual review of effectiveness.

findings.paper_title: Draft Financial Statements - Wholly Owned Companies and Outturn Update 2025/26
findings.headline: Council acquired 75% shareholding in Alliance Environmental Services from 1 April 2025
findings.detail: Cheshire East Council acquired a 75% shareholding in Alliance Environmental Services on 1 April 2025. Alliance has draft retained reserves of £0.669m, of which the council's 75% stake represents £0.502m. This acquisition occurred as the council simultaneously wound down its other two WOCs.
findings.matters: New shareholding acquisition affects the council's commercial portfolio; shows strategic consolidation while managing overall WOC strategy.
findings.figures: 75% shareholding, £0.669m total reserves, £0.502m council share
findings.quote: From 1 April 2025 the 75% shareholding has transferred to Cheshire East Council.

findings.paper_title: Draft Financial Statements - Wholly Owned Companies and Outturn Update 2025/26
findings.headline: Ansa and Orbitas reported balanced 2025/26 result with £339,000 management fee rebate offsetting closure costs
findings.detail: Ansa and Orbitas reported a balanced financial position in 2025/26, with transitional costs from the closure of operations on 31 March 2026 offset by a £339,000 management fee rebate from Cheshire East Council. This arrangement enabled break-even reporting despite the wind-down process.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the financial structure of the wind-down and shows the council is actively managing the transition costs.
findings.quote: ANSA and Orbitas reported a balanced position in 2025/26, this relates to the 2025/26 financial year transitional costs due to the closure of the companies on the 31 March 26 offset by rebated management fee of £339,000 to Cheshire East Council.

findings.paper_title: Draft Financial Statements - Wholly Owned Companies and Outturn Update 2025/26
findings.headline: Ansa and Orbitas reserves fell from £0.848m to £0.430m with £0.134m dividend and £0.284m written off
findings.detail: Combined opening reserves of £0.848m for Ansa and Orbitas fell to closing reserves of £0.430m, with movements including a £0.134m dividend payment to the council and £0.284m of assets and liabilities written off and funded from company reserves. This £0.418m net reduction reflects the wind-down process.
findings.matters: Material reserve depletion shows value being extracted from the companies as they close; relevant to council liquidity and cash flow planning during the transition.
findings.figures: Opening £0.848m, Dividend £0.134m, Assets written off £0.284m, Closing £0.430m
findings.quote: The movement in reserves reflecting net (after tax) commercial profits of Ansa and Orbitas were: Opening Balances £0.848m, Dividend Payment (£0.134m), Written off assets and liabilities to CEC – funded from company reserves (£0.284m), Closing Reserves £0.430m

findings.paper_title: Draft Financial Statements - Wholly Owned Companies and Outturn Update 2025/26
findings.headline: Ansa and Orbitas accounts unaudited; exemption under Companies Act section 479A
findings.detail: Both Ansa and Orbitas are entitled to audit exemption under section 479A of the Companies Act 2006 for subsidiary companies. Their 2025/26 financial statements will not be subject to external audit. This contrasts with Alliance Environmental Services, which is subject to full external audit by Grant Thornton.
findings.matters: Unaudited accounts during wind-down represent reduced financial oversight at a time of significant financial transactions (dividends, asset write-offs, liability transfers); material for governance assessment.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: For the year ending 31 March 2026 ANSA and Orbitas were entitled to exemption from audit under section 479A, audit exemption for a subsidiary company, of the Companies Act 2006. Therefore, the Financial Statements will not be audited.

findings.paper_title: Draft Financial Statements - Wholly Owned Companies and Outturn Update 2025/26
findings.headline: Ansa and Orbitas accounts prepared on break-up basis reflecting planned dissolution
findings.detail: The financial statements for Ansa and Orbitas use break-up basis accounting rather than going concern, reflecting the decision to dissolve both companies during 2026/27. Break-up basis is appropriate for entities ceasing operations and affects interpretation of reserves and asset valuations.
findings.matters: Break-up accounting signals companies are no longer assumed to be viable operations; material accounting change affecting how financial position should be evaluated.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: the draft Financial Statements for Ansa and Orbitas have been prepared on break up basis and comply with the Companies Act 2006.

findings.paper_title: Draft Financial Statements - Wholly Owned Companies and Outturn Update 2025/26
findings.headline: Ansa and Orbitas to be dissolved in 2026/27 following decision to bring operations back in-house
findings.detail: Following a Finance Sub-Committee decision in June 2024, Cheshire East is winding up its two wholly owned companies. Orbitas was brought back in-house from 1 February 2025, Ansa from 1 April 2025 (with the transport service following from 1 August 2025 due to operator licence issues). The 2025/26 accounts will be the final set before dissolution.
findings.matters: Material changes to group structure and governance arrangements directly affect lender assessment of the council's financial management and control.
findings.figures: 1 February 2025, 1 April 2025, 1 August 2025, 2026/27
findings.quote: This will be the last update for the two WoC's as they will be dissolved during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Strategic Asset Management Plan , item 21.
findings.headline: Statutory compliance in council buildings improved significantly (87% in 2018 to 97% in 2024), reducing regulatory and safety risk
findings.detail: The Facilities Management Service has lifted compliance scores from 87.11% (2018) to 97.20% (2024) through systematic inspection and maintenance. This is a genuine improvement in governance and statutory adherence (Health & Safety, building regulations, etc.), mitigating risk of enforcement action or safety failures.
findings.matters: Compliance failures create legal and safety liability; strong compliance reduces this exposure and demonstrates competent asset stewardship despite financial pressure.
findings.quote: The trend for the last few years has seen a steady improvement of performance with average compliance scores rising from 87.11% in 2018 to 97.20% in 2024.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Strategic Asset Management Plan , item 21.
findings.headline: Council is externally partnering on asset disposals to accelerate sales and unlock receipts faster
findings.detail: The internal disposal team achieved £5m in 15 months. Going forward, the council is exploring outsourcing to a private sector partner to increase disposal momentum and 'establish and optimise deliverable capital receipts'. This signals the internal team is not keeping pace with targets and the council needs external help to hit its £24m two-year goal.
findings.matters: Externalization costs money and dilutes the receipts the council retains. It also suggests the internal capacity to deliver disposals is insufficient, which is a delivery risk if the external partner underperforms.
findings.figures: Internal team achieved £5m April 2025–June 2026; target £24m over 2026/27–2027/28
findings.quote: Going forward from 2026/27, the Council is seeking to further increase the momentum of land and property disposals, and therefore will be exploring the opportunity to externalise to a private sector

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Strategic Asset Management Plan , item 21.
findings.headline: Council is implementing large-scale estate rationalisation to deliver financial savings, including consolidating operational depots and office locations
findings.detail: The council is reducing its property footprint to cut holding costs and generate disposal receipts. Highways is reducing from 3 depot sites to 2 (closing Congleton, retaining Macclesfield and Wardle). Environmental Services has closed multiple permanent depots and is moving to mobile waste services. The council is reviewing office rationalisation as well. These moves are explicitly driven by 'developing financial challenges' and aim to release assets and cut property-related costs.
findings.matters: Estate rationalisation is a forced cost-cutting measure during financial distress. While it can generate one-time receipts, it also signals structural pressure on the council's finances. Lenders should verify that service delivery is not compromised by acceleration of closures.
findings.figures: Highways consolidating 3 sites to 2; Environmental Services has closed multiple depots; no specific cost savings quantified in this paper
findings.quote: Since the pandemic and developing financial challenges, the council's operational estate is a significant factor in the implementation of financial savings and improvement in working practices.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Strategic Asset Management Plan , item 21.
findings.headline: Government abolished Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme, removing the council's primary funding route for carbon reduction projects
findings.detail: The council had been relying on PSDS grants to meet its carbon-neutral-by-2030 target. The scheme has been abolished with no confirmed replacement. This removes a major source of capital grant funding and creates uncertainty about how the council will fund low-carbon building upgrades (heating, lighting, thermal performance) across its £570m estate.
findings.matters: Loss of external grant funding narrows the council's financial headroom at a time of crisis. The council will need to either fund decarbonisation from revenue (unlikely given financial stress) or defer environmental commitments. A lender may view this as a regulatory risk if the council falls behind climate obligations.
findings.figures: No replacement scheme identified; PSDS abolished as of paper date (July 2026)
findings.quote: At the time of writing the government's main source of funding support through the former Public Sector Decarbonisation Scheme (PSDS) has been abolished with considerable uncertainty regarding any replacement.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Strategic Asset Management Plan , item 21.
findings.headline: Capital programme is dependent on asset disposal receipts; council forecasts £24m from property sales over two years but has achieved only £5m in first 15 months
findings.detail: The council relies on selling surplus assets to fund its capital programme instead of borrowing. It targets £24m in net receipts for 2026/27 to 2027/28 (with £8.19m additional in 2026/27 and £7.75m in 2027/28). However, its internal disposal team formed April 2025 has only achieved or committed £5m by June 2026, with a further £10–12m conditional on planning decisions. This is a structural dependency with execution risk.
findings.matters: If asset sales stall or fall short, the capital programme stalls and the council cannot fund essential projects. For a lender, this is a revenue-raising risk; for the finance director, it's a critical delivery risk.
findings.figures: Target £24m net receipts 2026/27–2027/28; achieved/committed £5m (April 2025–June 2026); further £10–12m conditional on planning approval; forecast breakdown: 2026/27 £10.94m total with £8.19m additional; 2027/28+ £12.75m total with £7.75m additional
findings.quote: Capital receipts from surplus property enable the delivery of the council's MTFS and the Capital Programme, reducing the need to borrow to deliver the schemes which have been recognised corporately as being important to the Council

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Strategic Asset Management Plan , item 21.
findings.headline: Council faces risk of S114 insolvency notice and is implementing asset strategy as part of financial recovery
findings.detail: The council has received a non-statutory best value notice and explicitly states it faces a risk of a future S114 notice (formal insolvency). The asset management plan is framed as part of the Transformation Programme to respond to these challenges. This is a governance crisis, not routine business.
findings.matters: An S114 notice means the council is formally insolvent and cannot spend money except on statutory obligations. A lender or finance director needs to know the council is under regulatory intervention.
findings.figures: S114 risk noted; council under non-statutory best value notice as of paper date (July 2026)
findings.quote: The Asset Management Strategy and Plan also seeks to recognise and respond to the Council's financial challenges at this time and the response to the non-statutory best value notice and risk of a future S114 notice being advanced.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Transformation costs are front-loaded; savings depend on upfront investment and capital receipts.
findings.detail: The council identifies a need to make 'reasonable investments' in the Estates Service to build capacity to realign assets. This requires transformation-funded resources. 'Recycling receipts' are required for capital works. Estates is identifying additional staff resources. This creates near-term cost pressure before savings are realized.
findings.matters: If capital receipts are delayed or lower than expected, upfront transformation investment will not be offset by receipts, leaving the council with higher costs and unachieved savings.
findings.figures: No figures provided; Transformation funded people resources to be sought
findings.quote: There is a need to make reasonable investments in the Estates Service to create the capacity to realign the use of the council's assets. This in turn will drive savings across the organisation.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: The existing Corporate Landlord model is not delivering and requires reinvention.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that its current Corporate Landlord model needs 'improvement and re-focus'. The model has operated on 'business as usual' basis with service-based building occupation patterns inherited from historical structures. The council recognises this approach has been difficult to change culturally and has failed to achieve effective asset management.
findings.matters: A transformation programme starting from a position of ineffective governance and requiring cultural change carries material delivery risk, particularly given the budget pressure and capital constraints already identified.
findings.figures: Portfolio comprises 2,800 defined assets; 421 substantive operational assets; 81 investment portfolio assets
findings.quote: The existing Corporate Landlord model needs improvement and re-focus as the current approach to asset management has been very much in the context of 'business as usual' (BAU), and often single service based building occupation often derived from long established local authorities' structures.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: MTFS assumes only £100,000 net saving from asset strategy refresh.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 MTFS includes a single £100,000 saving attributed to the asset strategy refresh. Against a combined Assets and Facilities budget of £18.753m, this represents 0.5% of the budget. For a transformation programme positioning asset optimization as a key enabler, this is a modest target.
findings.matters: The savings target appears small relative to the scale of transformation planned, signalling either low confidence in delivery or that material savings are unquantified and carry delivery risk.
findings.figures: £100,000 saving (reference S24); £18.753m combined Assets and Facilities management revenue budget
findings.quote: The MTFS for 2026/27 includes a £100,000 saving as a result of the asset strategy refresh (reference S24). The resulting combined Assets and Facilities management revenue budget is £18.753m.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Asset disposals are the critical mechanism for funding transformation and meeting MTFS targets.
findings.detail: The council states explicitly that disposal of assets is critical to deliver the capital receipts needed for transformation and to achieve its medium-term financial strategy. Currently 33 sites are in progress. The council is seeking private sector co-sourcing to accelerate a 5-year disposal pipeline programme, suggesting current pace is insufficient.
findings.matters: If the disposal programme underperforms, capital receipts will be lower than planned, transformation cannot be funded, and MTFS targets will be missed.
findings.figures: 33 disposal sites in progress for current year; 5-year disposal pipeline being established
findings.quote: Within the Asset Management Strategy, the disposal of assets will be critical for the delivery of capital receipts to enable transformation and to achieve the MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Asset Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Capital programme is tightly constrained by rising borrowing costs.
findings.detail: The council explicitly reports that its capital programme is limited due to increased cost of borrowing. Any schemes relying on prudential borrowing must now be reassessed through the Capital Programme Board to verify they remain affordable. This directly constrains the council's capital investment capacity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has exhausted its borrowing headroom or if debt capacity still exists for future needs.
findings.figures: Combined Assets and Facilities management revenue budget £18.753m
findings.quote: The service has a limited capital programme due to the increased cost of borrowing. Therefore, schemes funded by prudential borrowing need further review to ensure they remain affordable via Capital Programme Board.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: External borrowing is planned to fall to £106m by 2028/29 while the Capital Financing Requirement rises, forcing massive planned internal borrowing from reserves.
findings.detail: The council plans to hold external borrowing at £106m by 2028/29 (down from £397m today) while its Capital Financing Requirement reaches £560m. This creates internal borrowing of £454m—up from £150m today. The council is explicitly choosing to fund the bulk of its capital needs from reserves and working capital rather than external borrowing. While stated as deliberate strategy, this represents a significant drawdown of liquidity over the medium term and leaves the council vulnerable to any shortfall in reserves or unexpected capital needs.
findings.matters: This strategy works only if: (1) capital spending proceeds on plan, (2) reserves remain intact, (3) revenue income doesn't fall, (4) no major unexpected demands emerge. A lender would ask whether the council's liquidity is sufficient and what the downside scenario looks like if the plan breaks.
findings.figures: External borrowing: 2025/26 £397m, forecast 2028/29 £106m (a 73% reduction). Capital Financing Requirement: £547m to £561m. Internal borrowing: £150m to £454m (a 202% increase).
findings.quote: The Council's current strategy is to maintain borrowing and investments below their underlying levels, sometimes known as internal borrowing. Loans CFR 547.192, Less: External borrowing (397.028), Internal (over) borrowing 150.164. Forecast 2028/29: Loans CFR 560.749, External borrowing (106.475), Internal borrowing 454.274.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: The council is forecasting £40m in capital receipts over coming years but has only received ~£4m to date, creating a major execution risk.
findings.detail: Over 2024/25 and 2025/26, actual capital receipts total £6.19m (£2.100m + £3.990m). The council now forecasts £15m per year for 2026/27, 2027/28 and 2028/29, totalling £55m. If these asset sales do not materialise, the council faces a £40m+ funding gap. The capital financing tables show these receipts are being counted on to partially fund rising capital expenditure and to sustain borrowing below prudential limits.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are the discretionary, non-recurring source of funding. A lender would note that £40m of the council's funding plan depends on executing asset sales that have historically been slow (£2-4m per year). If the council's balance sheet contains imminent asset sales that fail to execute, it will need to borrow more than planned.
findings.figures: 2024/25 actual receipts: £2.200m. 2025/26 actual: £3.990m. 2026/27-2028/29 forecast: £15m + £15m + £10.2m = £40.2m. Forecast increase of more than 3.8x historical run-rate.
findings.quote: The Council received £2.677m of capital receipts from asset sales in 2025/26 and plans to receive a further £40m in future years. Any capital receipts in excess of those planned within the MTFS, and that are not already planned as funding for capital programmes, will be utilised at the discretion of the s151 Officer with a view to achieving the most beneficial longer term financial outcome for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: Non-Domestic Rates forecast missed by £0.938m due to a surge in appeals after the 2023 Rating List closed.
findings.detail: The council forecast a £0.967m surplus on NDR in its January return to government, but actual outturn delivered only a £0.029m surplus—a £0.938m gap against plan. The council attributes this to "a significant increase in the number of checks, challenge and appeals raised in March due to the closure of the 2023 Rating List." This represents a material variance in a £160m+ income stream and signals that forecast accuracy or risk identification is weak.
findings.matters: Business rates are the second pillar of local government income. A £0.938m miss suggests either poor forecasting or unmanaged risk in the business rate base. It also indicates businesses are actively challenging their ratings, which could signal economic stress or confidence to pursue disputes.
findings.figures: NNDR1 forecast surplus: £0.967m (£0.473m to council). Actual outturn: £0.029m surplus (£0.014m to council). Undeclared deficit vs. plan: £0.938m.
findings.quote: The reduction Non-Domestic Rates Collection Fund position since the NNDR1 declaration has been due to a significant increase in the number of checks, challenge and appeals raised in March due to the closure of the 2023 Rating List.

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: Council Tax collection rates have declined for three consecutive years, dropping from 98.2% to 97.5% in year-one collection.
findings.detail: The council's ability to collect council tax after one year has fallen from 98.2% in 2022/23 to 97.5% in 2025/26. This downward trend—from 98.2% to 98.0% to 97.8% to 97.5%—suggests growing difficulty in collection. The three-year target of 99% collection is now dependent on improving significantly in years 2 and 3, whereas previously the first-year rate was already close to that target.
findings.matters: Council tax is supposed to be a reliable revenue base. A declining collection rate signals either growing resident hardship or enforcement issues. This erodes the predictability of a key income stream and may indicate economic stress in the area or weakening collection performance.
findings.quote: Table 2 demonstrates that the target to collect at least 99% of Council Tax within three years continues to be achieved. After 1 year 97.8%, 2022/23 98.2%, 2023/24 98.0%, 2024/25 97.8% 2025/26 97.5%

findings.paper_title: Annex 3 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: Adult Social Care debt increased by £0.799m year-on-year and includes £0.231m stuck in complex legal property cases.
findings.detail: Service debt over 6 months old rose to £14.434m from £13.711m. Within this, Adult Social Care debt over 6 months jumped to £12.821m from £12.022m. A significant portion (£0.231m) is tied up in property-related disputes being handled by external legal providers. The council notes these cases are "expected to take a considerable length of time to resolve." Against £14.434m aged debt, the council has provisioned only £6.113m for doubtful debts.
findings.matters: Growing aged debt in social care signals either collection problems or liability that won't be paid. Either way, it represents revenue the council may not receive. A lender would worry whether the social care charging model is working or whether there's a structural collection issue.
findings.figures: Service debt over 6 months: £14.434m (up £0.722m). Adult Social Care portion: £12.821m (up £0.799m from £12.022m). Provision for doubtful debt: £6.113m.
findings.quote: The total amount of service debt over six months old is £14.434m, this has risen by £0.722m since FR3, this is due to an increase of £0.799m within Adult's Social Care, with a reduction of £0.146m within Growth & Enterprise. There is also £5.2m of debt which is deemed to be lower risk as its linked to areas such as probate, property sales or deputyship. A provision of £6.113m has been included in the accounts to 31 March 2026 to cover doubtful debt in the event that it needs to be written off.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: Growth in children's care demand cost 2.65× budget: £8.735m outturn vs £3.295m forecast
findings.detail: Council budgeted £3.295m for growth in current children's care demand based on MTFS projections but outturn was £8.735m (£5.440m overspend, marked Red). Despite being "closely monitored throughout the year," the underestimate was massive. This represents structural demand pressures, not a simple forecast miss, with MTFS growth figures now revised for 2026/27.
findings.matters: Demand forecasting accuracy is critical to multi-year financial planning. Missing by 165% on this category suggests underlying models are unreliable and future budgets for demand-led services may be equally inadequate.
findings.figures: Budget £3.295m; outturn £8.735m; variance £5.440m (marked Red)
findings.quote: This area has been closely monitored throughout the year to ensure that funding is sufficient to meet demand and complexity. This is also part of transformation work to ensure Edge of Care/Right Child Right home.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: £2.873m provision created for Special Guardianship Order backpay following ombudsman finding of incorrect payments
findings.detail: Ombudsman investigation found council was calculating Special Guardianship Order allowances incorrectly, resulting in underpayments to some individuals. Council has provisioned £2.873m to cover potential backpay liability for cases spanning 2023–2025. This reflects both a control failure (errors not caught internally) and a new contingent liability materializing.
findings.matters: Material contingent liability arising from governance failure. Raises questions about what other similar control gaps may exist across grants management or benefit administration.
findings.figures: £2.873m provision; covers potential cases 2023–2025
findings.quote: The creation of a provision for the Special Guardianship Order of £2.873m required to meet the potential costs relating to Special Guardianship Order (SGO) allowances. This is the result of a recent ombudsman case which evidenced incorrect calculations of funding due to some individuals which lead to incorrect lower payments being made.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: Council-wide transformation programme delivered nothing: £11.592m budgeted, £0 achieved, all programmes reprofiled to future years
findings.detail: Six major transformation initiatives budgeted to deliver £11.592m of savings in 2025/26 delivered zero and have been "reprofiled and agreed" to future years. Digital Blueprint (£4.0m), Target Operating Model (£3.0m), Digital Customer Enablement (£0.750m), Digital Acceleration (£0.600m), Workforce Productivity (£1.0m), and Agency Staffing (£0.352m) all marked Red. Core explanation: council shifted focus from cost savings to "enabling service change and redesign taking place in directorates."
findings.matters: Complete failure to deliver £11.6m of committed MTFS savings suggests either strategic capability gaps or unrealistic budget planning assumptions. Consistent reprofiling of savings raises questions about the council's ability to sustain financial control.
findings.figures: Total budgeted £11.592m; delivered £0; individual programmes: Digital Blueprint £4.000m, TOM £3.000m, Digital Customer Enablement £0.750m, Digital Acceleration £0.600m, Workforce Productivity £1.000m, Agency Staffing £0.352m
findings.quote: The Digital Blueprint saving, alongside all cross-cutting savings for 2025/26, have now been reprofiled and agreed by the Council as part of setting the budget for 2026/27 and MTFS 2026-30.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: Children in care numbers fell 16 but placement costs rose £7.860m, indicating structural cost pressures immune to volume reduction
findings.detail: Caseload declined from 550 to 534 children but placement costs increased to £48.631m vs £40.771m budget (£7.860m adverse). Residential placements overspent £4.134m (total £19.923m) and supported accommodation £2.436m (total £9.119m). Paper explicitly states this created "an un-budgeted pressure" despite the reducing caseload, suggesting unit costs or complexity are rising rather than costs falling with volume.
findings.matters: When activity decreases but costs increase, this signals structural pricing problems (market inflation, higher complexity cases, or poor commissioning) that will persist and worsen. Cost reductions cannot be achieved through volume management.
findings.figures: Placement costs £48.631m vs budget £40.771m (£7.860m adverse); residential placements £4.134m overspend; supported accommodation £2.436m overspend; caseload 534 vs prior year 550
findings.quote: Although numbers of children in care are reducing in the year, outturn position of 534 at 31st March 2026 compared to 550 at March 2025, the cost of placements in 2025/26 has continued to increase, creating an un-budgeted pressure.

findings.paper_title: Annex 1 for Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet) , item 19.
findings.headline: School DSG cumulative deficit rose £10.618m beyond plan to £156.596m driven by 12% EHCP demand surge
findings.detail: The High Needs Block saw 12% increase in EHCP demand (577 additional children), particularly in higher-cost independent special schools and post-16 specialist providers. This drove the cumulative DSG deficit to £156.596m compared to plan of £145.978m. In-year deficit was £44.447m against FR4 forecast of only £1.630m. Council states it is "seeing greater increased demand than anticipated despite best efforts to mitigate and control this demand."
findings.matters: DSG deficits must eventually be repaid by the council from reserves. Growing at 7% faster than planned (£10.6m above forecast) indicates demand models are inadequate and this financial exposure will likely worsen further.
findings.figures: Cumulative deficit £156.596m vs plan £145.978m (variance £10.618m); in-year deficit £44.447m vs FR4 forecast £1.630m; 577 additional EHCPs; 12% demand increase
findings.quote: The Council are seeing greater increased demand than anticipated despite best efforts to mitigate and control this demand. Increase in demand in EHCP of 12% has resulted in 577 more EHCPs in the system.

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet)
findings.headline: Non-Domestic Rates forecast collapsed from £0.967m to £0.014m after appeal challenges at end of rating list cycle
findings.detail: In January 2026, the NNDR1 return to government forecast a £0.967m surplus on the Non-Domestic Rates Collection Fund attributable to Cheshire East. The actual outturn was £0.014m, a swing of £0.953m. The council attributes this to 'a significant increase in the number of checks, challenge and appeals raised in March 2026 due to the end of the 3-year period of the 2023 Rating List', indicating the council faces rating appeals that may create further pressure.
findings.matters: This shows income forecasting volatility and suggests the council may face a deteriorating business rates position in the coming year as appeals are processed against the new rating list.
findings.figures: NNDR1 forecast surplus (January 2026) £0.967m; Outturn surplus £0.014m; variance £0.953m adverse
findings.quote: In January 2026, the NNDR1 return to Central Government forecast a £0.967m surplus on the Non-Domestic Rates Collection Fund. The reduced Non-Domestic Rates Collection Fund position since the NNDR1 declaration has recognised a significant increase in the number of checks, challenge and appeals raised in March 2026 due to the end of the 3-year period of the 2023 Rating List.

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet)
findings.headline: 23 maintained schools in deficit with net school deficit position of £3.291m
findings.detail: At the end of 2025/26, 23 maintained schools (out of 49) are in net deficit with a combined deficit of £3.291m. This is worsening from 2024/25 when 21 schools were in deficit with £2.175m deficit. Schools in deficit are required to submit deficit recovery plans, indicating financial stress across the school system.
findings.matters: Schools in financial difficulty can cascade into council pressures if the council needs to provide bailouts or if schools cannot fund services. The widening school deficit is an indicator of system-wide cost pressure in education.
findings.figures: Schools in deficit: 23 schools with £3.291m combined deficit (2025/26); 21 schools with £2.175m combined deficit (2024/25)
findings.quote: Schools with a net deficit (3.291) 23

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet)
findings.headline: Council reserves explicitly stated to be insufficient for financial sustainability
findings.detail: The council ends the year with total usable reserves of £28.520m (comprising £7.789m General Fund Balance and £20.731m Earmarked Reserves). The document explicitly states that 'the overall level of reserves held by the Council remains insufficient'. This is a direct statement from the S151 Officer that reserves do not meet the council's assessed financial risk.
findings.matters: If the S151 Officer believes reserves are insufficient, the council has inadequate financial buffers to absorb unforeseen pressures or volatility. This increases the risk of requiring further government support or emergency action.
findings.figures: Total usable reserves £28.520m; General Fund Balance £7.789m (increased by £1.490m); Earmarked Reserves £20.731m
findings.quote: As set out in the 2025/26 Budget/MTFS approved in February 2025, the overall level of reserves held by the Council remains insufficient.

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet)
findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only £122.180m against a revised budget of £208.491m (41% underspend)
findings.detail: The council's revised capital budget for 2025/26 was £208.491m. The outturn shows only £122.180m was spent, leaving an underspend of £86.311m (41.4%). This represents a significant gap between planned and actual capital deployment. Whilst some projects reprofiled to future years, the scale of underspend may indicate delivery difficulties.
findings.matters: A large capital underspend can indicate delivery or approval delays. It may also mean the council's capital programme planning is optimistic. Either way, a lender would want to understand why the council planned to spend £208m but only spent £122m.
findings.figures: Capital outturn £122.180m against revised budget £208.491m; underspend £86.311m (41.4%); FR4 forecast was £137.915m
findings.quote: Expenditure on the capital programme for the current year is £122.180m in year (FR4 £137.915m), an underspend of £86.311m against an original budget of £208.491m.

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet)
findings.headline: New £2.873m provision for Special Guardianship Order allowance underpayments following ombudsman case
findings.detail: The council has recognised a new provision of £2.873m at outturn to cover potential costs from a recent ombudsman case. The case found that the council made incorrect calculations when paying Special Guardianship Order allowances, resulting in individuals receiving lower payments than they were entitled to. The provision covers potential cases between 2023 and 2025.
findings.matters: This represents a control failure identified by the ombudsman and a potential financial liability for back-payments. It indicates weaknesses in the council's controls over social care payments and creates an unexpected liability that consumes resources.
findings.figures: £2.873m provision for SGO allowances; relates to cases between 2023 and 2025
findings.quote: At out-turn, a new provision has been recognised totalling £2.873m required to meet the potential costs relating to Special Guardianship Order (SGO) allowances. This is the result of a recent ombudsman case which evidenced incorrect calculations of funding due to some individuals which lead to incorrect lower payments being made.

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet)
findings.headline: Children and Families continued to overspend by £5.010m due to rising placement costs
findings.detail: The Children and Families directorate overspent its budget by £5.010m at outturn. Although this is an improvement of £2.770m since the FR4 forecast, it remains a substantial overspend. The document attributes this to 'increased costs of placements', indicating this is a structural demand pressure rather than a one-off issue.
findings.matters: A recurring service-level overspend in children's services indicates the council's budget assumptions for placement costs are not holding. Combined with the DSG SEND placement growth, this signals sustained demand pressure in a high-cost statutory service.
findings.figures: Children and Families overspend £5.010m; improvement of £2.770m since FR4 forecast of £7.780m
findings.quote: Children and Families have seen an improvement of £2.770m since FR4, however the out-turn overspend of £5.010m has continued to be the result of increased costs of placements.

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet)
findings.headline: DSG deficit has grown to £156.596m, increasing by £10.618m beyond the approved management plan
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant reserve began the year at a deficit of £112.149m. The in-year movement added £44.447m of deficit, bringing the year-end position to £156.596m. This exceeds the DSG Management Plan approved in September 2025 by £10.618m. The driver is a 16% increase in pupils with EHCP placements against a planned 6% increase.
findings.matters: The DSG deficit is a statutory liability that accumulates. Rapid growth in SEND placements (16% actual v 6% planned) shows demand is outpacing the council's planning assumptions. This creates a growing future liability that will require revenue budget recovery or further government support.
findings.figures: Year-end DSG deficit £156.596m; in-year movement £44.447m; exceeds DSG Management Plan by £10.618m; EHCP placements 16% increase (unplanned)
findings.quote: The year end position on the DSG reserve is a deficit of £156.596m compared to the FR4 forecast of £154.966m. This is an increase of £10.618m compared to the DSG Management Plan, approved in September 2025, of £145.978m. The key pressures relate to the High Needs Block where SEND service planned a 6% increase in placements, however out-turn reflects a 16% increase in numbers of pupils with EHCP placements.

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet)
findings.headline: Transformation savings programme fell short by £11.592m (47% of target), removing planned mitigation
findings.detail: The council planned to deliver £24.415m of cross-directorate transformation savings in 2025/26. The outturn shows only £9.903m delivered, a shortfall of £14.512m. This failure to achieve planned savings is a core reason the revenue budget overran. The shortfall is particularly acute in the 'Access to Services & Corporate Core' cross-cutting programme where £11.592m of the £13.452m target was not achieved.
findings.matters: A lender would see this as evidence the council cannot execute its efficiency programmes. If transformation plans are not delivering, future savings targets are at risk. This undermines the sustainability of the council's financial position.
findings.figures: £9.903m delivered of £24.415m target (40.5% delivery rate); shortfall of £14.512m; Access to Services shortfall of £11.592m of £13.452m target
findings.quote: A shortfall of £11.592m is being reported against in-year cross-directorate Transformation savings.

findings.paper_title: Final Outturn 2025/26 (Cabinet)
findings.headline: Revenue budget overspend of £18.510m (4.4%) must be funded through conditional government grant
findings.detail: The council overspent its £422.175m revenue budget by £18.510m in 2025/26. Although this is £6.751m better than forecast at FR4, it remains significant. The overspend is funded through conditional Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG, not from reserves or own resources. The council cannot balance its budget without this government grant.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that the council cannot live within its budget and is dependent on exceptional government support to stay solvent. The condition attached to the grant limits the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £18.510m overspend against £422.175m net revenue budget (4.4%); funded through conditional Exceptional Financial Support of £18.510m
findings.quote: The Outturn position for 2025/26 is an overspend of £18.510m, 4.4% against a net revenue budget of £422.175m. Whilst this is an improvement of £3.805m on the FR4 position of £22.315m, the overspend remains a significant challenge for the Council. The overspend is funded through conditional Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG).

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Council carrying historic borrowing costs that are expensive and difficult to refinance
findings.detail: The council has accumulated capital financing costs from historic borrowing that are described as 'sunk' costs. The paper notes these will be 'very difficult to refinance in the current environment at a lower cost than they currently cost', meaning the council is locked into expensive debt that cannot be replaced with cheaper financing.
findings.matters: High locked-in borrowing costs reduce the council's financial flexibility and consume budget that could otherwise go to services. If these costs are uncompetitive and cannot be refinanced, they represent a long-term structural drain on finances.
findings.figures: No specific amounts disclosed
findings.quote: capital financing costs that are a result of historic borrowing and are 'sunk' and will be very difficult to refinance in the current environment at a lower cost than they currently cost.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Council has low reserve levels that constrain financial flexibility
findings.detail: The paper identifies the council's 'current low levels of available reserves and balances' as a key vulnerability. Combined with a DSG deficit and high historic borrowing costs, low reserves limit the council's ability to absorb budget pressures or manage unexpected costs, increasing the risk of financial distress.
findings.matters: Reserves are a financial buffer that allow councils to manage unexpected costs and smooth budget pressures over time. Low reserves indicate the council has limited flexibility and is more vulnerable to budget shocks, increasing default risk.
findings.figures: No specific reserve figures disclosed in this report
findings.quote: the Council's current low levels of available reserves and balances alongside the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: 2027/28 faces £15.271m funding gap even after £13.302m planned savings
findings.detail: For 2027/28, the council has identified a net shortfall of £15.271m after accounting for £13.302m in savings already built into the MTFS. Closing this gap would require total savings of £28.573m (5.97% of the expenditure budget), equivalent to an additional 3.19% cuts beyond the planned savings.
findings.matters: A large funding gap in the medium term indicates the council has structural budget problems and will need to make significant service cuts or find new revenue sources. This affects the council's ability to maintain services and its financial resilience.
findings.figures: £15.271m gap; £13.302m existing savings; £28.573m total savings needed (5.97% of budget); additional savings of 3.19% of expenditure budget required
findings.quote: the current financial gap for 2027/28 is a forecast net shortfall of £15.271m. This position is after proposed savings of £13.302m that have already been included within the MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Council faces Section 114 notice risk if it cannot close funding gaps without exceptional support
findings.detail: The paper warns that without Exceptional Financial Support and with current low reserve levels, the council would face a Section 114 notice. This risk is compounded by a Dedicated Schools Grant deficit and historic borrowing costs that are difficult to refinance at lower rates.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration that a council cannot meet its financial obligations. This is a critical risk indicator for any lender considering the council's creditworthiness and ability to repay borrowing.
findings.figures: Section 114 risk conditional on failure to obtain EFS and close funding gaps
findings.quote: Without Exceptional Financial Support (EFS), this will result in a Section 114 notice based on the Council's current low levels of available reserves and balances alongside the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit and capital financing costs that are a result of historic borrowing and are 'sunk'

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy Assumptions and Reporting Cycle for 2027/28 to 2031/32
findings.headline: Council dependent on unsustainable Exceptional Financial Support of £24.995m to balance 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget was only balanced by using an 'in-principle' capitalisation direction for £24.995m. The council explicitly states this approach is 'not sustainable' and 'needs to be addressed in this year for the Council to become financially sustainable'. Without closing future gaps, the council will remain reliant on similar support.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can fund its operations from its own resources. Dependency on exceptional support signals the council cannot balance its budget and raises questions about financial viability.
findings.quote: The budget for the financial year 2026/27 could only be balanced using Exceptional Financial Support (£24.995m) by way of an 'in-principle' capitalisation direction. This is not sustainable and needs to be addressed in this year for the Council to be come financially sustainable.

findings.paper_title: Children and Families Capital Programme 2026/27 Decision Report Template (delete as appropriate)
findings.headline: School Condition Allocation declining from £2.552m to £2m due to academy conversions
findings.detail: The DfE grant for maintaining council-maintained schools is trending downward. The 2025/26 confirmed allocation was £2.552m; the council anticipates approximately £2m for 2026/27 (subject to DfE confirmation). This represents a 21.6% reduction, attributed to schools converting to academy status, which removes them from the council's maintained portfolio and the eligible base for this funding stream.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director monitoring the council's capital resources needs to track grant income trends. If academy conversions continue at this pace, the council's available capital for school building maintenance will shrink relative to the buildings it still maintains, potentially creating future maintenance backlogs.
findings.figures: 2025/26: £2.552m confirmed; 2026/27: £2m anticipated
findings.quote: Based on the confirmed 2025/26 School Condition Allocation (SCA) of £2.552m, the Council anticipates receiving approximately £2m in SCA for 2026/27, subject to formal DfE confirmation. This assumption aligns with previous years allocations and reduction for schools converting to academy status during the last financial year.

findings.paper_title: Addendum for Pension and EFS Update , item 77.
findings.headline: Pension contribution reduction provides temporary relief while pension fund confirms employer financial distress
findings.detail: The Cheshire Pension Fund reduced employer contribution rates from 20%/19%/18% to 18%/17%/17%, improving the budget by £2.444m. The Fund explicitly stated this change was to help employers 'facing financial challenges in the short-term', confirming sector-wide financial difficulty.
findings.matters: The pension fund's own rationale confirms councils are in financial distress; this temporary relief is a symptom of the problem, not a solution.
findings.figures: £2.444m budget improvement; rates reduced from 20%/19%/18% to 18%/17%/17%

findings.headline: Reserve depletion planned in later years to fund budget gaps
findings.detail: The MTFS includes planned drawdown of reserves: £10.5m in 2028/29 and £23.0m in 2029/30. This approach to funding budget gaps is unsustainable beyond the MTFS period and signals depletion of the council's financial buffer.
findings.matters: Reserves are the council's last financial buffer; drawing them down at scale to plug ongoing shortfalls shows inability to sustain from revenues and leaves the council vulnerable.

findings.matters: Multi-year structural deficits indicate the council cannot sustain itself from its own revenues and faces a persistent financial challenge that will require ongoing intervention.

findings.matters: Lenders need to know when a council cannot balance from its own resources and is dependent on government bailout, indicating material financial stress.

findings.headline: The Cheshire Pension Fund reduced employer contribution rates to provide financial relief to councils facing challenges.
findings.detail: The pension fund lowered employer contribution rates for the 2026-29 period to 18%, 17%, and 17% respectively, compared to initially projected 20%, 19%, and 18%. This £2.444m annual saving for Cheshire East was made because the fund explicitly acknowledged that employers are 'facing financial challenges in the short-term.' This concession, while beneficial, signals sector-wide financial stress among local authorities.
findings.matters: When pension funds and other external parties make concessions to help a council's finances, it signals the council is under stress; a lender should not assume such relief will continue and should assess the council's standalone financial sustainability.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Budget reaching £32.255m in 2026/27, growing to £32.606m by 2028/29, driven by DSG, EFS and capital borrowing interest and MRP
findings.detail: Capital Financing Budget comprises interest on DSG deficit (£4.358m), EFS interest (£1.147m), capital borrowing interest (£10.751m), less interest receivable, plus MRP. Budget grows year-on-year, with MRP rising from £18.647m to £22.305m by 2029/30, consuming material portion of available revenue.
findings.matters: Rising capital costs constrain available revenue for service delivery. Accumulating MRP indicates growing debt burden that will continue to consume revenue in future years.
findings.quote: In addition to funding from Council Tax, grants and other income, the Council also needs to appropriately manage its everyday cashflow through Treasury Management activity as well as consider how it funds its Capital programme. All of this has an impact on the revenue budget, particularly in relation to the costs of borrowing to fund the Capital programme.

findings.matters: Depleting reserves to cover recurrent overspends indicates the council's spending base is not sustainable from its revenue. Reserves exist for contingency and one-off items; using them annually is a sign of structural deficit.
