findings.headline: Children's services rated inadequate by Ofsted with improvement plan only 27% complete and ongoing funding commitments
findings.detail: Ofsted inspection in March 2024 found children's services inadequate for care leavers, triggering a DfE Improvement Notice. As of 2024-25, only 27% of improvement actions are completed with impact, 48% in testing phase, and 18% on track. Ongoing Ofsted monitoring visits are scheduled over 4-6 visits, with additional service capacity funded to support the improvement plan.
findings.matters: An inadequate rating indicates control and service delivery failures. Slow improvement pace (27% complete after one year) and requirement for additional ongoing funding creates sustained service and budget risk.
findings.figures: 27% of actions completed (Green); 48% in testing phase (Amber E); 18% on track (Amber); 4-6 Ofsted monitoring visits planned
findings.quote: Progress of the Improvement Plan now shows 27% of actions completed (Green) and impact achieved. A further 48% also have completed actions and we are in a phase of testing impact (Amber E) before these move to Green and 18% on track (Amber).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: Best Value Notice issued in May 2025 requiring Government assurance of financial sustainability
findings.detail: The council received a non-statutory Best Value Notice in May 2025, requiring it to provide Government with ongoing assurance of improvement and work towards financial sustainability. This formal escalation reflects concerns about the council's financial position and ability to meet obligations.
findings.matters: A Best Value Notice signals Government concern about the council's finances. The council must now demonstrate a credible sustainability plan or face more intensive intervention and potential loss of control over finances.
findings.figures: Best Value Notice issued May 2025
findings.quote: In May 2025, the Council was issued with a non-statutory Best Value Notice which requires the Council to provide the Government with further assurance of its ongoing improvement and work towards financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: Service overspend of £9.8m and overall budget deficit of £17.6m with declining reserves
findings.detail: The council's 2024-25 outturn showed a service overspend of £9.8m. Net of proposed reserve transfers of £7.8m, the overall overspend reached £17.6m. General reserves have been decreasing due to recurring overspends driven by funding uncertainty and demand growth. The council required exceptional financial support and a capitalisation directive to set a legally balanced budget.
findings.matters: Material ongoing overspends and reserve depletion indicate the council cannot live within its resources and has lost financial headroom for unforeseen demands.
findings.figures: £9.8m service overspend; £17.6m overall overspend net of transfers; reserves declining
findings.quote: the service overspend of £9.8m remains a significant financial challenge for the Council. The outturn position, net of proposed transfers to useable reserves of £7.8m, is an overspend of £17.6m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Risk Management Report 2024-25 , item 21.
findings.headline: Children's services received growth allocations of £10.8m (2024-25) and £4.6m+£2.7m (2025-26) but remain under pressure to find additional savings.
findings.detail: Children's Services Complexity and Demand risk (SR03) notes that despite MTFS growth of £10.8m for placement costs (2024-25) and further proposed growth of £4.6m for placement costs plus £2.7m for staffing (2025-26), the council states: "Significant action is still required to deliver savings to live within the budget as all indications are that demand, complexity and cost will continue to increase."
findings.matters: A lender would question whether growth allocations are keeping pace with demand growth, or whether the council is falling further behind in managing children's placement costs.
findings.figures: £10.8m growth 2024-25; £4.6m placement + £2.7m staffing growth 2025-26
findings.quote: The service received growth through the MTFS to help address the pressures but the challenge to deliver to budget and achieve the required savings remains present. Significant action is still required to deliver savings to live within the budget as all indications are that demand, complexity and cost will continue to increase.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Risk Management Report 2024-25 , item 21.
findings.headline: Adult social care demand and case complexity are rising, with individual care packages now reaching £2000+ per week.
findings.detail: Adult Services risk (SR01) reports: "Demand is constant especially for those who are 90+yrs, and for those with dementia. Cost of individual care packages remains very high with an increasing number £2000 per week." The paper notes that "As predicted the reduction of agency staff within the service has resulted in increased waiting times for assessments, this reduction has been seen in the services provided during quarter two. All waiting lists are monitored weekly."
findings.matters: Rising case complexity and unit costs indicate the council's mitigation strategies (reducing agency spend, redirecting demand) may be insufficient to contain the budget, particularly if new ICB-funded cases are shifted to social care.
findings.figures: Individual care packages: £2000 per week (and rising)
findings.quote: Demand is constant especially for those who are 90+yrs, and for those with dementia. Cost of individual care packages remains very high with an increasing number£2000 per week.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Risk Management Report 2024-25 , item 21.
findings.headline: Cheshire East children's services received an Ofsted "inadequate" judgement in February-March 2024 with improvement plan running to April 2026.
findings.detail: The ILACS Improvement Plan risk (SR19) notes that "children's services received an overall judgement of inadequate" from Ofsted inspection in February and March 2024. The paper identifies "significant reputational and financial risk to not delivering improvements. If services remain inadequate at the next inspection, further intervention measures may need to be put in place, for example escalation to a Statutory Direction notice, or Direction that another person or organisation performs the functions on the local authority's behalf. These measures will have a significant cost to the council." The improvement plan timeline runs to April 2026.
findings.matters: An inadequate Ofsted rating and risk of intervention (with associated commissioner costs, estimated elsewhere as up to £200k per commissioner, 2-6 commissioners, up to 5 years) represents a material reputational and financial risk for the council.
findings.figures: Intervention cost estimate: up to £200k per commissioner, typically 2-6 commissioners, up to 5 years
findings.quote: If services remain inadequate at the next inspection, further intervention measures may need to be put in place, for example escalation to a Statutory Direction notice, or Direction that another person or organisation performs the functions on the local authority's behalf. These measures will have a significant cost to the council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Risk Management Report 2024-25 , item 21.
findings.headline: The NHS Cheshire and Mersey ICB deficit may force the council to pick up additional funding for previously NHS-funded patients.
findings.detail: The Adult Services risk (SR01) notes: "The deficit within the Cheshire and Mersey ICB will increase pressure on the council to pick up funding for previously funded health patients and this will require robust challenge and discussion. We are currently in discussion with our NHS partners over a number of cases on which we disagree. It is possible that there will be an additional financial burden placed on ASC in the upcoming financial year."
findings.matters: This represents an unquantified and unplanned demand-led pressure that could emerge mid-year, adding to existing social care budget pressures.
findings.figures: unquantified potential burden
findings.quote: The deficit within the Cheshire and Mersey ICB will increase pressure on the council to pick up funding for previously funded health patients and this will require robust challenge and discussion. It is possible that there will be an additional financial burden placed on ASC in the upcoming financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Risk Management Report 2024-25 , item 21.
findings.headline: The council cannot afford care fee uplifts for social care providers despite 9.8% National Living Wage increase and inflation, creating market fragility.
findings.detail: The Social Care Market Risk (SR02) identifies that "The current financial position of the Local Authority precludes it from uplifting care fees for all care contracts in 2024/25" despite the 9.8% National Living Wage uplift from April 2024 and high inflation. Multiple care homes have placement embargos due to quality risks: Priestly Fields and St Catherine's Care Homes have embargos in place. Emmie Dixon Care Home is facing "financial sustainability challenges" due to 3 vacant voids. The care at home waiting list stands at 7 people representing 90 hours per week of unmet need.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether provider failures or service withdrawal could force emergency expenditure or service reduction, and whether the council has identified where the fee uplift will come from.
findings.figures: 9.8% National Living Wage uplift April 2024; 7 people on care at home waiting list = 90 hours per week; individual care packages reaching £2000 per week
findings.quote: The current financial position of the Local Authority precludes it from uplifting care fees for all care contracts in 2024/25. The major risk going forward is the financial impacts on providers resulting from the 9.8% uplift in National Living Wage from April 2024 and high rates of inflation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Risk Management Report 2024-25 , item 21.
findings.headline: £25m expended on Middlewich Eastern Bypass faces cancellation risk, which would "significantly worsen" the council's financial situation.
findings.detail: The Department for Transport decision on the Middlewich Eastern Bypass has been significantly delayed. The council's risk assessment notes "Medium to High" likelihood of ongoing delay coupled with "exceptionally high inflation rates in construction" creating budgetary challenges. The paper explicitly states: "Continued delay, or ultimately cancellation of the MEB would have significant financial and reputational implications for the Council...The very significant costs (c£25m) expended to date would need to be charged to revenue budgets in the year of cancellation. These costs would significantly worsen he Council's current financial situation." A positive DfT decision is expected by end of February 2025.
findings.matters: A lender would view a £25m write-off to revenue budgets in a year when the council is already forecasting £25m+ shortfalls as potentially triggering intervention thresholds. This is not a minor contingency.
findings.figures: c£25m expended to date on Middlewich Eastern Bypass
findings.quote: The very significant costs (c£25m) expended to date would need to be charged to revenue budgets in the year of cancellation. These costs would significantly worsen he Council's current financial situation.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Risk Management Report 2024-25 , item 21.
findings.headline: The council forecast an £18.3m overspend in 2024-25 and a £25.3m shortfall for 2025-26, relying on exceptional financial support to avoid Section 114.
findings.detail: The Third Financial Review (FR3) reported to Finance Sub-Committee on 9 January 2025 shows a forecast £18.3m overspend for the current financial year, an improvement of £1.8m on FR2 but still "a significant financial challenge". The council approved use of £17.6m conditional Exceptional Financial Support to balance the overspend. Forecast revenue reserves at 31 March 2025 are £9.2m. The 2025-26 shortfall is estimated at £25.3m, with Members to consider "options for further Exceptional Financial Support" at Corporate Policy Committee on 6 February 2025 prior to Budget Council on 26 February 2025.
findings.matters: A lender evaluating the council's credit strength needs to know: (a) whether Exceptional Financial Support will continue to be available; (b) what reserves depletion trajectory is sustainable; (c) what hard savings plans exist if grants end; (d) what threshold would trigger a Section 114 Notice.
findings.figures: £18.3m overspend FR3; £17.6m Exceptional Financial Support utilised 2024-25; £25.3m shortfall 2025-26; £9.2m forecast revenue reserves at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The Council's Third Financial Review (FR3) shows a forecast £18.3m overspend for the current financial year. Whilst an improvement on the Second Financial Review by £1.8m, the forecast overspend remains a significant financial challenge for the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Risk Management Report 2024-25 , item 21.
findings.headline: The DSG reserve deficit of £285m is unrecoverable without fundamental changes to funding.
findings.detail: The council holds a mitigated cumulative forecast DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) reserve deficit of £285m due to growth in pupils with EHCPs greatly exceeding funding. The Department for Education rejected the council's Safety Valve application in March 2024, stating the council's financial ask was "significantly above the level which the Department could reasonably afford" compared to other agreements. The latest 2024-25 forecast shows a £115.8m deficit. Without significant changes to funding, the position is acknowledged as "unaffordable and unsustainable."
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand whether this multi-year £285m liability represents a call on revenue budgets or if it remains contained to reserves, and what funding solution exists if the deficit continues to grow.
findings.figures: £285m cumulative mitigated forecast deficit; £79.5m 2023-24 outturn (improved from £89.6m forecast); £115.8m 2024-25 forecast; 8% EHCP growth (down from 13.6% prior year)
findings.quote: This position is unaffordable and unsustainable. The arrangements beyond March 2026 are not confirmed by the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities (DLUHC). Without significant changes to funding the DSG reserve deficit is not recoverable.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: The Cheshire and Merseyside Integrated Care Board requires £170m in cashable savings and the ICB Place Director role has been vacant since June 2025 with recruitment not yet engaged.
findings.detail: The NHS is undergoing significant restructuring following the announcement of NHS England abolition. The Cheshire and Merseyside ICB is one of the most financially challenged ICBs nationally and is formally in financial turnaround, required to make cashable savings of approximately £170m with 50% administrative cost reductions. The ICB Place Director, who facilitated partnership working at borough level and supervised jointly funded positions, retired in June 2025. The council has yet to be engaged in arrangements to recruit a replacement, creating immediate governance risk.
findings.matters: Large-scale NHS savings requirements and ICB instability will likely shift costs to the council for services jointly funded with the NHS including Continuing Health Care, Section 117 aftercare, and SEND services. Loss of ICB Place Director during major health restructuring creates partnership governance risk at a critical time.
findings.figures: ICB requires £170m cashable savings; 50% administrative cost reduction; Place Director vacant since June 2025
findings.quote: Cheshire and Merseyside ICB is one of the most financially challenged ICBs in the country and is formally in financial turnaround and required to make cashable savings of approximately £170 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: Material funding issues remain within the High Needs funding block of the Dedicated Schools Grant, and the Delivering Better Value scheme has not resolved these deficits.
findings.detail: The council faces ongoing material funding deficits in the High Needs block of the DSG, which funds special education needs services. Cheshire East participated in the Delivering Better Value Scheme, a national programme designed to help councils address DSG deficits, but the council explicitly states that 'it is clear this will not resolve the material deficits in this area.' These unfunded liabilities continue to accumulate with no viable mitigation.
findings.matters: Material unfunded DSG deficits represent a growing liability that the council must eventually fund from general revenues or reserves. A failed mitigation strategy (Delivering Better Value) indicates the structural problem is intractable under current policy, consuming general fund resources indefinitely.
findings.figures: Material High Needs deficit; Delivering Better Value scheme will not resolve it
findings.quote: Material funding issues remain within the High Needs funding block in the DSG, and Cheshire East Council took part in the Delivering Better Value Scheme, although it is clear this will not resolve the material deficits in this area.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: The Section 151 Officer (Chief Finance Officer) was on interim arrangements throughout 2024/25, with permanent replacement only joining in June 2025.
findings.detail: The incumbent Section 151 Officer announced their departure in February 2024 and left in May 2024. An interim arrangement was put in place and continued throughout the entirety of 2024/25. A permanent Executive Director of Resources (Section 151) joined only in June 2025. This prolonged period of interim leadership in the critical finance role during a period of significant financial challenge, overspending, and governance weakness represents instability in the council's most senior finance position.
findings.matters: Prolonged interim arrangements in the Section 151 Officer role during a period of significant financial stress, overspending, and audit weakness indicates instability in the council's financial leadership and capacity precisely when strong, permanent finance leadership is most needed.
findings.figures: S151 departed May 2024; interim throughout 2024/25; permanent appointment June 2025
findings.quote: In February 2024, it was announced that the Section 151 Officer would be leaving the Council in May 2024. Subsequently, an Interim Section 151 Officer was appointed, and this arrangement continued during 2024/25

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: External Auditors were unable to obtain sufficient evidence to sign off the 2023/24 financial statements before the 28 February 2025 backstop date.
findings.detail: The External Auditor provided an interim report to the Audit and Governance Committee on 24 February 2025 confirming they had not been in a position to obtain sufficient evidence to conclude that the 2023/24 financial statements were free from material and pervasive misstatement before the backstop date. The auditor also received a number of objections to the 2023/24 financial statements which remained under consideration. The 2023/24 accounts therefore remain unsigned and unaudited.
findings.matters: Failure to obtain audit sign-off on financial statements indicates material audit risk and possible errors or uncertainties in the council's reported financial position, directly impairing financial reporting credibility.
findings.figures: Backstop date 28 February 2025; 2023/24 accounts remain unsigned
findings.quote: The External Auditor had not been in a position to obtain sufficient evidence to be able to conclude that the financial statements were free from material and pervasive misstatement before the backstop date of 28 February 2025.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: The council received a non-statutory Best Value Notice in May 2025 and is now required to provide formal quarterly updates to central government on improvement.
findings.detail: The Minister of State for Local Government and Devolution issued a non-statutory Best Value Notice on 8 May 2025. The council confirmed on 20 May 2025 that required actions align with its improvement plans and progress has been made, but acknowledged 'there is more to do'. The council is now required to provide formal quarterly updates with MHCLG to demonstrate progress against the areas for improvement identified in the Notice.
findings.matters: A Best Value Notice indicates central government has assessed the council as requiring intervention to meet its Best Value duty, representing a significant reputational and governance concern that directly affects lender confidence.
findings.figures: Notice issued 8 May 2025; quarterly reporting commenced
findings.quote: On 8 May 2025, the Council received a letter from Jim McMahon OBE MP, Minister of State for Local Government and Devolution issuing a non-statutory Best Value Notice.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: General level of reserves has been decreasing due to year-on-year overspends, partly driven by funding uncertainty and demand growth in services.
findings.detail: The council has set a legally balanced budget each February, but reserves have been drawn down to achieve this position, including reliance on one-off funding sources. In February 2024, the council had to include an in-principle capitalisation directive as part of exceptional financial support to achieve a balanced budget. This pattern of declining reserves significantly limits the council's financial resilience and ability to manage future shocks.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves to balance the budget year-on-year indicates structural unsustainability in the revenue budget and reduced financial resilience to absorb shocks or unexpected costs.
findings.figures: General level of reserves decreasing year-on-year
findings.quote: General level of reserves has been decreasing due to over-spends within financial years, partly driven by the uncertainty of future funding aligned with growth in demand lead services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: The council ran a service overspend of £9.8m in 2024/25 with a net overspend of £17.6m after setting aside reserves for transformation.
findings.detail: While outturn figures for 2024/25 showed an improvement of £8.5m on the Third Financial Review position, the underlying service overspend of £9.8m remains a significant financial challenge. After setting aside £7.8m in proposed transfers to useable reserves (including resources for transformation and improvement activity), the net overspend reaches £17.6m. This continues a pattern of year-on-year overspends partly driven by funding uncertainty and demand growth.
findings.matters: Recurring year-on-year overspends of this magnitude, even after using reserves and one-off funding sources, indicate the council cannot balance its recurrent budget and is consuming financial resources unsustainably.
findings.figures: Service overspend £9.8m; net overspend £17.6m; proposed reserve transfers £7.8m
findings.quote: The outturn position, net of proposed transfers to useable reserves of £7.8m, is an overspend of £17.6m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Draft Annual Governance Statement 2024-25 , item 22.
findings.headline: Internal Audit has given a 'Limited' opinion on the Council's governance framework for the second consecutive year, the first time this has occurred since 2009.
findings.detail: The Head of Audit and Risk Management assessed the council's framework of risk management, control and governance as 'Limited' for 2024/25. This reflects a significant number of findings related to failure to apply existing controls or weaknesses in control design. While appropriate engagement with Internal Audit has occurred across the organisation, the 'Limited' opinion contributes to the significant governance issue identified as 'Governance and Internal Control'.
findings.matters: A 'Limited' audit opinion indicates material weaknesses in systems of control and risk management, signalling elevated financial and governance risk to lenders.
findings.figures: First 'Limited' opinion since 2009; also 'Limited' in prior year 2023/24
findings.quote: The Council's framework of risk management, control and governance is assessed as Limited for 2024/25

findings.paper_title: extract from Annex 1 Final Outturn 2024 25 , item 30.
findings.headline: Core Schools Budget Grant explicitly allocated to cover 2024 teacher pay award costs.
findings.detail: The £2.5m Core Schools Budget Grant from the Education and Skills Funding Agency is identified as supporting schools' overall costs 'in particular following confirmation of the 2024 teacher pay award'. This indicates teacher pay settlement impacts are a material cost factor requiring specific grant funding.
findings.matters: Recurring cost pressures from public sector pay settlements affect schools budget sustainability and wider council budget planning.
findings.quote: This grant is from the Education and Skills Funding Agency and is to support schools with their overall costs in the 2024 to 2025 financial year, in particular following confirmation of the 2024 teacher pay award.

findings.paper_title: extract from Annex 1 Final Outturn 2024 25 , item 30.
findings.headline: High Needs Capital Grant confirmed at £5.96m, nearly three times the provisional budget of £2m for 2025-26.
findings.detail: The High Needs Capital Grant for 2025-26 has been confirmed at £5,955,824, compared to the provisional amount of £2,000,000 included in the MTFS. This represents a supplementary capital estimate of £3,955,823 and reflects confirmed allocations from the Department for Education for special educational needs capital expenditure.
findings.matters: A nearly threefold increase to High Needs capital spending signals either significantly increased demand for SEND provision or a substantial change to the council's planned capital commitments, both of which affect borrowing needs and financial planning.
findings.figures: Provisional: £2,000,000; Confirmed: £5,955,824; SCE requested: £3,955,823
findings.quote: A provisional amount of £2,000,000 was included within the MTFS for High Needs Capital Grant. The 2025-26 allocation has now been confirmed as £5,955,824.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from Finance Sub Committee: Final Outturn 2024-25 - Approval of Supplementary Revenue Estimates and Capital Estimates
findings.headline: Capital programme severely underspent: only £88.4m of £215.8m approved budget used (59% variance)
findings.detail: Cheshire East spent £88.4m on capital projects against an approved capital programme of £215.8m in 2024-25, representing a 59% variance and spending only 41% of planned capital budget. This substantial underspend suggests either capital projects are not being delivered, budgets were unrealistic, or there are implementation barriers preventing project execution.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether a council can execute its capital plan. Large underspends suggest forecasting issues, project delivery problems, or changing priorities, all of which affect the council's infrastructure investment capability.
findings.figures: £88.4m actual capital spending, £215.8m approved programme, 59% variance
findings.quote: Capital Spending of £88.4m against an approved programme of £215.8m (59% variance).

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from Finance Sub Committee: Final Outturn 2024-25 - Approval of Supplementary Revenue Estimates and Capital Estimates
findings.headline: Significant cost pressures in Adult and Children's services persist as primary driver of overspend
findings.detail: The Finance Sub Committee noted that 'significant cost pressures in both Adults and Children's services remained a key issue.' These social care services are the primary cause of the council's £9.8m overspend. While the council improved its position by £18.3m from the previous quarter review, cost pressures in these areas persist, suggesting structural demographic or service demand challenges will continue.
findings.matters: Social care cost pressures are notoriously difficult to control and often reflect demographics outside the council's direct control, suggesting budget challenges will persist and recur.
findings.figures: No specific figures for these services disclosed; described as source of 'significant cost pressures' accounting for material portion of £9.8m adverse variance
findings.quote: It was noted that significant cost pressures in both Adults and Children's services remained a key issue.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from Finance Sub Committee: Final Outturn 2024-25 - Approval of Supplementary Revenue Estimates and Capital Estimates
findings.headline: Council's reserves remain inadequate for financial resilience despite £7.8m emergency borrowing to build them
findings.detail: The council proposed to increase reserves by £7.8m using money from the same emergency borrowing used to cover operational overspend (£5.3m for Change Reserves and £2.5m for General Fund Reserves). However, the report explicitly states reserves remain 'not at an adequate level' and that 'the issue of financial sustainability remained a key risk.' External auditors independently flagged reserve inadequacy as a key risk. The council's General Reserves closing balance is £6.3m.
findings.matters: Inadequate reserves limit a council's ability to absorb unexpected cost pressures or income shortfalls. External auditor concern about this is a significant governance risk flag for lending decisions.
findings.figures: £7.8m total added to reserves, £5.3m Change Reserves, £2.5m General Fund Reserves, £6.3m closing General Reserves balance
findings.quote: However, the reserves were still not at an adequate level and the issue of financial sustainability remained a key risk. This had also been highlighted as a key risk by the External Auditors.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from Finance Sub Committee: Final Outturn 2024-25 - Approval of Supplementary Revenue Estimates and Capital Estimates
findings.headline: Council required £17.6m emergency borrowing through Exceptional Financial Support to cover £9.8m revenue overspend
findings.detail: Prior to emergency support, Cheshire East recorded an adverse variance of £9.8m on 2024-25 service outturn. The council's net revenue overspend of £17.6m (4.8% of revised budget of £365.8m) was fully funded through conditional Exceptional Financial Support via borrowing. This means the council cannot balance its operational budget from normal income and relies on emergency borrowing capacity to continue operations.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can operate sustainably from its own income. Reliance on emergency borrowing to cover revenue shortfalls indicates structural budget problems that threaten long-term financial viability.
findings.figures: £9.8m adverse variance, £17.6m net revenue overspend, £365.8m revised budget, 4.86% PWLB interest rate on EFS
findings.quote: The committee noted that, prior to the application of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) and a proposed £7.8m transfer to reserves, the 2024-25 service outturn position was an adverse variance of £9.8m

findings.paper_title: Officer Decision re Funding for Phase 3 of the Transformation Programme
findings.headline: Audit report on officer decision-making procedures is underway following identified procedural weaknesses
findings.detail: The procedural errors in this ODR2 are not isolated. Similar issues have previously been identified, leading to a recent review of Officer Decision making procedures. An audit report on these systemic issues is in the process of being finalised.
findings.matters: Continuing procedural failures in financial decision-making suggest systemic governance weaknesses that could affect the integrity of other financial decisions and control environments
findings.figures: Not disclosed
findings.quote: Similar issues were previously identified leading to a recent review of the Officer Decision making procedures. An audit report is in the process of being finalised and will be reported to Audit and Governance Committee in due course.

findings.paper_title: Officer Decision re Funding for Phase 3 of the Transformation Programme
findings.headline: Transformation programme is essential to addressing a four-year £100m funding gap, and is already subject to external scrutiny
findings.detail: The transformation programme is designed to contribute to savings required to address a £100m funding gap across 2024/25 to 2028/29. The council explicitly identifies Financial Sustainability as a critical improvement item referenced in both the Corporate Peer Challenge and the Best Value Notice.
findings.matters: The council faces substantial structural funding pressures and is already operating under external scrutiny; failure to fund the transformation could cascade into wider financial difficulties
findings.figures: 4-year funding gap of £100m; transformation allocation £3.5m
findings.quote: Financial Sustainability is a key plank of the Transformation Programme. It is referenced as a critical improvement item in both the Corporate Peer Challenge and the Best Value Notice.

findings.paper_title: Officer Decision re Funding for Phase 3 of the Transformation Programme
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer has signalled that rejecting the virement could trigger a Section 114 notice
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer advises that Council approval of the reserves virement is necessary to allow transformation to continue. The officer explicitly warns that disregarding this advice places the council at risk of the budget ceasing to balance by law, which would require issuing a Section 114 notice.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals severe financial distress and is a major indicator to external parties (including lenders) of serious financial management problems
findings.figures: £3.5m virement required
findings.quote: To disregard this advice places the Council at risk of the budget no longer balancing by law and therefore requiring the Section 151 Officer to issue a Section 114 notice.

findings.paper_title: Joint Ltr to MHCLG Housing Targets , item 34.
findings.headline: SEND school funding decision at Sandbach 'significantly overdue' with no commitment; council states this is 'failing our SEND learners'.
findings.detail: The council reports it has written to Ministers about a SEND school project at the former Westfield site in Sandbach. The funding decision remains undetermined and 'significantly overdue'. The council explicitly states this is 'failing our SEND learners', indicating it is a priority unmet need.
findings.matters: A delayed capital project with unresolved government funding may eventually require local funding from reserves or borrowing; it also signals delivery risk on education provision.
findings.figures: One SEND school project at Sandbach
findings.quote: we recently wrote to Ministers McMahon / Phillipson about the lack of progress determining the funding to deliver a SEND school at the former Westfield site in Sandbach, a decision that is now significantly overdue, and one that is failing our SEND learners.

findings.paper_title: Joint Ltr to MHCLG Housing Targets , item 34.
findings.headline: Health care, drainage, and school capacity already under strain with no identified co-funding plan for infrastructure to support 166% increase in housing.
findings.detail: The council states health care is 'already under strain' and 'will struggle to cope' without new GP surgeries and walk-in centres. It flags drainage as critical to manage flooding risk and states it 'needs a clear drainage and infrastructure management plan in place ahead of increasing the delivery'. School places, particularly SEND, are insufficient.
findings.matters: If the council must fund major infrastructure to support housing growth, this directly affects its financial capacity and may require borrowing or reserve drawdown to fill funding gaps.
findings.figures: 2,603 homes per annum target vs. existing infrastructure capacity
findings.quote: Our local health care system and support. This is already under strain, and without national policies to bring forward new GP surgeries and health care walk in centres, the current infrastructure will struggle to cope.

findings.paper_title: Joint Ltr to MHCLG Housing Targets , item 34.
findings.headline: Housing target increased 166% to 2,603 units per annum; council requests 'incremental ramping up' period, indicating immediate delivery risk.
findings.detail: The council's annual housing target has been raised from 977 to 2,603 units per annum under the new standard method. The council explicitly requests an 'incremental ramping up or leading in period from the current 2,603 units pa to a jointly agreed new target', signalling it does not expect to deliver the full target immediately.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that growth plans are achievable; a 166% target increase with the council requesting a phase-in period indicates execution constraints and potential pressure on delivery.
findings.figures: 2,603 units pa (new target), 977 units pa (previous requirement), 166% increase
findings.quote: A 166% increase on the previous requirement of 977 per annum.

findings.paper_title: Service Budgets 2025-26 Finance Sub Committee , item 13.
findings.headline: Inflationary pressures in major social care budgets forcing immediate contingency use
findings.detail: Children's and Adults' services cannot absorb inflationary pressures from National Living Wage and National Insurance within their existing budgets. The council must immediately vire £0.7m to Children and £8m to Adults from central contingency. These are the council's two largest service budgets (£97.3m and £159.4m respectively), yet they are calling for contingency support within the first financial review cycle. This signals demand-side pressures are embedded and will recur annually.
findings.matters: Social care inflation is structural, not cyclical. Early contingency depletion to cover foreseeable wage inflation indicates future year budgets may also be inadequate, increasing default risk over the medium term.
findings.figures: £0.7m virement to Children and Families; £8m virement to Adults and Health; total £8.7m unplanned use of contingency
findings.quote: Recommendations 2 and 3 in this report request approval from the Finance Sub Committee to vire values from the Contingency budget to the service budgets, these requests are linked to proposed fee increases to providers.

findings.paper_title: Service Budgets 2025-26 Finance Sub Committee , item 13.
findings.headline: Capital programme requires significant borrowing; council actively trying to reduce it
findings.detail: Cheshire East has a four-year capital programme of approximately £0.6bn requiring substantial borrowing. The document states 'there remains a significant amount of borrowing required to fund the programme in 2025/26' and notes that the Capital Programme Board is undertaking review 'with a view to reducing the revenue cost impact.' This language indicates borrowing is at uncomfortable levels and the council is scrambling to reduce it.
findings.matters: High capital borrowing increases future revenue costs for debt service, constraining budget flexibility. Active efforts to reduce borrowing suggest the council recognizes unsustainable leverage.
findings.figures: Capital programme £0.6bn over four years; 2025/26 capital budget £173.077m; significant amount requiring borrowing
findings.quote: There remains a significant amount of borrowing required to fund the programme in 2025/26 and the Capital Programme Board will provide review of and challenge to projects with a view to reducing the revenue cost impact.

findings.paper_title: Service Budgets 2025-26 Finance Sub Committee , item 13.
findings.headline: Earmarked reserves being consolidated into general fund to cover existing deficits
findings.detail: Cheshire East is transferring money out of earmarked reserves (funds designated for specific purposes) into general reserves to plug current-year shortfalls. Earmarked reserves are forecast to drop from £11.539m to £9.386m in 2025/26. The document explicitly states these transfers are 'to support the forecast deficit position.' This is a one-time liquidity measure, not a structural fix.
findings.matters: Lenders look at reserves as a buffer against shocks and unforeseen costs. Converting designated reserves into operating cash reserves to cover recurring deficits indicates the council is burning through its safety margin.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves declining £2.153m from £11.539m to £9.386m; general reserves increasing from £3.696m to £5.0m
findings.quote: All remaining Earmarked reserves, excluding those held for ring-fenced purposes or forecast for use in 2025/26, are being transferred into the General Fund reserve during 2024/25 to support the forecast deficit position.

findings.paper_title: Service Budgets 2025-26 Finance Sub Committee , item 13.
findings.headline: £13.452m of transformation savings (55% of total) remain unallocated and still being designed
findings.detail: The council approved £24.4m of net transformation savings for 2025/26. However, £13.452m of this (over half) is held centrally as 'Council wide cross cutting savings' with no finalized delivery plan. The document states this work is 'continuing to refine how these savings will be delivered in detail.' If these savings do not land, there is no backup funding source and the budget will overspend.
findings.matters: Lenders evaluate whether savings plans are concrete or aspirational. Unallocated savings at this stage of the financial year present material risk of budget outturn failure and suggest weak financial control.
findings.figures: £13.452m unallocated of £24.4m total transformation savings; 19 transformation projects delivering the savings
findings.quote: Within this total budget saving, there are £13.452m of Council wide cross cutting savings which are held centrally; work is continuing to refine how these savings will be delivered in detail and these savings will be allocated to service committee budgets as soon as possible.

findings.paper_title: Service Budgets 2025-26 Finance Sub Committee , item 13.
findings.headline: Council requires £25.3m Exceptional Financial Support to balance 2025/26 budget
findings.detail: Cheshire East cannot balance its budget from normal resources. The 2025/26 budget of £427.6m is only covered by £402.4m in council tax, business rates and government grants. The £25.3m gap is closed using Exceptional Financial Support from government. This is effectively a bailout—the council's structural spending exceeds its revenue capacity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if a council can sustain itself on its own revenue base. Dependence on exceptional support signals underlying structural imbalance that could worsen if economic conditions change or government support is withdrawn.
findings.figures: £25.3m Exceptional Financial Support against total budget of £427.6m; normal funding of £402.4m covers 94% of need
findings.quote: The 2025/26 budget was approved at full Council in February 2025 including the use of up to £25.3m of Exceptional Financial Support to balance the overall budget, as expenditure outweighed the income forecast.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: Committee asked to assess whether resource constraints limit audit scope
findings.detail: The Committee is explicitly asked to consider whether the level of internal audit resources limits the scope of audit work or prejudices the ability to deliver assurance in line with professional standards. The plan is based on current resources, with acknowledgment that additional specialist capacity may be required.
findings.matters: If internal audit lacks sufficient capacity to deliver comprehensive assurance over governance and controls, this creates a gap in the control framework that affects the reliability of the governance statement and financial oversight.
findings.figures: Plan based on current resource levels; additional specialist support may be required during the year
findings.quote: Level of resources in any way limits the scope of Internal Audit or prejudices the ability to deliver a service consistent with the PSIAS.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Plan 2025-26
findings.headline: Internal Audit leadership posts remain vacant and filled through acting arrangements
findings.detail: The Internal Audit Manager role is filled by a Principal Auditor acting up on a longstanding basis. A Principal Auditor vacancy is also being filled by a Senior Auditor acting up. The substantive posts for both positions remain unfilled. The total Internal Audit team is 6.3 FTE.
findings.matters: Sustained vacancies in audit leadership undermine the independence, stability and effectiveness of internal audit — a critical control that lenders rely on to assess governance quality and the control environment.
findings.figures: 6.3 FTE team; Internal Audit Manager (acting up), 1 Principal Auditor (acting up), 3 Senior Auditors, 2 Auditors; 2 substantive posts vacant
findings.quote: The Internal Audit Manager post continues to be filled through a longstanding acting up arrangement by a Principal Auditor. A Principal Auditor vacancy also continues to be filled through an acting up arrangement by a Senior Auditor. The substantive Principal Auditor and Senior Auditor posts remain vacant

findings.paper_title: Companies Audited Financial Statements, External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023/2024
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s123745/Companies Audited Financial Statements External Audit Findings and Action Plan 20232024 Decision R.pdf
findings.headline: Ansa and Orbitas stopped holding annual shareholder meetings in December 2020; governance restored only in June 2024.
findings.detail: The council waived the AGM requirement for both subsidiary companies in December 2020. For over three years, accounts were reported to Audit Committees and Boards but without formal shareholder approval. In June 2024, governance changes now route reporting through Boards with external auditor (Grant Thornton) attendance.
findings.matters: A lender would view this as a control gap showing the council failed to exercise formal shareholder oversight of its subsidiaries for years; the recent fix is positive but the gap is concerning.
findings.figures: 2020-2024 (over three years without AGMs)
findings.quote: Ansa Environmental Services Ltd and Orbitas Bereavement Services Ltd have not been holding AGMs since a decision was taken in December 2020 by the then Director of Place to waive this requirement.

findings.paper_title: Certification of Housing Benefit Subsidy Claim and Teachers Pensions Return 2023-24
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s123735/Certification of Housing Benefit Subsidy Claim and Teachers Pensions Return 202324.pdf
findings.headline: Two audit exceptions identified in Teachers' Pension End of Year Certificate with acknowledged financial liability risk
findings.detail: The external auditor identified two exceptions in the 2023-24 Teachers' Pension EOYC. The council discussed these with Transactional Services managers and states corrections will be made. Teachers' Pensions processing is handled by a shared service hosted by Cheshire West and Chester Council. The Risk Management section explicitly flags that findings 'relate to a position where the Council may not meet the requirements of the certification process and a financial liability is incurred.'
findings.matters: Exceptions in pension contribution reporting indicate control weaknesses in payroll administration and create acknowledged financial exposure for the council.
findings.figures: two exceptions
findings.quote: Two exceptions were noted, the issues were discussed with managers within Transactional Services in order to resolve the problems and to prevent re-occurrence. Corrections will be made and notified to Teachers' Pensions as necessary.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C for Companies Audited Financial Statements, External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023/2024 , item 69.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s123748/Appendix C for Companies Audited Financial Statements External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023.pdf
findings.headline: Significant deficiencies identified in IT controls for Unit 4 ERP system covering security, technology acquisition, and infrastructure
findings.detail: The audit identified significant deficiencies in IT General Controls relevant to financial reporting within the Unit 4 ERP system's security management, technology acquisition/development/maintenance, and technology infrastructure. Despite these deficiencies, auditors issued a clean opinion on the current year financial statements.
findings.matters: IT control deficiencies in financial reporting systems indicate control gaps that could affect data reliability, even though not material in the current year; a lender would want to understand whether these strengthen before absorbing the company's records into the council
findings.figures: Three ITGC control areas flagged: security management, technology acquisition/development/maintenance, technology infrastructure
findings.quote: Significant deficiencies identified in IT controls relevant to the audit of financial statements

findings.paper_title: Appendix C for Companies Audited Financial Statements, External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023/2024 , item 69.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s123748/Appendix C for Companies Audited Financial Statements External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023.pdf
findings.headline: Cheshire East has decided to bring Orbitas Bereavement Services back in-house and cease it as a separate entity by 31 March 2025, triggering non-going concern accounting
findings.detail: The Council Finance Committee decided on 25 June 2024 to bring Orbitas back in-house by 31 March 2025. The company has begun transitioning operations, expected to complete by 1 April 2025. Management correctly prepared the accounts on a non-going concern basis, with assets and liabilities to transfer to the council at Net Book Value.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how the council's asset base will change as this subsidiary is absorbed and whether the operational consolidation affects the council's financial management or borrowing capacity
findings.figures: 31 March 2025 completion date; decision made 25 June 2024
findings.quote: on 25th June 2024 the Council Finance Committee made the decision to bring services provided by Ansa Environmental Services Limited and Orbitas Bereavement Services Limited back in house by 31 March 2025

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Companies Audited Financial Statements, External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023/2024 , item 69.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s123746/Appendix A for Companies Audited Financial Statements External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023.pdf
findings.headline: ANSA has incomplete VAT accruals due to invoices not yet physically delivered; this issue was re-raised in FY24
findings.detail: The auditor found multiple invoices dated before year-end but not yet invoiced by suppliers, resulting in incomplete accrued expenses and VAT recoverable not being recorded. This control point has been re-raised in FY24. Management responded that this accounting treatment is consistent with wider council (CEC) practice.
findings.matters: Incomplete accruals directly affect the council's balance sheet and cash position, which a lender would consider when assessing borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Re-raised in FY24
findings.quote: From the testing performed during the course of our audit work, it was noted that multiple invoices dated pre year end but not yet invoiced (i.e. physically delivered) by suppliers resulted in incomplete accrued expenses and VAT recoverable. This control point has been re-raised in FY24.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Companies Audited Financial Statements, External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023/2024 , item 69.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s123746/Appendix A for Companies Audited Financial Statements External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023.pdf
findings.headline: ANSA's headcount report has not been reconciling and this issue was re-raised in FY24
findings.detail: The auditor found that ANSA's headcount report was not appropriate and did not reconcile when adjusted for employee starters and leavers. This control issue has been re-raised in FY24, indicating it remains unresolved. Management is implementing monthly reconciliation procedures.
findings.matters: Payroll is typically the largest council cost; headcount reconciliation is a fundamental control over payroll accuracy and fraud prevention.
findings.figures: Re-raised in FY24
findings.quote: While performing the audit, it was noted that the headcount report was not appropriate. However, this was not reconciling and hence we continue to raise this matter. This control point has been re-raised in FY24.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Companies Audited Financial Statements, External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023/2024 , item 69.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s123746/Appendix A for Companies Audited Financial Statements External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023.pdf
findings.headline: ANSA had property, plant and equipment with negative net book values due to over-depreciation
findings.detail: The fixed asset register contained items held at negative net book value, indicating they had been depreciated beyond their original cost. This risks understating asset values and overstating future gains or losses on disposal. The issue is being resolved when ANSA insources to the council on 1.4.2025.
findings.matters: Incorrect asset valuation affects the balance sheet and financial metrics used in lending assessments.
findings.quote: On review of the PPE register, we noted that there were items held at a negative net book value (NBV). This indicates that they have been depreciated beyond their original cost. There is therefore a risk that the entity's asset values are understated.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A for Companies Audited Financial Statements, External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023/2024 , item 69.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s123746/Appendix A for Companies Audited Financial Statements External Audit Findings and Action Plan 2023.pdf
findings.headline: Revenue recognition controls lack supporting documentation in both ANSA and Orbitas; this issue was re-raised in FY24
findings.detail: The auditor found a lack of evidence demonstrating performance obligations were met for waste collection and other income in both companies. While the auditor performed alternative procedures to satisfy themselves, this control point has been re-raised in FY24, indicating the control weakness persists unresolved.
findings.matters: Revenue recognition is fundamental to financial reporting; a recurring control weakness affecting multiple council companies suggests the control environment may not be robust.
findings.figures: Re-raised in FY24
findings.quote: There is a lack of evidence that demonstrates where the entity has carried out its performance obligation for waste collection and other income. There is a risk revenue is recognised too early or when the service did not occur.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Internal Audit Plan 25-26 , item 72.
findings.headline: SEND and Dedicated School Grant management identified as areas of 'significant financial resilience challenges' requiring a recovery plan
findings.detail: The audit plan identifies DSG and SEND as areas where the council is 'continuing to make progress in managing those areas which offer significant financial resilience challenges'. Planned audits will 'review progress made against the recovery plan and its achievability moving forward'. The need for a recovery plan indicates DSG deficit, and audit emphasis on 'achievability' signals doubt whether the plan will succeed.
findings.matters: Dedicated School Grant deficits are structural funding shortfalls councils must cover from general reserves. An unachievable recovery plan means permanent drain on council reserves and reduced financial resilience for other council services.
findings.figures: No specific deficit amounts quantified
findings.quote: Assurance around the Council continuing to make progress in managing those areas which offer significant financial resilience challenges, including transformation, SEND and the DSG High Needs Management Plan

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Internal Audit Plan 25-26 , item 72.
findings.headline: Finance and governance leadership positions are held on interim or acting basis with substantive posts vacant
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer (chief finance officer) and Governance, Compliance and Monitoring Officer are in interim/acting roles. The Internal Audit Manager and Principal Auditor positions are also filled through 'longstanding acting up arrangements' with substantive posts remaining vacant. Multiple interim/acting arrangements across finance and governance leadership increases organizational risk.
findings.matters: Interim leadership in critical finance roles signals recruitment difficulties, recent departures, or organizational instability. Lenders require permanent, accountable leadership with demonstrable long-term commitment to financial stewardship.
findings.figures: Internal Audit team: 6.3 FTE with substantive Principal Auditor and Senior Auditor posts vacant
findings.quote: assurance work in this area is reported to the Acting Governance, Compliance and Monitoring Officer or Interim Executive Director of Resources, Section 151 Officer

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Internal Audit Plan 25-26 , item 72.
findings.headline: External auditors faced limitations completing work on the 2023/24 statement of accounts
findings.detail: The council's external auditors were unable to complete normal audit procedures on the 2023/24 financial statements. Internal Audit is providing continued assurance on key financial systems following the introduction of Unit 4 (the council's new ERP system). These audit limitations prevented standard sign-off and suggest either system defects or data integrity issues.
findings.matters: If external auditors cannot complete normal procedures, the reliability of the financial statements is in question. Lenders depend on audited accounts to assess council finances accurately. Audit limitations raise questions about hidden problems.
findings.figures: No specific amounts quantified
findings.quote: Continued assurance around the operation of Key Financial Systems since the introduction of Unit 4, and the limitations of work able to be undertaken by the Council's external auditors on the 2023/24 Statement of accounts

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Internal Audit Plan 25-26 , item 72.
findings.headline: Section 106 (developer contributions) management received a 'No Assurance' audit opinion in 2023/24, the lowest possible rating
findings.detail: The council's management of section 106 developer contributions received a 'No Assurance' opinion in 2023/24, the lowest audit opinion rating indicating the control environment was not providing reasonable assurance that risks were being managed. This reflects material control failures. A full-year audit follow-up is planned for 2025/26 to assess whether control weaknesses have been remedied.
findings.matters: Section 106 contributions fund critical local infrastructure. 'No Assurance' opinions indicate material control failures where funds could be misallocated, delayed, or lost.
findings.figures: No specific amounts quantified
findings.quote: To provide assurance that the systems and processes in place to manage s106 agreements are embedded and effective following the No Assurance audit report issued in 2023/24.

findings.paper_title: Reporting of Urgent Decisions taken by the Chief Executive
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer directed to seek 5% above-standard Council Tax referendum limit for 2025/26
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer is instructed to make a formal submission to the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government seeking authority for the Council Tax referendum limit to be increased by an additional 5% above the standard amount for 2025/26 only. The paper does not explain the reason for this request.
findings.matters: A council seeking above-standard council tax increases signals additional revenue pressure or planned major expenditure, both material to lending risk assessment.
findings.figures: 5% increase above standard amount
findings.quote: seeks authority for the Council Tax referendum limit for Cheshire East Council to be increased by an additional 5% above the standard amount for 2025/26 only

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from the Appointments Committee: Appointment of the Executive Director Resources (S151)
findings.headline: Governance Officer recruitment abandoned after interview stage
findings.detail: After receiving 5 applications for the Governance, Compliance and Monitoring Officer role and progressing one candidate to formal interview on 12-13 February, the Appointments Committee decided not to proceed with appointment. Temporary acting arrangements will continue, with recruitment to recommence in March 2025.
findings.matters: The Governance, Compliance and Monitoring Officer is a statutory designated officer role responsible for legal compliance and governance controls. Leaving it vacant with temporary acting arrangements represents a control weakness.
findings.figures: 5 applications received; 1 candidate interviewed
findings.quote: The Appointments Committee decided not to proceed with the appointment to the role of Governance, Compliance and Monitoring Officer.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from the Appointments Committee: Appointment of the Executive Director Resources (S151)
findings.headline: Experienced finance leader appointed as Chief Finance Officer
findings.detail: Ashley Hughes has been appointed as Executive Director Resources (S151) at an annual salary of £142,951. He brings extensive experience as Director of Resources at Tameside MBC since 2023, Deputy S151 at Barnet (2020-2023), and Head of Finance at Westminster and Kensington & Chelsea councils (2018-2020) managing budgets exceeding £200 million.
findings.matters: The S151 is the council's statutory chief finance officer responsible for financial management and control. Their experience and competence directly affect the council's financial governance.
findings.figures: £142,951 annual salary; budgets exceeding £200 million
findings.quote: Ashley Hughes be appointed as Cheshire East Council's Executive Director Resources (s151) as the Chief Finance Officer at an annual salary of £142,951

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from Corporate Policy Committee: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: Change to Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) accounting policy, effective 1 April 2024
findings.detail: The council is implementing a change to how it accounts for debt repayment (MRP policy), with effect backdated to 1 April 2024. The effects are reflected in the 2025/26 MTFS. The specific details of the policy change are not disclosed in this extract, so it is unclear whether this reduces or increases the council's prudent provision for debt repayment.
findings.matters: MRP policy changes can materially affect the council's published financial position. A change with retrospective effect (April 2024) raises questions about whether this improves the council's position or merely masks underlying pressures.
findings.figures: Effective date: 1 April 2024; reflected in 2025/26 MTFS
findings.quote: which includes a change in the MRP Policy, with effect from 1 April 2024

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from Corporate Policy Committee: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: Council tax is being increased by 4.99%, just below the referendum threshold
findings.detail: The council is increasing B and D band council tax by 4.99%, which includes 2% ringfenced for Adult Social Care. This is the maximum permissible increase without triggering a local referendum. The increase is necessary to help balance the budget.
findings.matters: A council pushing council tax to the referendum threshold while running low reserves and needing to borrow £25m signals financial stress. It also indicates limited room for further tax rises, which narrows the council's options for addressing future shortfalls.
findings.figures: 4.99% increase; B and D band council tax £1,882.04
findings.quote: Approve the setting of B and D Council Tax of £1,882.04 representing an increase of 4.99%. This is below the referendum limit (including 2% ringfenced for Adult Social Care)

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from Corporate Policy Committee: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: Budget relies on £72m of transformation savings that have not yet been delivered
findings.detail: The council's MTFS assumes gross transformation savings of £72m over the four-year period, with £10.8m allocated to digital programmes to support delivery. The committee noted that transformation costs and savings are being accounted for within individual service areas, but the total quantum (£72m) is substantial and the track record of councils delivering transformation savings is mixed.
findings.matters: If transformation savings do not materialise at pace, the council will need to find alternative sources of funding (more borrowing, more council tax, or service cuts). A lender needs confidence that savings are real and likely to land.
findings.figures: £72m estimated transformation savings over the MTFS; £10.8m for digital programmes
findings.quote: the gross transformation savings were estimated to be in the region of £72m over the period of the MTFS and that the £10.8m for digital programmes would help support and deliver on some transformation savings.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from Corporate Policy Committee: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: Reserves are at a low level and flagged by the Section 151 Officer as a significant risk
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer (Chief Finance Officer) has identified that the council's reserves are low and flagged this as a significant risk that needs urgent attention. The committee agreed and noted that 'robust management of the budget was critical.' The Reserves Strategy sets out how reserves might be built up over the MTFS period, but the current position is a concern.
findings.matters: Reserves are a council's shock absorber. Low reserves mean the council has little buffer for unexpected costs or income shocks, and signals weak financial management or prior overspending. A lender sees this as material default risk.
findings.figures: Specific reserve levels not disclosed in this extract
findings.quote: The low level of reserves was highlighted within the report as a significant risk that needed to be addressed urgently.

findings.paper_title: Recommendations from Corporate Policy Committee: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: Council must borrow £25.3m to balance the 2025/26 budget
findings.detail: The council cannot balance its revenue budget without using £25.3m of conditional Flexible Finance Support (a borrowing mechanism). This is not a one-off; the need for Flexible Finance Support to balance a budget signals structural deficit. The council is also increasing its use of Flexible Capital Receipts (which are effectively borrowing against future asset sales) from £1m to £1.518m in 2024/25.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can balance its budget from its own resources. Reliance on borrowing to plug a revenue gap in a single year raises questions about whether the council has identified the same savings recurring councils are finding, or whether it is behind the curve.
findings.figures: £25.3m conditional EFS; £1.518m Flexible Capital Receipts (increase of £0.518m from £1m)
findings.quote: Approve the utilisation of up to £25.3m conditional EFS (Capitalisation Direction) via borrowing to balance the 2025/26 budget shortfall

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: External assurance review by CIPFA completed with recommendations the council must implement
findings.detail: Following the in-principle support agreed in February 2024, the government commissioned an external assurance review by the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA). The review has been completed and identified recommendations that the council is required to implement, though the details have not yet been published.
findings.matters: An external assurance review indicates the government identified governance, management or financial control weaknesses, and the council must remediate these as a condition of continued support.
findings.figures: CIPFA review following February 2024 in-principle support
findings.quote: I would be grateful if you could begin or continue to take steps to implement the review's recommendations.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: Capitalisation directions impose 20-year asset life cap on MRP charges, constraining the council's flexibility
findings.detail: Any capitalisation direction will require the council to charge annual MRP using asset life method with a maximum proxy asset life of 20 years. This is a constraint imposed by government, suggesting it has concerns about how the council would otherwise manage the capitalised debt.
findings.matters: Government-imposed constraints on how the council can spread repayments indicate lack of confidence in the council's financial management and restrict the council's ability to manage its own debt profile.
findings.figures: 20-year maximum asset life
findings.quote: Where expenditure is capitalised, the authority shall charge annual MRP using the asset life method with a proxy 'asset life' of no more than 20 years.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support is capitalisation (borrowing) not cash grant, creating future repayment costs
findings.detail: The letter explicitly states the support 'does not come in the form of cash' and 'brings additional costs to following years'. The council must charge annual Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) on any capitalised expenditure, meaning future budgets bear the repayment cost.
findings.matters: The council is not receiving a grant to solve its structural deficit; instead it is accumulating debt that must be repaid, meaning the underlying budget problem remains and worsens with MRP charges.
findings.figures: £25.3m capitalisation plus £17.6m for prior year
findings.quote: While this reduces the immediate pressures in the short-term, the support is not in the form of cash, it does bring additional costs to following years, as set out in the council's draft medium-term financial strategy 2025 to 2029.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: Previous year's EFS for 2024-25 increased from £6m to £17.6m, indicating worsening position
findings.detail: The council's revised EFS for 2024-25 has been increased from the originally approved £6m to £17.6m. This revised amount covers the council's forecast funding shortfall in 2024-25. The upward revision suggests the council's financial position deteriorated.
findings.matters: Escalating EFS requirements across consecutive years suggest structural budget problems rather than one-off pressures, and point to deteriorating financial management or demand-driven deficits.
findings.figures: £6m revised to £17.6m for 2024-25; £25.3m for 2025-26
findings.quote: The Deputy Prime Minister is also minded to approve a revision to the previously agreed in-principle capitalisation direction of £6 million to £17.6 million for 2024-25.

findings.paper_title: Item 7 Medium Term Financial Strategy 2025/26-2028/29
findings.headline: Council requires £25.3m in Exceptional Financial Support to balance 2025/26 budget
findings.detail: The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government has approved in principle Exceptional Financial Support of £25.3m for 2025/26. This matches the assumptions in the council's MTFS. The support is essential to close the council's budget shortfall.
findings.matters: A council dependent on government bailout support to balance its budget signals unmanageable structural financial problems and reputational fragility relevant to any lending decision.
findings.quote: The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) confirmed in principle Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) up to £25.3m, to balance the budget shortfall for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Council Tax Statutory Resolution
findings.headline: Minimal government grant (£0.8m) means financial viability depends on council tax collection and growth in the tax base.
findings.detail: The council's general government grant for 2025/26 is £0.8m, while its Council Tax Requirement is £307.3m. This represents 99.7% dependency on council tax revenue. The council's stated strategy is pursuing 'economic independence from government grant', requiring growth in the local tax base to fund service demand and inflation.
findings.matters: A lender assesses resilience by examining funding diversification. Heavy reliance on council tax means the council is exposed to collection risk and property valuation changes. Economic downturn or demographic shifts affecting the tax base could quickly create financial stress.
findings.figures: £0.8m government grant; £307,263,921 Council Tax Requirement; tax base 163,261.10 dwellings
findings.quote: In 2025/26, there continues to be minimal general government grant support to the revenue budget of Cheshire East Council (£0. 8m).

findings.paper_title: Council Tax Statutory Resolution
findings.headline: Council tax increases driven by Adult Social Care demand pressures, with a 2% dedicated ASC precept for the eighth consecutive year.
findings.detail: Cheshire East has used the special 2% Adult Social Care precept every year from 2017/18 through 2024/25 (years: 3%, 3%, 2%, 3%, 1%, 2%, 2%), and is proposing it again for 2025/26. The 4.99% total council tax increase for 2025/26 includes this 2% ASC component. The council explicitly cites 'increases in demand related to protecting vulnerable people and inflation in costs' as driving the need to continue raising council tax.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether ASC cost growth is structural (ongoing) or cyclical (temporary). Eight years of ASC precept use suggests structural funding gaps that could constrain the council's ability to invest in other services or maintain reserves, affecting creditworthiness.
findings.figures: 4.99% increase (including 2% ASC); 2% ASC precept used 2017/18–2024/25 (3%, 3%, 2%, 3%, 1%, 2%, 2%) and proposed 2025/26
findings.quote: The Provisional Fina nce Settlement in December 202 4 confirmed a further 2% ASC precept could be levied in 202 5/26 to help alleviate the continuing growth pressure.

findings.paper_title: Audit and Governance Committee Annual Report 23-24 - Final , item 86.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122567/Audit and Governance Committee Annual Report 23-24 - Final.pdf
