findings.matters: DSG deficits are overspends in a ring-fenced, mandatory grant that often signal cost pressures (typically SEND placements or transport costs) that either consume reserves or require council contributions, directly affecting council financial position.
findings.figures: DSG deficit (amount not quantified)
findings.quote: The Committee are engaged with the Children and Families committee to receive assurances over its plan to develop an effective SEND (Special Educational Needs and Disabilities) Policy and management of the DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit.

findings.paper_title: Audit and Governance Committee Annual Report 23-24 - Final , item 86.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122567/Audit and Governance Committee Annual Report 23-24 - Final.pdf
findings.headline: Internal audit of Section 106 agreements found 'no assurance' opinion with significant risk areas not effectively managed.
findings.detail: In September 2023, internal audit review of Section 106 agreement management concluded with a 'no assurance' opinion. The Committee escalated this to the Annual Governance Statement as a significant governance issue and requested regular updates on remedial actions, indicating concerns serious enough to involve multiple committees in oversight.
findings.matters: Lenders track audit weaknesses over material contractual obligations and reserved contributions; a 'no assurance' rating signals control failures in planning gain administration.
findings.figures: no assurance opinion
findings.quote: The report provided a 'no assurance' opinion and highlighted that there were significant areas of risk that were not being effectively managed.

findings.paper_title: Additional Information on MTFS , item 78.
findings.headline: Council is drawing down £17.6m of previously approved EFS to cover the 2024/25 shortfall, indicating recurring structural deficit
findings.detail: The council is using all previously approved EFS from 2023/24 and 2024/25 (£17.6m total) to cover the 2024/25 funding shortfall. This is the second consecutive year requiring exceptional support.
findings.matters: Exceptional support in two consecutive years indicates the financial pressures are structural and ongoing rather than temporary, suggesting deteriorating financial trajectory.
findings.quote: The MHCLG announcement also confirms, in principle, that the council can use all of the previously approved EFS for years 2023/24 and 2024/25 – a total value of £17.6m – to cover the forecast funding shortfall in the 2024/25 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Additional Information on MTFS , item 78.
findings.headline: EFS support brings additional costs to following years, worsening the medium-term outlook
findings.detail: Although supporting immediate pressures, the document notes that EFS 'is not in the form of cash, it does bring additional costs to following years, as set out in the council's draft medium-term financial strategy 2025 to 2029.' These additional costs are not quantified in this paper.
findings.matters: Unquantified future liabilities from EFS use indicate that budget pressures will worsen from 2026 onwards, requiring either further exceptional support or more radical savings.
findings.figures: None quantified in this extract
findings.quote: While this reduces the immediate pressures in the short -term, the support is not in the form of cash, it does bring additional costs to following years, as set out in the council's draft medium-term financial strategy 2025 to 2029.

findings.paper_title: Additional Information on MTFS , item 78.
findings.headline: EFS is explicitly described as a short-term solution; the council must find additional savings the underlying problem is not solved
findings.detail: The document states this is 'only a short-term solution' and the council must 'continue to find additional funding, income and efficiency savings to reduce the need to use this support over the coming financial year.' The savings required are not yet identified.
findings.matters: If the underlying budget problem persists and required savings are not delivered, the council will remain dependent on exceptional support, signalling structurally unsustainable finances.
findings.figures: None specified for required savings
findings.quote: This is only a short-term solution, and it will be important to continue to find additional funding, income and efficiency savings to reduce the need to use this support over the coming financial year.

findings.paper_title: Additional Information on MTFS , item 78.
findings.headline: Council requires £25.3m in exceptional financial support to balance the 2025/26 budget
findings.detail: The MHCLG has confirmed in principle Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) up to £25.3m to balance the budget shortfall for 2025/26. This represents a structural deficit that cannot be covered from the council's own resources.
findings.matters: A £25.3m shortfall requiring government support indicates significant financial stress and raises material concerns about the council's financial sustainability and creditworthiness.
findings.quote: The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) confirmed in principle Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) up to £25.3m, to balance the budget shortfall for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX B - Budget Engagement Report , item 78.
findings.headline: Accumulated DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) deficit of £120.1m for 2025/26 represents a latent liability to the general fund
findings.detail: Analysis included in resident budget suggestions identifies a Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit of £120.1m forecast for 2025/26. DSG deficits are statutory accumulated deficits that councils must eventually recover from their general fund unless central government grants relief. This compounds the pressure from SEND and other education spending.
findings.matters: A £120m DSG deficit represents a significant latent liability; unless the government extends the deficit relief scheme, the council will be forced to fund this from its general fund, further constraining resources.
findings.figures: £120.1m DSG deficit forecast for 2025/26
findings.quote: Address the growing Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit (£120.1m forecast for 2025/26).

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX B - Budget Engagement Report , item 78.
findings.headline: Capital borrowing is rising to £449.6m by 2028/29, with reserves of only £10m identified as insufficient for projected shortfalls
findings.detail: A detailed resident budget analysis notes current borrowing of £375.2m rising to £449.6m over the planning period, with current annual borrowing costs of £15.6m-£16.4m. The same analysis identifies current reserves of £10m as 'insufficient for projected shortfalls,' creating vulnerability to interest rate increases or unexpected costs without adequate buffer.
findings.matters: Rising debt with inadequate reserves increases financial vulnerability; the council would have limited capacity to absorb interest rate shocks, unexpected liabilities, or revenue shortfalls.
findings.figures: Borrowing £375.2m (2025/26) to £449.6m (2028/29); reserves £10m; borrowing costs £15.6m-£16.4m annually
findings.quote: Current Borrowing: £375.2m (2025/26) to £449.6m (2028/29)...Current Reserves: £10m, insufficient for projected shortfalls

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX B - Budget Engagement Report , item 78.
findings.headline: Council proposing 9.99% Council Tax increase while residents report they cannot afford it
findings.detail: The council is consulting on a 9.99% Council Tax increase. Throughout the feedback, residents express severe affordability concerns, with some stating they are 'at my wits end,' cannot pay their bills, and would face hardship if the increase proceeds. Multiple residents describe the increase as 'scandalous' given current financial pressure. There is risk of collection problems or political opposition if residents cannot afford the increase.
findings.matters: If residents cannot afford the planned tax increase, the council may face collection shortfalls or political pressure to abandon it, undermining the funding assumptions in the financial plan.
findings.figures: 9.99% Council Tax increase proposed; some residents note that pay rises do not match Council Tax increases year on year
findings.quote: How deep do you think our pockets are, I like many others are struggling with paying our bills as it is.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX B - Budget Engagement Report , item 78.
findings.headline: Adult social care demand is growing faster than the council can fund it, with providers describing the service as close to crisis
findings.detail: Multiple respondents describe adult social care as 'unsustainable,' 'unfit for purpose,' and 'close to crisis.' One notes the service is 'neglected for far too long' and 'impossible to access' unless presenting high complexity. Another states the council has 'no clear strategy' and is making 'irresponsible' commitments without understanding the scale of the problem. The council proposes investing more, but respondents argue this cannot continue indefinitely.
findings.matters: Growing demographic demand for an expensive statutory service that the council describes as already underfunded creates structural financial pressure that cannot be solved through local effort alone, without central government intervention or rationing.
findings.figures: No specific figures provided in service description; broader budget shows significant allocations to adult social care
findings.quote: The service is close to crisis. Adult services have been neglected for far too long. It's pretty impossible to access this for anyone who isn't highly complex and even then it's a battle.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX B - Budget Engagement Report , item 78.
findings.headline: Children's services received an inadequate CQC rating, signalling regulatory concern about service quality
findings.detail: A respondent references that children's services have received an inadequate CQC (quality regulator) rating. Multiple respondents describe the service as 'in chaos' and requiring 'total overhaul.' The council proposes recruiting additional staff to deliver an improvement plan, but respondents question whether staffing is the root problem.
findings.matters: An 'inadequate' regulatory rating in a high-cost statutory service (the largest budget item after SEND) signals quality and governance issues that create risk of further cost escalation or service failure.
findings.figures: CQC inadequate rating for children's services
findings.quote: Children's services received an inadequate CQC rating, not recruiting to an improvement plan is not an option if you want this to improve.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX B - Budget Engagement Report , item 78.
findings.headline: SEND costs are four to five times higher per capita than peer councils, far beyond peer benchmarks
findings.detail: A respondent comparing Cheshire East to peer authorities notes that SEND debt exceeds eight surrounding authorities combined (despite those authorities having ten times more children), and costs are five times higher per head than Surrey and four times higher than Kent. Individual out-of-county placements cost £12.5k per week. The council is described as having some of the most expensive but some of the worst children's services in the country.
findings.matters: SEND costs that are multiples of peer authorities suggest either demand management failures, cost control failures, or underlying service delivery problems that will persist until fundamentally addressed, consuming an unsustainable share of council resources.
findings.figures: 5x higher per head than Surrey County Council, 4x higher than Kent County Council, £12.5k per week for individual placements
findings.quote: Cheshire East already has some of the most expensive children's services in the country. Its SEND debt is bigger than its eight surrounding neighbouring authorities put together, despite the fact that those eight local authorities have ten times more children than Cheshire East. It is five times higher per head of children's population than Surrey County Council and four times higher than Kent County Council.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A - MTFS 2025-2029 FINAL , item 78.
findings.headline: The Council's Core Spending Power is 5.77% lower than statistical neighbours, despite appearing to be in a stronger position.
findings.detail: While Cheshire East has experienced strong taxbase growth and lower reliance on grant funding (which initially appears positive), paragraph 1.52 reveals the Council is actually 'relatively underfunded by comparison' to nearest neighbours. Additionally, Band D Council Tax is 1.94% lower than comparators, meaning the Council is collecting less per property than peers.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the Council has capacity to raise income through Council Tax or other means. Being below peer average funding while facing above-peer pressures suggests limited flexibility.
findings.figures: Core Spending Power 5.77% lower than statistical neighbours average; Council Tax Band D 1.94% lower than comparators
findings.quote: Cheshire East Core Spending Power compared to our statistical nearest neighbours is 5.77% lower than the average meaning we are relatively underfunded by comparison.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A - MTFS 2025-2029 FINAL , item 78.
findings.headline: The Council holds £10.8m of sundry debt over six months old, including £9.3m from Adult Social Care.
findings.detail: As at November 2024, total outstanding debt was £16.9m, of which £10.8m is over six months old. Adult Social Care debt alone accounts for £9.3m of this aged debt. The Council made a bad debt provision of £6.8m as at March 2024 and is conducting reviews to potentially reduce this, but the existence of significant aged social care debt indicates collection difficulties or inability of service users to pay.
findings.matters: Aged debt in social care typically reflects either service users unable to pay or the council's inability to collect. Large bad debt provisions are an implicit admission that forecast income may not be received.
findings.figures: Outstanding debt £16.9m (November 2024); aged debt (over 6 months) £10.8m; Adult Social Care debt £9.3m; bad debt provision £6.8m
findings.quote: The total amount of service debt over six months old as at November 2024 is £10.8m; split as £9.3m of Adult Social Care debt and £1.5m of Sundry Debt.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A - MTFS 2025-2029 FINAL , item 78.
findings.headline: Adult social care is generating budget overspends against forecast, driven by high demand.
findings.detail: Paragraph 1.54 identifies 'high demand on social care services resulting in budget overspends against forecast levels' as one of the key budget pressures. The Council has introduced weekly financial recovery reviews for Adults Services chaired by the Section 151 Officer to manage overspends. Any directorate off target by more than 5% faces detailed weekly review, indicating this is a material issue.
findings.matters: Adult social care demand is demographic and largely inelastic—councils cannot easily reduce this spending. Persistent overspends suggest the budget assumptions are unrealistic or demand management is failing.
findings.figures: Adults, Health and Integration budget: £138.0m (2024/25), £159.4m (2025/26); identified as subject to weekly financial recovery reviews
findings.quote: high demand on social care services resulting in budget overspends against forecast levels

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A - MTFS 2025-2029 FINAL , item 78.
findings.headline: Capital Financing costs have increased by £9.5m in one year due to rising interest rates and increasing borrowing.
findings.detail: Capital Financing jumped from £19m to £28.5m in 2024/25, an increase of £9.5m. Paragraph 1.56 notes 'Interest Rates have a particularly high impact due to the overall level of borrowing for the Council. This impact is exacerbated by the high and increasing level of short-term borrowing, which means that rate rises have an immediate impact on council finances.'
findings.matters: Rising interest costs reduce the amount available to spend on services. If rates continue to rise, this trend will accelerate. The reliance on short-term borrowing means the Council has no protection against further rate increases.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Budget increased from £19m to £28.5m (increase of £9.5m); £4.9m of this increase solely for DSG interest
findings.quote: the annual Capital Financing Budget had to increase for 2024/25 from £19m to £28.5m to support the increased interest rates and borrowing costs

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A - MTFS 2025-2029 FINAL , item 78.
findings.headline: A Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £78.6m is generating £4.9m in annual interest costs and is expected to worsen.
findings.detail: The DSG reserve moved into deficit in 2019/20 due to growth in pupils with Education Health and Care Plans. The deficit stood at £78.6m by 31 March 2024 and interest payments now consume £4.9m per annum. This was flagged as part of the reason the Capital Financing budget had to increase from £19m to £28.5m in 2024/25. The Council notes this is a national issue but specifically impacts Cheshire East.
findings.matters: A £78.6m DSG deficit is a structural problem that cannot be resolved by the Council alone—it requires government override. The £4.9m annual interest cost is a permanent drain on revenue that crowds out spending on other services.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £78.6m by 31 March 2024; interest payments £4.9m per annum; Capital Financing Budget increased to £28.5m (from £19m), with £4.9m of this solely attributable to DSG interest
findings.quote: DSG deficit of £78.6m by 31 March 2024– interest payments on the deficit balance currently c.£4.9m per annum

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A - MTFS 2025-2029 FINAL , item 78.
findings.headline: The Council used General Fund reserves to balance the 2024/25 budget for the first time and cannot repeat this approach.
findings.detail: Paragraph 1.6 states 'The 2024/25 budget was balanced by the use of General Fund reserves for the first time and this cannot happen in subsequent years.' This indicates the Council has exhausted the one-time use of reserves and must now find sustainable solutions through either significant savings or increased income, neither of which the MTFS demonstrates is achievable.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fill a budget gap is unsustainable and signals that the underlying budget cannot be balanced through normal operations. This is a red flag for creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Reserve drawdown in 2024/25 to balance budget; forecast replenishment in 2025/26 of £1.3m (Table 1)
findings.quote: The 2024/25 budget was balanced by the use of General Fund reserves for the first time and this cannot happen in subsequent years.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A - MTFS 2025-2029 FINAL , item 78.
findings.headline: General Fund reserves have fallen to crisis levels and are forecast to drop below minimum safe levels.
findings.detail: Reserves fell from £37.9m (2023/24) to a forecast £15.2m (2024/25 outturn). The General Fund reserve specifically is forecast to be only £3.7m against a minimum requirement of £20m. The Council notes these are 'historically low levels' that are 'barely adequate' for current risks and 'insufficient to cover future projected funding shortfalls'. This represents a loss of 60% of reserves in one year.
findings.matters: Reserves are the buffer a council holds to manage unexpected pressures or shortfalls. At £3.7m versus £20m required, the Council has minimal capacity to absorb any financial shock or savings slippage.
findings.figures: £37.9m (end 2023/24), £15.2m (forecast 2024/25), General Fund Reserve £3.7m actual vs £20m required minimum
findings.quote: The forecast closing balance position for 2024/25 is just £15.2m; of which, the General Fund Reserve is forecast to be only £3.7m instead of the £20m that should be the minimum level held

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A - MTFS 2025-2029 FINAL , item 78.
findings.headline: The Council cannot balance its budget beyond 2025/26 despite exceptional financial support.
findings.detail: The MTFS explicitly states that 'it has not been possible to present a fully balanced budget beyond 2025/26' due to unprecedented financial circumstances. Table 1 shows projected funding shortfalls of £21.6m in 2026/27, £13.0m in 2027/28, and £15.4m in 2028/29. The Council is requesting capitalisation directions of up to £31.4m for 2025/26 and £23.7m for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can meet its obligations in the medium term; unbalanced budgets beyond the current year indicate structural problems that cannot be addressed by one-year fixes.
findings.quote: Due to the unprecedented financial circumstances that the Council continues to be in it has not been possible to present a fully balanced budget beyond 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors - Audit of Accounts 2023-24
findings.headline: A disclaimed audit in 2023-24 will likely prevent a full unmodified opinion for multiple subsequent years due to loss of opening balance assurance
findings.detail: Once a disclaimed opinion is issued, the auditor will not have assurance over opening balances and comparatives from the prior year. This means the 2024-25 audit will face similar constraints. The council's audit opinion may not recover to an unmodified opinion for several years.
findings.matters: Multiple years of disclaimed or qualified audit opinions mean lenders cannot reliably assess the council's financial position or year-on-year trends, significantly increasing credit risk and limiting lenders' ability to monitor financial performance.
findings.figures: Impact extends across multiple years from 2024-25 onwards
findings.quote: It is likely therefore that a disclaimed audit in year 2023/24 may not recover for a number of years to an unmodified opinion.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors - Audit of Accounts 2023-24
findings.headline: The council will miss the 28 February 2025 statutory deadline for publishing audited accounts and must explain the failure to the Secretary of State
findings.detail: The council will not meet the 28 February 2025 backstop deadline for publishing audited accountability statements. The Interim S151 Officer is required to publish an explanation on the council's website and send it to the Secretary of State. The government will publish a list of bodies that missed backstop dates.
findings.matters: Missing a statutory reporting deadline indicates governance or capacity issues. Public identification as a body that failed to meet regulatory reporting deadlines raises concerns about the council's ability to meet other statutory obligations.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 28 February 2025
findings.quote: As the backstop date will not be met, the Interim Executive Director of Resources (S151) is required to publish an explanation and subject to finalisation of the audit work by EY, aim to publish audited accountability statements as soon as practicable.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors - Audit of Accounts 2023-24
findings.headline: An error in pension accounting (IAS19) dating back to March 2022 required restatement of accounts across three financial years
findings.detail: The Cheshire Pension Fund's actuary identified an error in the council's IAS19 report from March 2022 in November 2024. The council was required to restate the 2021-22 prior year comparatives and update the 2023-24 draft accounts. Although the council states there was no change to bottom-line figures, the multi-year restatements indicate control weaknesses in pension accounting.
findings.matters: An accounting error that took eight months to discover and affected multiple years of accounts indicates potential weaknesses in the council's internal financial controls and account preparation processes.
findings.figures: Error dating from March 2022; restatements affected 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24 accounts
findings.quote: In late November 2024, the Council were made aware via the Cheshire Pension Fund that the Actuary, Hymans Robertson, had identified an error which had occurred in the Council's IAS19 report for March 2022.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors - Audit of Accounts 2023-24
findings.headline: Four objections from a local elector to the 2023-24 accounts remain unresolved and are delaying the audit opinion
findings.detail: Ernst & Young accepted four objections from a local elector on the 2023/24 financial statements. Until these objections are fully considered by the auditor, the disclaimed opinion cannot be issued. The formal objections suggest that someone has raised concerns about amounts or disclosures within the accounts.
findings.matters: Elector objections indicate there may be errors or questionable items within the financial statements, raising concerns about account quality and whether proper governance controls were applied.
findings.figures: Four objections accepted
findings.quote: EY have accepted four objections from a local elector on the 2023/24 financial statements and until these objections have been considered, EY will not be in a position to issue the disclaimed opinion.

findings.paper_title: External Auditors - Audit of Accounts 2023-24
findings.headline: External auditor will issue a disclaimed opinion on 2023-24 accounts, unable to provide independent assurance on financial statements
findings.detail: Ernst & Young cannot obtain sufficient evidence to conclude the financial statements are free from material misstatement before the 28 February 2025 backstop date. A disclaimed opinion means substantive assurance cannot be provided on parts of the financial statements, leaving no independent verification of the council's financial position.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on independently audited accounts to verify council financial position and assess creditworthiness. A disclaimed opinion means lenders have no external assurance that the accounts are accurate.
findings.figures: Backstop date: 28 February 2025
findings.quote: EY advise that they are not in a position to obtain sufficient evidence to be able to conclude that the financial statements of the Council are free from material and pervasive misstatement before the backstop date for the 2023/24 accounts and therefore anticipate issuing a disclaimed 2023/24 audit opinion.

findings.paper_title: Audit and Governance Committee Supplementary Agenda

findings.headline: Audit timescales compressed to 4 months from standard 9 months; prior year audit incomplete during fieldwork period
findings.detail: EY's appointment came late. Normal audit planning and fieldwork takes 9 months but was compressed to 4 months (October 2024 to end of January 2025). During EY's fieldwork, the previous auditor Mazars was still completing the 2022/23 audit (not signed off until 12 December 2024). Only 2023/24 accounts remain outstanding.
findings.matters: Compressed audit timescales increase audit risk and may indicate challenges in finance function capacity; incomplete prior year audits delay resolution of historical issues and audit continuity problems.
findings.figures: normal audit duration 9 months; actual duration 4 months; prior year audit completion 12 December 2024
findings.quote: Ordinarily, audit planning work would commence in February/March of that year, however the 2023/24 planning and fieldwork, which would usually cover a nine-month period has been condensed to four months as a consequence of the late appointment and the introduction of statutory 'backstop date' deadlines.

findings.paper_title: Audit and Governance Committee Supplementary Agenda
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/b27752/Audit and Governance Committee Supplementary Agenda 24th-Feb-2025 10.00 Audit and Governance Commi.pdf?T=9
findings.headline: Pension fund accounting error in IAS19 valuations identified and corrected, indicating control weaknesses
findings.detail: In late November 2024, the Cheshire Pension Fund actuary identified a system error in the Council's IAS19 pension report for March 2022. The error was corrected and cascaded through revised valuations for 2023 and 2024. Whilst stated to have no impact on bottom line figures reported, the error's discovery indicates gaps in internal financial controls.
findings.matters: Pension accounting errors, even if ultimately immaterial, indicate internal control weaknesses that could mask more significant issues and undermine confidence in financial data integrity.
findings.figures: Error identified in March 2022 IAS19 report; revised reports prepared for 31 March 2022, 2023, and 2024; stated bottom line impact £0
findings.quote: In late November 2024, the Council were made aware via the Cheshire Pension Fund that the Actuary, Hymans Robertson, had identified an error which had occurred in the Council's IAS19 report for March 2022. The error had been identified as part of preparations by the Actuary ahead of the 2025 valuation.

findings.headline: Council identifies 'urgent' medium-term financial sustainability crisis requiring transformation; situation 'must be addressed now'
findings.detail: The council's narrative states that service pressures in Adults and Children's services 'will almost certainly affect the medium-term finances of the Council' and that 'This situation must be addressed now and as part of the MTFS process for 2025 to 2029'. The council is working with a transformation partner on medium-term sustainability.
findings.matters: The council's explicit acknowledgment of urgent structural imbalance requiring transformation signals multi-year financial recovery needed, indicating elevated risk profile for credit decisions over MTFS period.

findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/b27752/Audit and Governance Committee Supplementary Agenda 24th-Feb-2025 10.00 Audit and Governance Commi.pdf?T=9
findings.headline: Adult Social Care crisis with 'extraordinary' demand and 'unexpected and unfunded' costs with 'consequences for 2024/25'
findings.detail: Performance overview explicitly describes 2023/24 as 'extraordinarily difficult year for adult social care' driven by increased complexity of need among younger adults, ongoing inflation pressures on care providers, and NHS hospital discharge pressures. Council states this produced 'unexpected and unfunded level of expenditure, which will have consequences for 2024/25'.
findings.matters: Unfunded demand pressures in social care (61% of net budget) indicate structural budget gap that cannot be resolved through one-year actions, signaling multi-year financial distress ahead.
findings.figures: Adult and Children's Social Care represents 61% of total expenditure; £11.8m overspend in Adults in 2023/24
findings.quote: 2023/24 has been an extraordinarily difficult year for adult social care, locally and nationally, as it has sought to respond to increased complexity of need, particularly amongst younger adults, increased costs arising from ongoing inflation pressures affecting care providers and the need to support the NHS with hospital discharge pressures. These issues have driven an unexpected and unfunded level of expenditure, which will have consequences for 2024/25.

findings.paper_title: Audit and Governance Committee Supplementary Agenda
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/b27752/Audit and Governance Committee Supplementary Agenda 24th-Feb-2025 10.00 Audit and Governance Commi.pdf?T=9
findings.headline: General reserves collapsed 60% from £14.1m to £5.6m; council explicitly states reserve depletion is 'not sustainable in the medium term'
findings.detail: General fund reserves fell from £14.1m to £5.6m. Total revenue reserves decreased from £83.1m to £45.2m. The council's own narrative explicitly states that when setting the 2024/25 budget, it 'was highlighted that the use of reserves was not sustainable in the medium term' and that 'Net spending therefore needs to be contained within the estimates of expenditure that form the budget'.
findings.matters: Reserves at £5.6m provide minimal buffer against shocks for a £768m spending council; lenders view reserve depletion as a leading indicator of financial distress and loss of financial flexibility.
findings.figures: General reserves £14.1m to £5.6m (60% reduction); total reserves £83.1m to £45.2m
findings.quote: When the 2024/25 budget was set, in February 2024, it was highlighted that the use of reserves was not sustainable in the medium term. Net spending therefore needs to be contained within the estimates of expenditure that form the budget.

findings.headline: 2023/24 revenue overspend of £8.5m with social care responsible for £20m of unfunded cost pressures
findings.detail: Final outturn shows £8.5m overspend after reserve allocations. Adults Social Care overspent by £11.8m against revised budget of £138.0m; Children and Families overspent by £8.2m against revised budget of £81.9m. These two services alone generated £20m of overspend partially offset by underspends elsewhere.

findings.headline: Ernst & Young will issue a disclaimed audit opinion, unable to obtain sufficient evidence financial statements are free from material misstatement

The disclaimed opinion results from compressed audit timescales (4 months instead of normal 9), late auditor appointment, and ongoing consideration of four audit objections from a local elector.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion is a fundamental loss of financial credibility; lenders typically treat this as material adverse information, and it cascades to future years' audits losing opening balance assurance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122929/Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee.pdf
findings.headline: Bank reconciliation was not performed on a monthly basis and the year-end reconciliation was not completed until October 2024—seven months after the balance sheet date.
findings.detail: Bank reconciliation is a fundamental financial control. The council did not maintain monthly reconciliations during 2023/24 due to changes in the finance team and capacity issues. The year-end bank reconciliation for 31 March 2024 was not completed until October 2024, meaning the council could not promptly detect or investigate unexplained differences between the bank statement and the accounting records. This delay and breakdown in a basic control increases the risk of undetected errors or irregularities in the cash position.
findings.matters: Delayed bank reconciliation is a significant control weakness and red flag for audit risk. It suggests the finance function lacks capacity and discipline. Cash is the most liquid asset and the most vulnerable to misuse; failure to reconcile it promptly and regularly is a material control deficiency that undermines confidence in financial reporting.
findings.figures: Year-end bank reconciliation completed: October 2024 (7 months after year-end balance sheet date of 31 March 2024).
findings.quote: As a result of changes in the finance team and capacity issues during the year the bank reconciliation was not undertaken on a monthly basis. We noted that the year end 31 March 2024 bank reconciliation was not completed until October 2024.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122929/Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee.pdf
findings.headline: Internal audit gave a limited assurance opinion on the council's control framework and only 48% of management recommendations are being implemented on time.
findings.detail: During 2023/24, internal audit issued 23 assurance reports: 13 at 'Limited Assurance' and 1 at 'No Assurance'. Weak areas include Purchase Cards, Use of Agency Workers, Debt Management (both sundry and adult social care), and Section 106 compliance. The Head of Internal Audit concluded the overall opinion on the council's framework of risk management, governance and internal control was 'Limited'. Critically, only 48% of agreed recommendations were implemented within the agreed timescale, indicating management is not addressing known control gaps rapidly.
findings.matters: Limited assurance from internal audit means the council's own control environment is weak and controls cannot be relied upon to prevent or detect fraud, error, or misstatement. Combined with the disclaimed external audit opinion, this creates a picture of an uncontrolled financial environment where large misstatements could exist undetected. Lenders cannot have confidence in the accuracy of reported financial position or the reliability of management's financial disclosures.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance opinions: 13 out of 23. No Assurance: 1. Recommendations implemented on time: 48%.
findings.quote: During 2023/24, Internal Audit produced 23 assurance reports with 13 "Limited Assurance" opinions and 1 "No Assurance" opinion. Internal Audit also reported that during 2023/24 only 48% of agreed recommendations were implemented with the agreed timescale.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122929/Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee.pdf
findings.headline: Children's social care services rated inadequate by OFSTED and a Secretary of State improvement notice has been issued.
findings.detail: In May 2024, OFSTED inspected Cheshire East's children's services and rated them overall as inadequate, citing systemic failures in senior leadership oversight, consistency of practice, quality of supervision, sufficiency of placements, and effectiveness of child protection arrangements. On 24 July 2024, the Secretary of State issued a formal improvement notice requiring the council to establish an improvement plan with an appointed Improvement Adviser. The council must show sustainable improvement across multiple service areas or face potential central government intervention.
findings.matters: Children's services inadequacy is a governance failure affecting both service quality and financial risk. The council faces reputational damage, potential intervention costs, and regulatory risk. If the service does not improve, the council could face government takeover or forced restructuring, both of which destabilize the organisation and distract from financial recovery. This also signals weak internal governance and risk management to external stakeholders.
findings.figures: OFSTED inspection: May 2024. Secretary of State improvement notice: 24 July 2024.
findings.quote: The May 2024 OFSTED report on the Council's children's services rated the service overall as inadequate and outlined that the Council needs to improve

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122929/Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee.pdf
findings.headline: General fund balances have depleted by £37.9m in one year and are approaching dangerously low levels.
findings.detail: General fund reserves fell from £81.1m at 31 March 2023 to £43.2m at 31 March 2024—a drop of 46.7% in a single financial year. At this rate of depletion, reserves will be exhausted within two years. The 2024/25 budget assumes £22m of reserve use and delivery of £30m of savings, neither of which appears certain given the £18.3m forecast outturn breach and internal audit findings that only 48% of management's agreed recommendations are implemented on time.
findings.matters: Local authority reserves are the buffer that allows a council to absorb service overspends, unexpected costs, or revenue shortfalls. Depletion at this rate is unsustainable and forces increasingly difficult choices (service cuts, price increases, reduced investment). Lenders see reserve erosion as a leading indicator of solvency stress.
findings.figures: Reserve depletion: £37.9m (46.7% reduction) in one year. Remaining: £43.2m. 2024/25 planned use: £22m. If trend continues, reserves exhausted by 2026/27.
findings.quote: the Council exceeded budget by £6m in 2022/23 and £8.5m in 2023/24 with general fund balances reducing from £81.1m at the 31 March 2023 to £43.2m at the 31 March 2024

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122929/Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee.pdf
findings.headline: The council is at risk of issuing a Section 114 notice and its Medium Term Financial Strategy is not sustainable without central government support.
findings.detail: The council has overshooted its budget by £6m in 2022/23 and £8.5m in 2023/24. General fund balances have collapsed from £81.1m to £43.2m in a single year. For 2024/25, despite planning to use £22m of reserves and deliver £30m of savings, the forecast revenue outturn shows an adverse variance of £20.1m as at November 2024, with the Section 151 officer reporting a forecasted overspend of £18.3m in February 2025. Earmarked reserves of £32.3m are nearly depleted, with over 70% (more than £22m) already committed to supporting the revenue budget for 2024/25. General fund reserves stand at only £5.6m.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is issued when a local authority cannot balance its budget and must effectively freeze all non-essential spending. It is a sign of financial crisis and makes the council unable to meet its obligations. Lenders view S114 risk as existential and would likely recall facilities or demand covenant strengthening.
findings.figures: Budget overruns: £6m (2022/23), £8.5m (2023/24). General fund: £81.1m (31 Mar 2023) → £43.2m (31 Mar 2024). 2024/25 forecast overspend: £18.3m. Earmarked reserves: £32.3m. General fund reserves: £5.6m. Reserves committed to revenue: £22m+ (70.5% of earmarked total).
findings.quote: The Council's Medium Term Financial Strategy 2024-28 is not sustainable without central Government support and the Council is at risk of issuing a S114 notice in the future.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122929/Appendix B - EY Interim Completion Report to Audit and Governance Committee.pdf
findings.headline: Auditor will issue a disclaimed audit opinion and cannot assure the 2023/24 financial statements.
findings.detail: EY cannot complete planned audit procedures or obtain sufficient evidence to conclude the financial statements are free from material misstatement before the 28 February 2025 backstop date. Late audit appointment (October 2024), the unfinished prior-year 2022/23 audit, and delays in supporting information from the finance team have made the deadline impossible to meet. Four elector objections to the accounts are also still pending consideration, which must be resolved before the opinion can be issued.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditor provides no assurance that the council's accounts are accurate. Lenders cannot assess the council's true financial position without an unqualified audit, making this a critical red flag for creditworthiness and covenant compliance.
findings.figures: Backstop deadline: 28 February 2025. Audit start: October 2024.
findings.quote: we were not in a position to complete our planned procedures and obtain sufficient evidence to enable us to conclude our financial statements audit of the Council before the 28 February 2025 backstop date and as a result we anticipated issuing a disclaimed audit opinion

findings.headline: 2024/25 budget relies on unprecedented use of reserves to balance
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that using reserves to balance the 2024/25 budget 'was an unprecedented step'. When setting that budget in February 2024, the council highlighted that 'the use of reserves was not sustainable in the medium term' and that spending 'needs to be contained within the estimates of expenditure that form the budget'—yet did the opposite, indicating inability to align spending to available resources.
findings.matters: When reserves must fund recurring spending gaps, the council is technically operating at structural deficit; this is unsustainable and typically leads to service cuts or borrowing

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Statement of Accounts 2023-24 v4 - AGC240225 , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122928/Appendix A Statement of Accounts 2023-24 v4 - AGC240225.pdf
findings.headline: DSG deficit forecast to reach £150m over three years with no funding solution
findings.detail: The council states 'The levels of expenditure on pupils with special educational needs and disabilities are unaffordable within the current funding levels provided to the Council'. The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is 'still forecast to increase over the next three years to as much as £150m'. Currently managed through a Department accounting override due to expire 31 March 2026, with council noting 'the underlying financial risk has not changed'.
findings.matters: A £150m unfunded liability for SEN represents a structural imbalance with no identified solution; the accounting override is temporary and masks a real liability
findings.figures: DSG deficit forecast to increase to £150m over next three years; override expires 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The levels of expenditure on pupils with special educational needs and disabilities are unaffordable within the current funding levels provided to the Council, a result of higher demand and complexity...the deficit is still forecast to increase over the next three years to as much as £150m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Statement of Accounts 2023-24 v4 - AGC240225 , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122928/Appendix A Statement of Accounts 2023-24 v4 - AGC240225.pdf
findings.headline: £42m shortfall published for 2025/26; transformation partner appointed
findings.detail: The Medium Term Financial Strategy published a shortfall of £42m for 2025/26. The council states this 'means that the Council must undertake a transformation process during 2024/25 to live within reduced budget levels and focus on priority areas.' A transformation partner has been appointed but 'aims to generate proposals for consultation purposes later in 2024', meaning the savings plan is not yet defined.
findings.matters: A £42m savings programme (12% of net budget) across four years is material; transformation is urgent but not yet scoped, creating delivery risk
findings.figures: £42m shortfall for 2025/26; net budget £356.2m
findings.quote: The Medium Term Financial Strategy is clear that the financial challenge remains with a published shortfall of £42m for 2025/26. This means that the Council must undertake a transformation process during 2024/25 to live within reduced budget levels and focus on priority areas.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Statement of Accounts 2023-24 v4 - AGC240225 , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122928/Appendix A Statement of Accounts 2023-24 v4 - AGC240225.pdf
findings.headline: General reserves depleted to £5.6m, declared unsustainably low
findings.detail: General reserves fell from £14.1m to £5.6m during 2023/24. The council explicitly states that combined with using reserves for 2023/24 overspend, this 'is forecast to leave general reserves at an unsustainably low level without urgent action'. Finance analysis notes current general reserves are 'significantly lower than our nearest neighbours' according to CIPFA resilience data.
findings.matters: Reserves below 2% of budget indicate the council cannot absorb service shocks; inability to manage within annual budget without drawing reserves signals structural deficit
findings.figures: General reserves £14.1m to £5.6m (61% reduction); total group reserves £83.1m to £45.2m
findings.quote: combined with the use of reserves to manage the 2023/24 overspend , is forecast to leave general reserves at an unsustainably low level  without urgent action.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Statement of Accounts 2023-24 v4 - AGC240225 , item 59.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122928/Appendix A Statement of Accounts 2023-24 v4 - AGC240225.pdf
findings.headline: Adult and Children's Social Care overspend £20m against combined budget of £220m
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspent by £11.8m and Children's Services by £8.2m against revised budgets of £138m and £81.9m respectively. The council describes 2023/24 as 'an extraordinarily difficult year' driven by 'unexpected and unfunded level of expenditure' from complexity of need, inflation pressures on care providers, and hospital discharge support. These pressures 'will almost certainly affect the medium-term finances of the Council'.
findings.matters: Social care is 61% of council net budget; uncontrolled overspends in this area threaten overall financial stability and indicate forecasting difficulties
findings.figures: Adults overspend £11.8m, Children's Services overspend £8.2m, combined overspend £20m against £219.9m revised budget
findings.quote: In terms of comparisons to these budgets it represents an overspend of £20m , mitigated by underspends across the rest of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication , item 61.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122755/Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication.pdf
findings.headline: 57 audit actions remain outstanding past their agreed implementation dates as of 31 January 2025
findings.detail: While the council has improved action implementation (75% of due actions completed vs 49% a year earlier), 57 recommendations remain overdue. The paper notes this 'remains high' and requires 'additional focus' to ensure agreed dates are achievable and timely.
findings.matters: Delayed implementation of audit recommendations means identified control weaknesses persist for extended periods; the pattern of overdue actions suggests either weak action planning or inadequate accountability for remediation.
findings.figures: 57 actions in progress past agreed date (31/01/2025); 75% completion rate vs 49% a year prior; 199 of 279 total actions completed.
findings.quote: It is noted, however, that the number if actions having exceeded the agreed implementation date remains high and this is an area that requires additional focus to ensure that all agreed implementation dates are achievable as well as timely.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication , item 61.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122755/Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication.pdf
findings.headline: Grant audit found improvements needed in monitoring contractor expenditure on a £344k substance misuse treatment project
findings.detail: The audit of the Supplementary Substance Misuse Treatment and Recovery Grant (Limited Assurance) concluded that the council's monitoring arrangements for contractor spending require improvement to ensure expenditure complies with grant conditions.
findings.matters: Weak monitoring of grant-funded spending creates risk that funds are not used in accordance with grant conditions, potentially triggering fund recovery or jeopardising future grant allocations.
findings.figures: Family Focus DWP grant value £344,000.00 (shown in Table 5). Specific substance misuse treatment grant value not disclosed.
findings.quote: The review concluded that improvements need to be made over the monitoring arrangements on expenditure incurred by the contractor in delivering this project.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication , item 61.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122755/Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication.pdf
findings.headline: Schools audit found errors in the procurement module leading to duplicate payments and inconsistent application of purchase card policy
findings.detail: The consolidated schools audit identified errors in the Unit4 procurement module causing duplicate payments, errors in HR forms, and inconsistent application of purchase card policies across schools. All actions were agreed with management but implementation status is not detailed.
findings.matters: Duplicate payments indicate failing controls over spending approval and processing; inconsistent purchase card policy application suggests inadequate oversight of discretionary school spending, both material control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Limited to one consolidated report covering the full school audit programme. Specific payment values not disclosed.
findings.quote: The report identified common issues in relation to: • Errors in completing Unit4 HR forms. • Errors in the use of the procurement module on Unit 4 leading to duplicate payments, and • Inconsistent application of the purchase card policy.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication , item 61.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122755/Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication.pdf
findings.headline: A 'No Assurance' report was issued on the council's arrangements for Section 106 developer contribution funds
findings.detail: During 2023/24, Internal Audit issued a No Assurance opinion on the control arrangements governing Section 106 funds—the highest level of audit concern. No details of remediation are provided in this paper.
findings.matters: Section 106 funds are developer contributions held in trust for specific infrastructure purposes. A No Assurance opinion on their arrangement indicates the council cannot demonstrate adequate controls over receipt, holding, or spending of these funds.
findings.figures: One No Assurance report issued; quantum of Section 106 funds not disclosed in this paper.
findings.quote: A significant 'No Assurance' report was also provided during the year in relation to the arrangements of Section 106 funds.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication , item 61.
findings.paper_url: https://moderngov.cheshireeast.gov.uk/ecminutes/documents/s122755/Appendix 1 - Internal Audit Plan Update Q1_Q3 202425 Final for Publication.pdf
findings.headline: The council's audit opinion on governance, risk and control was 'limited' in 2023/24, the first limitation since 2009
findings.detail: The Head of Audit gave a 'limited' opinion on the council's governance framework for 2023/24, reflecting a significant number of findings related to failures to apply existing controls and absence of expected or actual controls. This represents a material deterioration from prior years.
findings.matters: A limited audit opinion signals fundamental weaknesses in internal control and governance that expose the council to financial irregularity, fraud, and mismanagement of public funds—key risks any lender would need to assess.
findings.figures: 2023/24 opinion: limited. First occurrence since 2009.
findings.quote: The Head of Audit and Risk Management's opinion as the Chief Audit Executive on the Council's framework for governance, risk management and internal control for 2023/24 was given as 'limited'. This is the first time since 2009 that there has been a limitation on this opinion.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2023-24 (Verbal Update)
findings.headline: Eight significant governance issues identified in 2023-24
findings.detail: The council has identified three new significant governance issues beyond those in prior years, plus five previously identified governance issues continuing as areas of concern, plus one prior issue restated to reflect latest challenges. Details are in the full AGS but not this covering report.
findings.matters: Multiple unresolved governance issues can indicate control weaknesses; lenders need to understand what these are and management's remediation plan.
findings.figures: 3 new significant governance issues + 5 continuing + 1 restated
findings.quote: The Council's assessment of its governance arrangements for 2023/24 as presented to the July and December 2024 meetings had already identified three additional significant governance issue to those included in previous years.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2023-24 (Verbal Update)
findings.headline: Statutory publication deadline will be missed by at least four days
findings.detail: The Accounts and Audit (Amendment) Regulations 2024 require accountability statements to be published by 28 February 2025. The council has confirmed this deadline will not be met and will publish an explanation instead.
findings.matters: Missed statutory deadlines indicate process constraints or resource issues; lenders depend on timely, audited financial reporting and timely compliance signals operational discipline.
findings.figures: Deadline: 28 February 2025
findings.quote: As the accountability statements will not be published by the backstop date, the Council will publish an explanation and subject to finalisation of the audit work by EY, aim to publish audited accountability statements as soon as practicable.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2023-24 (Verbal Update)
findings.headline: External audit delayed by objection to the 2023/24 accounts
findings.detail: The Committee cannot approve the final Annual Governance Statement until external auditors EY complete their work on an objection to the 2023/24 accounts. Final approval and publication timescale is now uncertain pending resolution of this audit matter.
findings.matters: Audit objections delay sign-off of accounts and raise questions about what triggered the objection—a material risk signal for lenders assessing financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the covering report
findings.quote: The Committee will be asked to approve a proposed final version of the AGS once the External Auditors are in a position to provide their audit opinion, following completion of their work on the objection to the 2023/24 accounts.

findings.paper_title: Commissioners proposed precept 2025-26 , item 50.
findings.headline: Pay award sensitivity: 0.5% movement in pay award creates £1.1m budget impact
findings.detail: The budget is exposed to pay award volatility. The paper states 'a 0.5% movement in the pay award would have a potential £1.1m impact on the budget'. Pay awards are negotiated nationally and mandatory across forces. The 2025/26 budget assumes a 2.8% pay award from September 2025.
findings.matters: National pay negotiations are outside the force's control. A 1% overshoot versus budget assumption would create a £2.2m pressure with limited headroom to absorb it without drawing reserves or cutting services.
findings.figures: 0.5% pay movement = £1.1m impact; estimated pay award 2.8% for September 2025
findings.quote: There are key assumptions included within this proposed budget that could significantly affect the proposed budget such as pay awards where a 0.5% movement in the pay award would have a potential £1.1m impact on the budget.

findings.paper_title: Commissioners proposed precept 2025-26 , item 50.
findings.headline: Litigation costs rising significantly but not quantified beyond 2025/26 budget headroom
findings.detail: The budget includes £484k for litigation and collision damage, described as having 'seen a significant increase over the last few years'. The paper acknowledges 'increasing litigation activity within policing across all forces' but does not project these costs in the medium-term financial strategy or model their trajectory.
findings.matters: Rising litigation costs are a risk that could emerge as a pressure mid-year. If litigation activity continues its upward trend, the reserve buffer may not be sufficient to absorb cost overruns without service impact.
findings.figures: £484k for litigation and collision damage in 2025/26 budget
findings.quote: Finally, this budget recognises the increasing litigation activity within policing across all forces both in terms of operational activity and collisions. The cost of such litigation includes court costs, defence, and where appropriate payments to claimants, all of which have seen a significant increase over the last few years.

findings.paper_title: Commissioners proposed precept 2025-26 , item 50.
findings.headline: Reserves declining 48% over five years: £23.3m forecast to fall to £12.1m by 2030
findings.detail: Reserves held at 31 March 2024 were £23.3m. They are forecast to decrease to £15.1m by end of March 2025, then continue falling to £12.1m by March 2030. Best practice for general reserves is 3% of net budget (approximately £8.2m). The declining reserve position leaves less flexibility to absorb unforeseen costs or variances.
findings.matters: Declining reserves indicate the force is consuming accumulated buffers to manage current spending. If reserves fall too far, the organisation loses flexibility to handle inflation spikes, pay award surprises, or operational pressures.
findings.figures: £23.3m (2023/24 actual); £15.1m (forecast March 2025); £12.1m (forecast March 2030); General reserve 3% target = ~£8.2m
findings.quote: Reserves are held to provide flexibility in-year for such incidences and the Reserves Strategy included within this report covers this in more detail.

findings.paper_title: Commissioners proposed precept 2025-26 , item 50.
findings.headline: Major capital investment requiring £4.2m borrowing, with £5.9m Estates Strategy spend in year one
findings.detail: The capital programme totals £13.4m for 2025/26. Government capital grants have ended, forcing reliance on capital receipts (£4.32m), revenue contributions (£4.17m), and borrowing (£4.24m). A major Estates Strategy scheme for Crewe and Northern stations is budgeted at £5.9m in 2025/26 alone. Borrowing incurs ongoing revenue costs for interest and repayment, increasing reliance on revenue contributions.
findings.matters: Borrowing increases future revenue commitments and reduces financial flexibility. The loss of government capital grant support forces higher debt financing just as the council faces cost pressures.
findings.figures: £13.365m total capital; £4.237m borrowing; £5.9m Estates Strategy; capital receipts £4.32m; revenue contribution to capital £4.173m
findings.quote: As direct capital funding is no longer provided, and as part of the Reserve Strategy, funding is set aside each year to support the annual replacement cycles of items such as laptops, phones, and vehicles. However, this is not always sufficient, and borrowing is used to fund any shortfall.

findings.paper_title: Commissioners proposed precept 2025-26 , item 50.
findings.headline: Budget gap being met by precept increase: £20m cost inflation against £6.3m savings identified
findings.detail: Pay and price inflation added almost £20m to costs in 2025/26. A comprehensive Priority Based Budgeting exercise identified £6.3m of savings to address a budget gap. The £14 Band D precept increase (£6.4m) is assumed within the funding increase; without it, this amount would be 'lost to the base budget going forward', creating a structural shortfall.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know if a council can sustain its services if precept assumptions slip. This precept is at the maximum threshold before referendum is required.
findings.figures: £20m inflation pressures; £6.3m savings identified; £6.4m from £14 precept increase; 5.3% precept increase
findings.quote: If I do not increase the precept by £14 per annum at Band D, this would result in a significant loss of funding to Cheshire in 2025/26 and this amount would be lost to the base budget going forward.

news_drafts.headline: Adult Social Care debt grown £2.350m to £20.823m and now represents 87% of all council sundry debt
news_drafts.lead: Growing ASC debt and particularly the over-6-month segment suggests service users are unable to pay charges or the council is experiencing collection difficulties, indicating financial pressure in adult social care.

news_drafts.headline: Non-Domestic Rates collection down 2.36 percentage points; Collection Fund in £1.157m deficit
news_drafts.lead: Declining collection rates could indicate weakness in the local business base or economic stress; the deficit requires use of reserves and reduces future liquidity.

news_drafts.headline: Net financing costs forecast £2.897m above budget for the full year
news_drafts.lead: A persistent cost overrun signals that the council's budget assumptions are not holding; a lender would view this as evidence of financial pressure and reduced budget resilience.
